papers.abstract: Host-parasite interactions exist along a continuum from parasitism to mutualism, yet the environmental drivers governing transitions along this spectrum remain underexplored. Here we show that chronic thermal stress systematically attenuates virulence across multiple natural RNA viruses in Drosophila melanogaster and shifts persistent Nora virus infection into conditional mutualism, enhancing host lifespan, reproductive output, and behavioral performance without compromising viral persistence. Driven by host immunometabolic reprogramming and aging deceleration rather than viral genomic adaptation, this phenotypic switch demonstrates that thermal stress can invert the sign of biotic interactions. Our findings establish that persistent infections can expand host thermal reaction norms in animals, revealing how climate warming can fundamentally alter selection pressures and host-pathogen coevolutionary trajectories.
papers.title: Parasitism to mutualism shift during a viral infection in Drosophila under thermal stress

papers.abstract: Understanding whether environmental conditions bias the statistical weight of specific genomic configurations requires a framework connecting molecular interactions, thermal fluctuations, and sequence-level observables. Here, we model DNA as an open quantum system coupled to an environmental thermal bath (represented as an external bosonic field) and parameterize the underlying molecular interaction energies (effective Hamiltonian terms) directly from prescribed nucleotide sequences. To evaluate sequence distributions at thermodynamic equilibrium, we compare two finite-temperature strategies at fixed inverse temperature ($\beta=1$): classical Bayesian optimization targeting the exact thermodynamic equilibrium distribution (the Gibbs state), and quantum simulation using a Variational Quantum Thermalizer (VQT) implemented via a nine-layer parameterized quantum circuit. Both methods optimize the same interaction energy model and target-sequence objective across short oligomers ($N=2$--$5$ base pairs), using 200 outer evaluations. Benchmarking against a uniform sequence distribution, exact-Gibbs optimization enhances target-sequence probabilities by factors of $9.11$, $25.64$, $54.51$, and $159.87$. The VQT approach similarly yields substantial target enrichment across all sequence lengths, achieving enhancement factors between $9.85$ and $62.77$. By evaluating the VQT-selected Hamiltonians against exact Gibbs calculations, we decouple optimization errors in parameter learning from approximation errors inherent to the variational quantum circuit. While concordance with the exact-Gibbs optimum is high in shorter oligomers, larger systems exhibit heightened sensitivity to variational thermal approximations. These results demonstrate that environment-induced sequence biases can be systematically captured within a variational quantum simulation framework, bridging biophysical models of DNA thermodynamics with quantum algorithms for finite-temperature state preparation. Crucially, the resulting equilibrium probabilities represent intrinsic thermodynamic biases rather than realized evolutionary substitution rates, which remain governed by kinetic activation barriers, replication fidelity, and enzymatic DNA repair.
papers.title: Variational quantum thermalization of environment-coupled DNA sequence biases

papers.abstract: Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping studies in model organisms have long been used to infer the structure of genotype-phenotype maps. However, prior work has largely focused on analyzing the genetic architecture of complex traits individually. Here, we sought to instead infer genotype-phenotype maps for a large set of related phenotypes simultaneously. To do so, we used bulk assays to measure the competitive fitness of each of 100,000 individuals from a large budding yeast QTL mapping panel across a set of 101 phenotypes related by a ``hub-and-perturbation'' pattern, and then used a forward search approach to jointly infer the genetic basis of all phenotypes together. Our results reveal complex patterns of pleiotropy in the genetic architecture of these traits. We find that these patterns of pleiotropy reflect the structure of the environmental relationships as well as functional information about individual variants and the interactions between them. This suggests that high-throughput QTL mapping across structured environments can help uncover biologically meaningful genetic interactions, along with their variation across related environmental contexts.
papers.title: Joint QTL mapping reveals patterns of pleiotropy across structured environments in budding yeast

papers.abstract: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) coordinates viral and cellular proteins during infection. While proteins associated with HSV-1 genomes have been identified, changes in proteins associated with the host genome during infection remain poorly understood. We adapted accelerated native isolation of proteins on nascent DNA (aniPOND) to label and purify cellular and viral DNA then identify associated proteins by mass spectrometry. Using this approach, we confirm observations that cellular transcription, DNA replication, and repair proteins are enriched on viral genomes after the onset of viral DNA replication. We assessed how protein interactions with cellular DNA change during infection relative to protein abundance. Targets of the viral E3 ubiquitin ligase, ICP0, are depleted from the nucleus and cellular genome during infection. Transcription regulatory factors, Pol II, and the proteasome are depleted from the host genome, while association with DNA damage response and nuclear pore proteins increases. We also provide evidence for HSV-1 disruption of ribosome biogenesis. Results demonstrate reorganization of the nucleus during infection and validate this technique to identify changes to host genome-associated factors during infection.
papers.title: Distinct labeling of host and viral genomes highlights redistribution of nuclear proteins during HSV-1 infection

papers.abstract: Dopaminergic replacement therapy via L-DOPA is the major medical therapy for Parkinsons Disease. Long-term L-DOPA administration is known to cause dyskinetic movements, L-DOPA Induced Dyskinesia (LID). It remains unclear if the LID related, maladaptive changes in brain structure/function are localized to neural circuits within the nigrostriatal DA system or have brainwide impact. We employed multi-shell diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and correlational tractography to investigate structural brain networks associated with daily administration of L-DOPA and the development of LID in the unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine rat model. 53% of rats receiving L-DOPA therapy developed severe LID. Tractography found brainwide statistical maps positively and negatively associated with LID severity highlighted by bilateral neural circuits contained in the lesioned nigrostriatal system as well as others including the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex. These results suggest that systemic dysfuntion in brainwide neural circuits forms the mechanistic basis the maladaptive changes underlying LID.
papers.title: Levodopa induced dyskinesia severity is linked to distinct microstructural alterations in nigrostriatal and brainwide neural circuits

papers.abstract: Intellectual disability is a hallmark of Down syndrome (DS), caused by the triplication of human chromosome 21. Abnormal neuronal connectivity and impaired myelination are consistently observed in DS, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we used DS-derived isogenic induced pluripotent stem cell-derived forebrain assembloids (FAs) to investigate oligodendrocyte lineage cell (OLLC) development and neuron-glia interactions. Trisomic FAs exhibited an expansion of BCAS1+ pre-myelinating OLLCs, without a corresponding increase in myelin basic protein (MBP) expression. Transcriptomic analyses identified a euploid-enriched, trophic and maturation-supportive state (OLLC_2-TMS) and a trisomy-enriched synaptic interactions and differentiation state (OLLC_3-SID), lacking coordinated enrichment in myelination-promoting programs. Corresponding transcriptional signatures were identified in OLLCs from early postnatal human cortex. Increased excitatory neuronal contacts with pre-myelinating OLLCs accompanied ultrastructural myelin abnormalities in trisomic assembloids. Our findings suggest that trisomy redirects OLLC development toward a pre-myelinating state, uncoupling oligodendrocyte differentiation from productive myelination.
papers.title: Trisomy 21 Perturbs Oligodendrocyte Developmental States and Oligo-Neuron Communication in Human Forebrain Assembloids

papers.abstract: Perception and decision-making rely on distributed cortical circuits that transform sensory inputs into choices and actions. Such cortical processing varies with behavioral state, such that the same inputs can be handled differently across states. However, how behavioral state shapes sensory processing across distributed brain regions remains unclear. To address this question, we trained mice to perform a two-alternative choice task that required discrimination between paired auditory and whisker cues. During task training, we simultaneously recorded neuronal population activity from the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), using two-photon imaging of neurons expressing the fluorescent calcium indicator GCaMP6f. Using a Hidden Markov Model with Generalized Linear Models (GLM-HMM), we identified three latent behavioral states, including one optimal-performing stimulus-guided state and two sub-optimal biased states. We found that the optimal state was associated with stronger sensory representation in S1 and PPC, as well as stronger bottom-up information transfer from S1 to anterior PPC (PPC-A). In contrast, biased states showed weaker sensory coding and relatively stronger involvement of rostrolateral PPC (PPC-RL). State-dependent differences were present in both task-related and task-orthogonal population activity. These results show that internal states modulate not only local sensory encoding, but also the routing of task-relevant information across cortical networks.
papers.title: State-dependent modulation of cross-area sensory processing in mouse neocortex

papers.abstract: The Columbretes archipelago in the Mediterranean is an example of deep isolation and sporadic human interaction during the Holocene. We recovered ancient DNA from 2,600-year-old microfauna and historical museum specimens to investigate the island's extinct fauna. Despite challenging preservation conditions, we successfully recovered mitogenomes from historical Vipera latastei specimens, and partial mitogenomes from snake, skink, and lizard subfossils. Phylogenetic analyses confirm the extinct Columbretes snake as Vipera latastei, sharing a haplotype with the historical specimen and clustering with modern populations from northeastern Iberia, validating its provenance and suggesting a single mitochondrial lineage since isolation. The extinct skink, Chalcides bedriagai, also shows affinities with eastern Iberia. These results point to a vicariant origin for the herpetofauna, likely isolated on the island following sea level rise after the Last Glacial Maximum. Conversely, a 2,600-year-old mouse incisor yielded a Mus musculus mitogenome, indicating Iron Age human-mediated introduction. Additionally, genomic analysis of a 11th-century CE human burial revealed an individual with genetic affinities to the Central Mediterranean and Balkans, highlighting medieval maritime mobility. This study resolves the long-debated Columbretes snake identity, traces biogeographic origins and illustrates the interplay of natural isolation and anthropogenic influence on the island biodiversity.
papers.title: Hic sunt dracones: ancient DNA from the extinct palaeofauna of the tiny Mediterranean archipelago of Columbretes and its implications for human visitation

papers.abstract: A century of fire suppression has made historically fire-adapted forests across the western U.S. denser and dominated by fire-intolerant trees, leading to severe fires. Fuel treatments aim to reduce wildfire impact and restore fire-adapted forests. Ecological theory suggests these objectives need not align: protecting the existing, fire-maladapted stand may prevent fire-tolerant seedling recruitment. Using Forest Inventory and Analysis data on 81,621 trees and 41,328 seedlings across 11 western U.S. states, we show that fuel treatments increase tree survival, but benefits are largest for fire-intolerant trees, fade within nine years, and come with no seedling composition shift towards fire-tolerant species. Concluding, fuel reduction reduces wildfire impacts but does not restore fire-adapted forests. Without changes in treatment design, long-term resilience will require repeated intervention.
papers.title: A mismatch in wildfire impact reduction and ecological restoration in western U.S. fuel treatments

papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in HERC1 are associated with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by macrocephaly, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and psychomotor dysfunction. Although genetic and molecular studies suggest a loss-of-function mechanism, definitive in vivo evidence that HERC1 deficiency is sufficient to cause neurodevelopmental abnormalities is lacking. Using a HERC1 knockout mouse model, we investigated the behavioural, neuronal, and synaptic consequences of complete HERC1 loss. HERC1 deficiency caused motor coordination and cognitive deficits in both sexes, while male mutants additionally displayed hyperactivity and increased anxiety-like behaviour. Histological analyses revealed selective hippocampal abnormalities, including disruption of dentate gyrus organization, whereas Purkinje cells survival and cerebellar compartmentalization remained preserved. HERC1-deficient mice exhibited a marked increase in hippocampal GABAergic interneurons, impaired maturation of dendritic spines in CA1 pyramidal neurons, and altered adult neurogenesis, indicating widespread defects in hippocampal circuit organization. Consistent with these structural abnormalities, glutamatergic synaptic components were significantly altered throughout the hippocampus. These molecular changes showed a sex-dependent pattern, with predominantly presynaptic defects in males and postsynaptic alterations in females. Despite these differences, whole-cell recordings revealed a common functional phenotype in both sexes. At both mossy fibre-CA3 and Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses, HERC1-deficient neurons exhibited a progressive inability to sustain excitatory neurotransmission during repetitive stimulation, resulting in impaired steady-state glutamatergic transmission. Together, these findings demonstrate that loss of HERC1 function is sufficient to produce a neurodevelopmental phenotype and identify HERC1 as a critical regulator of hippocampal circuit assembly and function. Our results provide mechanistic insight into the pathogenesis of HERC1-associated disorders and establish the Herc1 knockout mouse as a preclinically relevant model for investigating disease mechanisms and therapeutic approaches.
papers.title: HERC1 Loss of Function Causes a Developmental Disorder with Impaired Hippocampal Function

papers.abstract: Natural selection embeds distinct genomic signatures as populations adapt to environmental pressures. Machine learning approaches, particularly deep neural networks, have emerged as powerful tools to detect adaptive signatures from genomic data. While machine learning has dramatically improved our ability to extract these signals from sequence variation, distinguishing among multiple evolutionary processes remains challenging. We introduce SHADES, a deep learning framework that employs information about sequence differences and their frequencies at various spatial resolutions to capture evolutionary signatures at different genomic scales. We found that SHADES has the capacity to distinguish among neutrality, selective sweeps, balancing selection, and adaptive introgression and outperformed several contemporary methods evaluated for both classification accuracy and power. In addition, SHADES remained robust to a number of confounding factors, with only modest changes in classification performance. Furthermore, application of SHADES to empirical haplotypic variation from European humans recovered previously reported signals for selective sweeps, balancing selection, and adaptive introgression, while also identifying novel genes broadly involved in immune defense, inflammatory regulation, and epithelial barrier biology.
papers.title: Multi-scale haplotype signatures distinguish among evolutionary processes

papers.abstract: Diversity-generating retroelements (DGRs) are genetic elements that use error-prone reverse transcription to hypermutate specific target genes, most often the receptor-binding proteins of phages. They are enriched in human gut viruses, where they are hypothesised to enable phages expand their host range. Yet DGR-mediated host-range expansion across bacterial species has so far only been predicted in silico and has not been examined directly within complex microbial communities. To test this hypothesis in situ, we tracked phage-host interactions in the human gut, combining bulk metagenomic, virus-like particle (VLP), and Hi-C sequencing of longitudinal faecal samples collected over a five-week period. This culture-independent approach identified 380 interactions between 97 phages and 76 bacterial hosts. Nearly a third of these phages (31 of 97) encoded a DGR, and DGR-encoding phages were more likely to interact with multiple bacterial species. Moreover, nucleotide diversity in DGR-targeted genes increased with the number of hosts a phage interacted with and was concentrated in the surface-exposed, DGR-targeted variable region of its receptor-binding proteins. Together, these results provide in situ evidence that DGRs enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut.
papers.title: Diversity-generating retroelements enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut.

papers.abstract: Background. Helicobacter pylori colonises 40-45% of the global population, is a WHO Group I carcinogen, and is increasingly hard to eradicate amid rising resistance; no vaccine is licensed. CagW, a VirB6-family cagPAI component, has been advanced as a DNA-vaccine antigen that protects mice; a codon-optimised CagW-Fc mRNA in lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNP) is a candidate antigen design intended to engage humoral and cellular immunity. To define the infected gastric mucosal niche in which such a vaccine must operate, we mined public sequencing, single-cell and metabolomics repositories. Methods. NCBI GEO, MetaboLights and NCBI Protein were interrogated. Bulk transcriptomes of H. pylori-infected vs uninfected gastric epithelial cells (GSE295523; 24 libraries: HGC27, AGS, MKN45, GES-1) were re-analysed with a cell-line-blocked design; DEGs (BH-adjusted) were annotated via g:Profiler (GO, KEGG, Reactome) and 13 functional signatures scored. Single-cell composition was quantified from a mouse gastric scRNA-seq atlas (GSE224840; 16,434 cells) and sorted gastric CD8+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) vs splenic memory T cells (GSE216894). Targeted gastric metabolomics was re-analysed for epithelial ornithine decarboxylase (Odc) deletion (MTBLS3235) and cystathionine-gamma-lyase (Cth) deletion (MTBLS2851). CagW conservation was computed across 400 NCBI records (286 variants) with Kyte-Doolittle topology and four B cell epitope scales. Results. Infection induced 326 up- and 115 down-regulated genes (FDR < 0.05, |log2FC| > 1), dominated by TNF/NF-kappaB (KEGG hsa04668, P=5.5x10-11), integrated stress response (ATF4-CHAC1-DDIT3-TRIB3-ASNS) and Th17 chemokines (CXCL8 +3.43, CCL20 +1.32, CXCL1 +1.30, IL23A +1.02). MHC-I presentation rose (Delta-z +0.76; MHC-II unchanged); the arginine/polyamine module (SLC7A1 +1.19, ARG2 +1.33, SAT1 +1.50, ODC1 +0.58) was co-induced. scRNA-seq showed immune expansion in infected mucosa (39.8% vs 21.2% cells; OR 2.46; cell-level frequencies reported descriptively because cells are not independent; direction confirmed at sample level, n=4 vs 4), driven by plasmacytoid DCs (OR 8.9), neutrophils (OR 3.0), macrophages (OR 2.7) and cDCs (OR 2.1), with epithelial de-differentiation. Gastric CD8+ TRM cells showed a residency-effector program (Itgae +6.2, Cd69 +2.3, Gzmb +4.8, Ifng +5.3) with egress-gene loss (Sell -11.4, S1pr1 -9.7, Klf2 -5.2). Metabolomics confirmed both nodes: Odc deletion raised arginine (+3.08) and Cth deletion raised spermidine (+0.40) while lowering leukotriene B4 (-0.33). CagW was conserved across 286 variants (median 98.3% identity; 96.4% residues >=95% conserved), carried four transmembrane helices, and showed a surface-biased conserved epitope envelope at residues 505-530 and 63-79. Conclusions. Public multi-omics define an NF-kappaB/ATF4-driven, Th17-polarised, metabolically stressed niche where antigen-presenting cells expand, epithelium de-differentiates, and CD8+ TRM cells act locally. Here CagW is exceptional among cagPAI antigens: near-universal conservation plus an accessible, conserved surface. These findings provide a systems-level rationale for prioritising CagW as a conserved, epitope-accessible vaccine antigen and inform next-generation multi-antigen designs.
papers.title: Integrative multi-omics re-analysis of public sequencing and metabolomics repositories defines the mucosal immune and metabolic landscape of Helicobacter pylori infection and supports CagW as a rational mRNA-LNP vaccine antigen

papers.abstract: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is built from phospholipids synthesised at the inner membrane, but how they cross the periplasm remains unresolved. YhdP is the leading candidate for anterograde phospholipid transfer and is predicted to form an envelope-spanning bridge. Here we purify YhdP at endogenous levels and show by cryo-electron microscopy that it contains a continuous cavity, alongside an additional density that proteomics identifies as the cell wall-binding protein DedD. Liposome co-sedimentation shows that the C-terminal helices of YhdP bind membranes directly, and single-molecule tracking reveals that endogenous YhdP is as immobile as an outer membrane protein, indicating an envelope-spanning architecture in vivo. Native mass spectrometry demonstrates that the YhdP groove accommodates all major classes of E. coli phospholipid without headgroup preference. DedD engages YhdP through its disordered region and increases lipid density at the groove entrance, suggesting a potential role in lipid loading.
papers.title: YhdP forms an envelope-spanning phospholipid-binding bridge in complex with DedD

papers.abstract: Type I interferons (IFN) help clear a viral infection, but IFN levels can then decline to reset the antiviral state and avoid innate immune dysregulation. Such dysregulation can occur following infection with highly pathogenic and pandemic RNA viruses, such as H5N1 influenza A viruses or SARS-CoV-2. In spite of the strong innate immune response that these viruses induce, pandemic viruses replicate and spread successfully, suggesting that they can circumvent the effects of IFN. Innate immune activation is triggered when host cells detect viral RNA, especially defective viral genomes (DVGs). A strong IFN response (e.g. to DVGs or a highly immunogenic wild-type infection) must then decline through negative feedback involving the IFN receptor. How DVGs modulate this feedback remains poorly understood. To quantify positive and negative IFN regulation, we first performed in vitro experiments combining different doses of viral RNA and exogenous IFN, and measured subsequent IFN expression. We next developed an in vivo Bayesian computational model that captures the impact of influenza virus DVGs on both positive and negative IFN feedback. Competition between DVGs and virus is also considered. Finally, we calibrated this model on published in vitro and in vivo influenza virus infection data. Our model suggests that the cumulative IFN exposure of a host cell, rather than the instantaneous IFN level, shapes further IFN induction; this gives DVGs a dual role: beyond triggering IFN induction, they can also lower it through negative feedback. Our model further predicts that these effects are important locally, shaping the spatial dynamics of the response, allowing suppression of innate immune responses in neighbouring, uninfected cells. Through this model, we can explain two important biological observations: i) IFN levels can decline while virus and DVG levels continue to rise in tissue culture and mouse infections; and ii) pandemic viruses that produce high levels of immunogenic RNA molecules can successfully replicate through local innate immune suppression. Overall, we propose that heterogeneity within viral populations (including DVGs and other noncanonical viral RNAs) can modulate positive and negative feedback loops and shape infection outcomes. More broadly, our work may support studies into the therapeutic use of these viral RNA populations.
papers.title: Defective Viral Genomes Reveal History-dependent Self-regulation of Type I Interferon Dynamics

papers.abstract: Modeling substitution rate heterogeneity as a discretized Gamma distribution is standard in phylogenetic inference. Ferretti et al. (2026) have recently demonstrated that the most commonly used equiprobable Gamma rate discretization, known simply as the discrete Gamma model (DGM), substantially overestimates average branch lengths in reconstructed phylogenies when the true rates are drawn from a continuous Gamma distribution. We propose an alternative method to discretize the Gamma rate distribution that considerably reduces the bias in estimated branch lengths and can be used as a drop-in replacement for the standard DGM. The method works especially well on large trees with short branches, yielding up to a 20-fold reduction in bias on simulated phylogenies. It is developed by applying quantization-theoretic tools to the analysis of a simplified star-phylogeny abstraction introduced by Ferretti et al. (2026), where the new method is unbiased by construction. We explain Ferretti et al.'s counterintuitive observation that increasing the number of rate categories can exacerbate the bias of the standard DGM, even though this should in principle make DGM a better approximation to the continuous case, and offer our method as an immediately available alternative.
papers.title: DGM Is Dead; Long Live DGM-Star! A Quantization-Theoretic Approach to Gamma Rate Discretization

papers.abstract: Dietary fiber deficiency shifts the gut microbiota to degrade host mucus, compromising intestinal homeostasis. Mechanistically linking in vitro metabolic dynamics of fiber degradation to in vivo outcomes remains challenging due to a lack of representative model systems. Introducing spatial mucin structures to a defined Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota (OMM12) in vitro consortium allowed us to recapitulate the spatio-temporal dynamics of xylooligosaccharide (XOS) processing in gnotobiotic mice. XOS supplementation rapidly established a stable community state in vitro and in vivo across compositional, metabolic and transcriptional levels. XOS supplementation established distinct functional guilds: Bifidobacterium animalis and Blautia coccoides partitioning xylose and arabinose catabolism, whilst profiting from XOS degradation by Bacteroides caecimuris. Along the colonic axis, a spatial XOS gradient exposes Bl. coccoides's substrate preference for xylose and drives longitudinal functional adaptations. Altogether, our predictive platform proves that regional microenvironments govern prebiotic efficacy, highlighting spatial cascades as essential parameters for targeted microbiome interventions.
papers.title: Metabolic cascades drive spatial prebiotic fermentation in a defined gut consortium

papers.abstract: ATCC 17978 is one of the most utilised lab strains of Acinetobacter baumannii. Current literature suggests ATCC 17978 can have either a sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype or have the type VI secretion system (T6SS) switched on depending on the presence/absence of the large conjugative plasmid pAB3, which encodes the antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) sul2 and T6SS repressors tetR1/tetR2. Here, we show that pAB3 integrates into the ATCC 17978 chromosome, which enables a large inversion resulting in the chromosomal arrangement labelled GS2.24 by Socru. This integration has no transcriptional impact on nearby genes or tetR1/tetR2. We find several instances were a portion of integrated pAB3 containing tetR2 is lost but the rest of the sequence, including sul2, is maintained, suggesting pAB3 integration may serve to make further rearrangements more tractable, enabling a putative T6SS+ sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype.
papers.title: The large conjugative plasmid pAB3 integrates into the chromosome of Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC 17978

papers.abstract: During infection, fungal pathogens must adapt to multiple environmental challenges, including changes in temperature, nutrient availability, and immune stress. Although transcriptional regulators are central to these adaptations, how individual regulators contribute to distinct environmental responses and how these responses are functionally interconnected remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functions of infection-associated transcription factors under distinct host-relevant conditions in Cryptococcus neoformans. Integrating in vivo expression profiling with infectivity data from signature-tagged mutagenesis, we prioritized 24 transcription factors, 12 of which were induced under host-mimicking conditions. Initial functional analyses revealed distinct roles for these transcription factors in adaptation to temperature, carbon, and nitrogen availability. Further characterization of Mln1, a fungal basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, uncovered an unexpected connection between carbon source adaptation and thermotolerance. Mig1-dependent repression limited MLN1 expression in the presence of glucose, whereas Mln1 accumulated in the nucleus in the presence of trehalose or ethanol, but not glucose. Loss of MLN1 impaired carbon-starvation gene expression and growth on non-preferred carbon sources, particularly trehalose. Conversely, mln1{Delta} cells accumulated more intracellular trehalose and exhibited enhanced thermotolerance, yet showed reduced melanization, titan cell formation, virulence in Drosophila, and brain fungal burden in mice. Together, these results suggest that Mln1 contributes to metabolic flexibility and fungal virulence while differentially influencing thermotolerance. More broadly, these findings highlight a potential physiological trade-off between nutrient utilization and stress resistance, suggesting that these adaptive processes may be interconnected in fungal pathogens.
papers.title: Systematic analysis reveals an Mln1-dependent trade-off between metabolic flexibility and thermotolerance in Cryptococcus neoformans

papers.abstract: Mitochondrial Complex I generates reactive oxygen species at its flavin cofactor, where spin dependent reaction pathways have been proposed. Models of this chemistry treat the flavin oxygen radical pair in isolation, although the flavin is wired to a chain of eight iron sulfur clusters. Here we model the pair with this chain using the human Complex I structure and open quantum system models of spin coupling and electron transfer. In the simulated network, spin coherence decays rapidly along the chain, whereas proximal clusters alter the calculated radical-pair singlet yield. Their influence is kinetically gated: a downstream cluster affects the modelled yield when its electron-transfer rate competes with radical pair recombination, a threshold robust to driving force and to the transfer model. Modelling does set the sign: one directional spin hops predict suppression and inflate coherence transport, whereas charge resolved transfer drives the singlet yield towards its spin-randomized limit unless triplet recombination dominates. Detectable spin dependent effects in this framework require superoxide spin relaxation to be substantially slower than in free solution, a condition not yet established for Complex I.
papers.title: Kinetic gating by an iron sulfur chain modulates flavin radical-pair spin chemistry in mitochondrial Complex I

papers.abstract: The Asian citrus psyllid Diaphorina citri (Insecta: Hemiptera), a major agricultural pest, harbors the unusual obligate bacterial symbiont "Candidatus Profftella armatura" (Profftella), which is intimately integrated with its host yet devotes a remarkably large proportion of its highly reduced genome to the production of diaphorin, a bioactive polyketide. To gain insight into the evolution of this distinctive symbiont, we determined the genomes of Profftella and the co-resident nutritional symbiont "Candidatus Carsonella ruddii" (Carsonella) from Diaphorina lycii and compared them with previously characterized counterparts from D. citri and D. cf. continua. The Profftella and Carsonella chromosomes from D. lycii were 471 and 174 kb, respectively, and Profftella harbored an 8-kb plasmid. Genome organization and gene content were highly conserved across the three lineages. The diaphorin biosynthetic system likewise retained its overall organization, consistent with an important role for diaphorin in the Diaphorina symbiotic system. Remarkably, however, pronounced lineage-specific structural variation was observed in diaphorin synthases DipP and DipT, encoded by two of the 20 diaphorin biosynthetic genes. These synthases contained three extensively amplified tandem arrays of acyl carrier protein (ACP) domains that carry growing polyketide intermediates, with up to seven copies compared with one or two at corresponding positions in the related pederin synthases. All three regions of tandem ACP repeats showed copy-number variation among the Profftella lineages. This variation indicates that ACP amplification remains evolutionarily dynamic despite the otherwise highly constrained symbiotic genome. Together, our findings show that even highly integrated obligate symbionts retain evolutionary flexibility in specialized functional systems.
papers.title: Dynamic evolution of diaphorin biosynthetic genes against a background of genome conservation in Profftella

papers.abstract: Introduction: Sapovirus (SaV) is an emerging enteric pathogen of rising public health importance, responsible for acute gastroenteritis in people of all ages and most often in children under five. Its genome is approximately 7.1-7.7 kb long, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, comprising two principal open reading frames; processing of the ORF1 product yields seven non-structural proteins and the major capsid protein VP1, while ORF2 encodes the minor structural protein VP2. Given the absence of therapies or an approved vaccine and the low yields of recombinant capsid protein, improving expression remains a priority. Methods: VP1 and VP2 sequences from twelve selected human SaV strains were aligned, phylogenetic trees were reconstructed by maximum likelihood method under the Tamura-Nei model with 1,000 bootstrap replicates, and both genes were optimized in silico for Escherichia coli using the OPTIMIZER. Results: The trees resolved three genogroups, GI, GII and GV, each strain placed alike by both genes. Every optimized sequence reached the ceiling value of 1.000 for the codon adaptation index (CAI). Mean CAI and GC% increased by 3.07 (207.0%) and 1.11 (11.1%) fold for VP1, and 3.11 (210.9%) and 1.14 (14.1%) fold for VP2, while AT% decreased. All changes were statistically significant (p < 0.001) and the encoded amino acid sequences were unaltered. Conclusion: Our findings indicate that Optmization raised host-matched codon usage in both capsid genes with no truncated proteins produced. The redesigned VP1 and VP2 sequences warrant further investigation as potential candidates for biotherapeutic and vaccine development. KEYWORDS: Sapovirus,CAI, codon optimization, VP1 capsid protein, GC content, DNA, phylogenetic analysis, vaccines
papers.title: In silico codon optimization and phylogenetic analysis of various strains of Sapovirus

papers.abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal RNA modification with established roles in mRNA metabolism. Although m6A has been characterized in several well-known long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), its transcriptome-wide landscape and roles remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized the m6A landscape of lncRNAs at single-base resolution, identified m6A deposition-associated features, and investigated potential roles of m6A in lncRNA processing. Unlike in mRNAs, m6A sites are broadly distributed along lncRNAs. We further found that these differences in m6A patterns between lncRNAs and mRNAs may reflect contributions from transposable element-derived sequence to motif availability and local RNA structure, together with splicing-related constraints on m6A deposition near exon junctions. Additionally, m6A may be relevant to the regulation of lncRNA polyadenylation. Together, these findings define the single-base-resolution m6A landscape in lncRNAs, and connect lncRNA methylation to transposable elements, RNA structure, splicing, and polyadenylation. This study broadens our understanding of m6A in the lncRNA epitranscriptome.
papers.title: Single-base mapping of m6A in lncRNAs reveals a distinct landscape linked to transposable elements and RNA processing

papers.abstract: Combinatorial assembly of transcription factors (TFs) opens chromatin at cis-regulatory elements (cREs) to establish cell-type-specific gene expression. Dissecting the role of individual TFs and their collective function has been limited by the diversity of TF binding-site arrangements across cREs. A single regulatory sequence can support multiple configurations of TF and nucleosome occupancy, raising the possibility that distinct chromatin states reflect different TF assemblies. Predictive models linking regulatory sequence to chromatin accessibility collapse these distinct molecular states into population averages, obscuring how TF assemblies shape accessible chromatin. Here, we introduce SMFNet, a generative diffusion model that predicts distributions of single-molecule chromatin accessibility profiles from DNA sequence, and PRISM, which identifies sequence features associated with individual molecular states. Together, these approaches enable us to systematically associate single molecule chromatin states at cREs with specific TF binding motifs. Experimental perturbation of these motifs redistributes the corresponding states as predicted by SMFNet, supporting their interpretation as TF-dependent configurations underlying chromatin opening. We then use controlled in silico motif screens to systematically dissect individual and combinatorial TF contributions to chromatin opening. Individual TFs show distinct chromatin-opening signatures, differing in accessible-region width and nucleosome-positioning precision even when associated with similar levels of chromatin accessibility. Combining motifs reveals partner- and spacing-dependent effects on chromatin accessibility, TF occupancy and nucleosome positioning. Genetic perturbation of TF binding sites using natural variation at endogenous cRE confirms that TF-specific properties shape chromatin accessibility in vivo. Together, our findings reveal sequence-encoded principles of combinatorial TF assembly during chromatin opening.
papers.title: SMFnet reveals principles of combinatorial transcription factor assembly

papers.abstract: Whether similar phenotypes evolve through shared substitutions or alternative molecular routes is a central question in evolutionary genomics. Grey-coated taurine cattle provide a powerful system for investigating this question using geographically distinct Podolian and Alpine lineages. We combined whole-genome resequencing data, complementary selection scans (hapFLK, DCMS and FST) and contrasts between grey-coated and non-grey-coated breeds to investigate the molecular evolution of grey coat colour. Selection analyses identified candidate regions associated with Podolian/steppe divergence and a prominent pigmentation-related signal on BTA18 contaning FANCA, MC1R, and SPIRE2. Most grey breeds shared a BTA18 haplotype containing MC1R p.Arg223Trp and additional candidate variants. Tyrolean Grey cattle lacked this predominant haplotype but carried the coding duplication p.Gly220_Arg223dup, together with differentiation near the ASIP regulatory region. Thus, different candidate coding changes affect the same MC1R residue in different cattle lineages. Haplotype comparisons supported independent Podolian and Alpine origins for p.Arg223Trp and p.Gly220_Arg223dup insertion, respectively. Ancient-genome screening yielded no validated evidence of either variant except p.Arg223Trp in medieval cattle. Comparisons across 1,108 mammalian taxa identified independent recurrence of p.Arg223Trp in the white-coated mountain goat, Oreamnos americanus, where the derived allele was fixed in surveyed individuals (JTT-based neutral probability = 0.0043). Our findings support a model in which grey coat colour in cattle evolved through at least two partially distinct molecular routes within interacting pigmentation pathways. More broadly, they identify MC1R residue 223 as a candidate recurrent target of coat-colour lightening and illustrate how domesticated and wild lineages can repeatedly target constrained functional positions during phenotypic evolution.
papers.title: MC1R residue 223 is a convergent target for coat-colour lightening in domestic and wild bovids

papers.abstract: Urbanization imposes unique selective pressures on organisms, but connecting specific urban environmental differences to trait adaptation requires detailed characterization of environmental heterogeneity across urbanized landscapes and tests for adaptation to it, rarely done to date. The Plant Economic Spectrum (PES) predicts that plants invest in different life strategies according to resource availability, ranging from an acquisitive strategy favoring fast growth and aboveground biomass where resources are abundant, to a conservative strategy favoring belowground investment where resources are limiting. Here, we leverage previous work describing the mosaic of urbanized environments in California, USA as a set of Environmental Zones, and use this framework to test for trait differentiation predicted by the PES in the invasive annual plant Centaurea melitensis. Seeds from 31 populations across California were grown in greenhouse conditions for two generations. In the second generation, we measured growth, reproductive, and phenology traits to test for genetically-based differentiation and whether variation follows PES predictions. Variation across all genotypes was not structured along the multivariate trait axes predicted by the PES. Individual traits were associated with environmental variables, including impervious surface cover and tree cover, following some PES expectations, but multi-trait strategies were absent. We found evidence that C. melitensis traits have differentiated genetically across environments with different features of urbanization but did not exhibit the multi-trait strategies predicted by the PES. Our study pairs detailed knowledge of urbanized environments with tests of trait-environment relationships to reveal how urbanization may be selecting on the species that inhabit these spaces.
papers.title: Trait differentiation across urbanized environments in invasive Centaurea melitensis is not predicted by the Plant Economic Spectrum

papers.abstract: Among the multiple cortical glutamatergic neuron classes, intratelencephalic (IT) neurons represent the largest class and project within the cortex and striatum. IT neurons have been amplified and diversified throughout mammalian evolution and are thought to underlie increasingly complex mammalian cognition. However, despite their diversity and significance in cortical processes, few existing tools connect the molecular signatures to the projection patterns of distinct IT subtypes, limiting our ability to understand their organization and function at a subtype resolution. Here, we illustrate six novel gene knock-in mouse lines based on IT-specific markers, labeling subpopulations with unique cortico-cortical and corticostriatal projection patterns. These include two broad subpopulations with upper-layer (Cux1-Flp) versus lower-layer (Kcnh5-CreER) expression biases, two narrow upper-layer subpopulations with contrasting callosal (Wfs1-Flp) and local (Igfn1-Flp) projection patterns, and two narrow lower-layer subpopulations with contrasting bilateral (Deptor-CreER) versus ipsilateral-predominant (Ptprm-CreER) corticostriatal projection patterns. Upper-layer Wfs1+ and lower-layer Ptprm+ IT neurons also project to perirhinal/ectorhinal cortex with densities that vary across cortical areas. Finally, we use in vivo calcium imaging in mice performing a reach-withdraw-drink task to demonstrate subtype-specific temporal dynamics in upper-layer Wfs1+ versus lower-layer Deptor+ neurons. Our work expands the toolbox of transgenic mice to access molecularly defined IT neuron subpopulations.
papers.title: An expanded toolbox for genetic access to molecularly defined cortical intratelencephalic neuron subtypes

papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is managed as a single clinical entity despite substantial biological heterogeneity. We established a cross-species framework to define etiology-specific molecular programs and determine how these programs relate to molecular heterogeneity and pathobiology in human AKI. We performed parallel sequencing of totalRNA (mRNA) and miRNA (kidney, whole blood) in 3 murine models (mild AKI: ischemia-reperfusion injury, IRI; cecal-ligation and puncture, CLP; endotoxemia, LPS); kidney mRNA and miRNA clearly distinguished the models, blood mRNA maintained model-specific separation, and blood miRNA was less distinct. IRI was characterized by epithelial injury/repair, and extracellular matrix remodeling (i.e., miR-125b-1-3p, Vim, Sprr2g); CLP, broader inflammatory, metabolic programs (i.e., miR-692, Pfkfb3, Cdo1); LPS, inflammatory signaling (i.e., miR-155-5p, Irf7, Gbp3). We then compared these signatures to human whole blood RNAseq. Human blood samples varied along a shared gene axis that correlated to differing degrees with all three murine models, consistent with the heterogeneous nature of clinical AKI rather than discrete assignment to a single experimental etiology. Orthologs were linked to immune processes (i.e., SIGLEC14, DAAM2, CD177, DEFA3), and the presence of tubular casts in human biopsies, reflecting that mild murine AKI models capture etiology-specific biology relevant to severe human AKI. Integration of injury etiology, severity, and time may provide a framework for developing circulating biomarkers that may resolve the biological heterogeneity of human AKI.
papers.title: Shared and Specific miRNA-mRNA in Human and Murine Acute Kidney Injury

papers.abstract: Remipedes are enigmatic blind, venomous crustaceans endemic to anchialine cave ecosystems (aphotic, hypoxic subterranean environments) and occupy a pivotal phylogenomic position within Pancrustacea as the sister group to Hexapoda. A high-quality genome assembly has long proven elusive for this taxon, due to accessibility challenges and the fragility of remipedes when removed from their habitat. Here we present a highly contiguous, chromosome-level genome assembly for the remipede Xibalbanus tulumensis (Xibalbanidae) spanning 8.05 Gb on 30 chromosome-scale scaffolds, placing it among the largest arthropod genomes reported to date. The protein-coding gene repertoire was highly conserved, with over 97% of arthropod orthologs recovered, and microRNA surveys showed a high level of completeness (94%) relative to pancrustacean genomes. Genome expansion appears to be driven primarily by proliferation of intronic and repetitive elements, which comprise ~71% of the genome. Comparative genomic analyses reveal extensive gene family turnover, with relatively few families showing lineage-specific expansions and contractions. Venom-associated gene families included the remipede-specific Xibalbins, while significant expansion and episodic positive selection affected other venom-associated gene families. Comparative analysis of macrosynteny revealed that the remipede genome retains the signature of ancient fusion-with-mixing events that unite Pancrustacea and Allotriocarida, with considerable similarity in the chromosome architecture of remipedes and basally branching insect orders. Our findings provide the first genomic framework for Remipedia and reveal a highly expanded, repeat-rich genome that retains deep phylogenetic signals in its architecture, despite being adapted to a highly unusual environment.
papers.title: Genomic expansion in the dark: A repeat-rich genome of a cave-dwelling remipede sheds light on the evolution of the hexapod sister group.

papers.abstract: Bacterial capsules are formed by individual capsular polysaccharide (CPS) polymers and are the outermost extracellular layers of many Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Capsules affect several aspects of bacterial biology, including resistance to host immune factors, survival in unfavorable environments and antimicrobial resistance. Research on CPS biology has largely focused on its synthesis and the pathogenic consequences of its presence or absence. Beyond synthesis, our understanding of its retention (attachment) on the cell surface is limited. Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important Gram-negative pathogen and expresses more than 80 capsular serotypes using the common Wzy-dependent CPS biosynthesis system and phenotypically manifests in various forms, making this species an attractive bacterial model to study the underexplored aspects of CPS biology. Here, we identified and characterized bacterial components involved in CPS retention in K. pneumoniae and assessed the importance of CPS retention on bloodstream fitness. Our examination revealed that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and the outer-membrane protein, Wzi, collectively retain K. pneumoniae CPS on the bacterial surface. We demonstrate that the core-oligosaccharide domain of LPS and the extracellular surface of Wzi likely provide anchoring sites for CPS on the bacterial surface. Furthermore, CPS retention depends on divalent cation availability. Importantly, CPS retention on the bacterial surface is important for survival in serum and bacterial fitness at secondary infection sites in a murine bacteremia model. Together, our findings demonstrate that the functional importance of CPS to bacteria extends beyond synthesis and its overall abundance. Bacterial control over other CPS properties, like cell surface retention, are also important for K. pneumoniae fitness during bacteremia.
papers.title: Lipopolysaccharide and Wzi retain capsular polysaccharide at the Klebsiella pneumoniae cell surface and promote bloodstream infection fitness

papers.abstract: Carotenoid cleavage dioxygenases (CCDs) are a superfamily of non-heme iron-containing enzymes ubiquitous across all kingdoms of life. Previously, we identified a new subfamily of CCDs termed beta-carotene oxygenase-like (BCOL) proteins, a chordate expansion of an ancestral sister clade of metazoan CCDs, which are widely distributed in marine invertebrates, including mollusks and lancelets. Here we present the three-dimensional structure of a representative BCOL protein from the lancelet Branchiostoma floridae (BCOLg) at 2.4 [A] resolution and its functional properties. BCOLg symmetrically cleaves {beta}-carotene into all-trans retinal. RNAseq of wild-caught animals detected six of the seven annotated BCOL transcripts in Branchiostoma gut tissue. We expressed and crystallized recombinant BCOLg. BCOLg is heavily glycosylated, with four N-linked glycosylation sites, and adopts the seven-bladed propeller fold characteristic of the superfamily, with one disulfide bond contributing to structural stability. BCOLg and several other BCOL proteins contain Asp substitutions at two of three Glu positions found in other CCDs, stabilizing three of four His residues involved in Fe2+ coordination. Notably, BCOLg lacks the canonical -PDPCK- motif characteristic of other metazoan CCDs.
papers.title: Structure of a secreted lancelet carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase (CCD), from an ancestral CCD clade

papers.abstract: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis-regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.
papers.title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility

papers.abstract: Ancestral balancing selection may facilitate evolutionary rescue following migration into a new habitat by providing founder populations with adaptive alleles, even when those alleles were not the fittest in the ancestral habitat. However, recent studies emphasize the roles of immigration history and admixture on colonization success. The extent to which balanced polymorphism may contribute to colonization success and the conditions under which it matters remain unclear. We use computer simulations to investigate how the mode of selection in the source population influences colonization success in new habitats under eco-evolutionary population dynamics, different invasion scenarios, and different selection regimes in the new habitat. We model source populations under balancing selection, directional selection, and neutrality, and allow founder groups of different sizes to invade a novel stable or perturbed habitat. We find that balancing selection in ancestral populations leads to higher rates of establishment in new habitats than are observed under source neutrality or directional selection when founder populations are relatively small, which would occur with a population bottleneck. This trend is observed regardless of whether invaders experience stable or variable conditions in a new habitat and persists under increasingly harsh conditions or greater environmental perturbations. When the colonizing populations are large, selection in the source population has little effect on invasion success. This study elucidates the interaction between genetic diversity and propagule pressure on colonization success, highlighting the number of adaptive alleles as a unique metric.
papers.title: Eco-evolutionary Dynamics of Colonization: When Does Source Selection Matter?

papers.abstract: Developmental stuttering has been repeatedly linked to decreased white matter integrity and structural connectivity differences in major white matter tracts. Prior diffusion-weighted MRI studies reporting such white matter structural differences involved voxel-averaged tensor measures (e.g., fractional anisotropy (FA)). A well-acknowledged limitation of this approach, however, has been that it cannot resolve distinct fiber populations within crossing-fiber regions. Fixel-based analysis addresses this limitation by quantifying individual fiber populations within a voxel and providing complementary measures of fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their combined measure (FDC).Here we applied Fixel-based analysis to diffusion MRI data from 171 children aged 3 - 13 years, including 84 children who stutter and 87 typically developing controls, to test whether white-matter differences associated with developmental stuttering were expressed as differences in FD, FC, and FDC and whether these measures show group-specific age-related patterns. We evaluated this at both the whole-brain level and within a priori white-matter tracts.FC, but not FD or FDC, showed significant Group and Group by Age effects, indicating that white-matter differences were primarily expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure. Tract-of-interest analyses identified developmental differences in bilateral arcuate fasciculus FC that remained significant across tracts, with controls showing greater age-related increases in FC than children who stutter. Additional FC differences were observed across corticospinal and thalamocortical pathways, although these tract-wise effects were less robust to across-tract correction. These findings suggest that white-matter differences in developmental stuttering are prominently expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure rather than fiber density and highlight divergent development of bilateral arcuate pathways. FBA provides fiber-specific information that complements conventional tensor-based diffusion measures and may improve characterization of white-matter development in childhood stuttering.
papers.title: Fixel-wise Differences in White Matter Fiber-bundle Cross-section identified in Children who Stutter

papers.abstract: Animal mating signals can communicate both species-specific recognition information and male phenotypic quality persuasion information to females. Using a comparative framework across an entire clade, we show that mating signal traits specifically associated with conspecific signal recognition show fast initial divergence during speciation, followed by relative stasis at equilibrium, and that this effect is enhanced among species pairs with the potential for gene flow. In contrast, sexually selected persuasion mating signal evolution is not associated with initial species divergence. These results reveal mechanistically how and when rapid mating signal evolution facilitates speciation and challenge the prevailing view that traits experiencing intrapopulation sexual selection are likely to be the major traits which promote interspecific divergence. In particular, the results suggest that the mechanistic link between sexual selection and speciation is ephemeral. We expect that the distinction between recognition and persuasion traits, and the particular importance of divergence in recognition traits for speciation, should be a widespread phenomenon.
papers.title: Speciation, sexual selection, and the macroevolution of cricket mating signals

papers.abstract: Single-molecule footprinting methods are rapidly transforming chromatin biology. They resolve nucleosome positioning, regulatory-factor occupancy, and accessibility on individual DNA fibers, revealing combinatorial heterogeneity that bulk measurements average away. Emerging footprinting methods leverage diverse enzyme systems and sequencing platforms, necessitating tools that can accommodate these systems. We present FiberBrowser, a unified platform that converts these diverse datasets into a common per-molecule representation of nucleosomes, accessible DNA, and subnucleosomal footprints for interactive and scripted analyses. Its inference engine, FiberHMM, weighs each observation against the assay's informative sites and sequence-specific modification probabilities, separating missing information from protection in four assays. FiberBrowser clusters, sorts and compares these calls across thousands of molecules in seconds, linking chromatin architecture to haplotype, CpG methylation and non-reference structural variants on the same molecules. Because the representation is independent of chemistry, models also transfer between assays. A classifier trained on Fiber-seq footprints identifies 12 scDAF-seq cells as lymphoblastoid without retraining, whereas models trained on raw modification patterns fail to transfer. FiberBrowser thus provides a unified, expandable analytical framework for single-molecule chromatin footprinting.
papers.title: FiberBrowser: a unified framework for single-molecule genomics

papers.abstract: Inhibitory neurons (INs) at the stratum radiatum/stratum lacunosum-moleculare border of hippocampal CA1 comprise diverse populations, including long-range-projecting neurons that innervate the retrosplenial cortex (RSCtx). However, their molecular organization and developmental connectivity remain poorly understood. Here, we combine multimodal transcriptomic profiling, intersectional genetics, and retrograde tracing to characterize CA1 border INs. We identified two major caudal ganglionic eminence-derived, Cxcl14-enriched populations distinguished by Syt6/Cck-related and Ntng1-expressing transcriptional profiles. We then generated a Cxcl14-Cre mouse line that, when combined with an IN-specific viral enhancer, provides genetic access to CA1 border INs. Retrograde labeling established that CA1 INs projecting to the RSCtx belong to the Ntng1-expressing population, and that this long-range projection emerges during postnatal mouse development, between postnatal days 3 and 5. Finally, analysis of genes encoding cell-surface proteins, key regulators of connectivity, revealed distinct expression profiles in RSCtx-projecting and SYT6-positive INs. Together, these findings establish a molecular and developmental framework for CA1 border IN diversity and provide a genetic strategy for investigating the assembly and function of these inhibitory circuits.
papers.title: Multimodal profiling and intersectional genetics reveal CA1 border inhibitory neuron diversity and postnatal emergence of retrosplenial connectivity

papers.abstract: Background: Females are more likely to be diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD) than males. Cognitive symptoms of MDD include negative cognitive bias, the perception of ambiguous situations as negative, which predicts MDD episode onset and severity. MDD is associated with changes to functional connectivity between regions involved in cognition, emotion, attention, and memory. Methods: Here we examined the impact of chronic unpredictable stress (CUS) on negative cognitive bias in male (n=18) and female (n=22) Sprague-Dawley rats. We assessed hippocampal neurogenesis and c-Fos expression in response to an ambiguous context across 15 regions of the frontal cortex, amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and hippocampus, including in newborn dentate gyrus (DG) neurons, to examine functional connectivity during cognitive bias testing. We conducted a graph-based network analysis and constructed linear models to predict freezing in the ambiguous context based on regional activation. Results: CUS-exposed rats froze more to the ambiguous context than non-CUS-exposed rats, regardless of sex. CUS decreased neurogenesis in the ventral DG of both sexes, and increased activation of new neurons in the dorsal DG of males only. In response to the ambiguous context, CUS males had an increase in c-Fos expression in the amygdala. CUS produced extensive, sex-specific network reorganization, decreasing global network efficiency in males but not in females. Freezing in the ambiguous context was predicted by activation of new neurons in combination with the ventral CA1 in opposing directions across sex. Conclusions: These findings suggest that sex-specific pathways drive the expression of CUS-induced negative cognitive bias, underscoring the necessity of sex-stratified preclinical and clinical research on negative cognitive bias in depression.
papers.title: Chronic unpredictable stress induces negative cognitive bias in rats with sex-specific changes in neurogenesis and functional connectivity

papers.abstract: Siphonophores are associated with prey, parasites, microbes, and other organisms in the open ocean, but little is known about these siphonophore cobionts. To learn more about them, we investigated molecular bycatch: their DNA captured during siphonophore genome sequencing. We reanalysed 213 specimens of Physalia, Nanomia, Bargmannia and other siphonophores sequenced in four previously published studies. We recovered 104 bacterial genomes forming 32 genome clusters, including recurrent Metamycoplasmataceae and diverse proteobacteria, groups also found with other cnidarians. Bacterial communities differed among Physalia species sampled in the southwestern Pacific. We identified non-siphonophore eukaryotes from ribosomal markers in 38 specimens, including fish and copepods consistent with prey, parasitic flatworms, and Perkinsela-like relatives of amoeba endosymbionts. Alfonsino (Beryx) sequences in one Hawaiian P. utriculus specimen are consistent with capture of pelagic young of deepwater fishes. Molecular bycatch reveals the diversity of siphonophore associates from specimens already collected for genome research.
papers.title: Organisms associated with siphonophores revealed by short-read whole-genome sequencing

papers.abstract: Aquatic species of economic and ecological importance are increasingly threatened by environmental change, yet their genetic diversity and population structure remain poorly characterised, limiting effective conservation and management. To address this gap, we initiated a multi-species genomic monitoring programme in 2022, targeting key marine and freshwater taxa. A total of 2,420 individuals from 104 locations were sampled across six species: turbot (Scophthalmus maximus), zander (Sander lucioperca), European eel (Anguilla anguilla; both glass eel in the marine environment and adult eel in freshwater environments), blue mussel (Mytilus edulis), flat oyster (Ostrea edulis), and Pacific oyster (Magallana gigas). Using genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) and SNP arrays, we generated genome-wide SNP datasets to assess population structure, genetic diversity, inbreeding, and relatedness. Among fish species, population structure was generally weak, consistent with high connectivity. However, significant variation in genetic diversity and kinship among localities indicates the presence of distinct source populations that may be critical for maintaining adaptive potential and guiding restoration efforts. In bivalves, cultured populations in the Oosterschelde and Waddenzee were genetically homogeneous, whereas wild populations in Grevelingen and Veerse Meer retained distinct genetic signatures, representing important reservoirs of diversity for conservation and breeding. Together, these results provide a genomic baseline for key aquatic species in the Netherlands and demonstrate the value of coordinated, multi-species genomic monitoring. The identification of genetically distinct and diverse populations offers direct guidance for conservation prioritisation, restoration strategies, and the sustainable management of aquatic genetic resources under ongoing environmental change, in the Netherlands but also applied in other national and transnational monitoring contexts.
papers.title: A genomic baseline for long-term monitoring of economically important aquatic species in the Netherlands

papers.abstract: In a rapidly warming world, species must either adapt to changing environmental conditions, shift their distributions through the movement and survival of individuals, or face local or global extinction. Within ecosystems, structural complexity of either environmental or biogenic origin may provide microclimate buffering, promoting persistence. In coastal environments, it has long been stated that macroalgae act as important ecosystem engineers that can moderate thermal extremes, however the magnitude of this buffering has rarely been quantified. Moreover, the extent to which thermal buffering varies among macroalgal species, and how it relates to thermal heterogeneity across scales remains poorly understood. Here, we measured thermal buffering provided by intertidal macroalgae using high-frequency, high-spatial-resolution in situ temperature logging. We compared microclimates beneath algal cover with those on experimentally cleared bare rock across two tidal levels, two solar exposures and two seasons along six shores within a biogeographical transition zone. Thermal buffering was highly heterogeneous across the study area, varying with species identity, algal cover, tidal level, and solar exposure. Together, these factors generated a complex thermal mosaic, with even small algal specimens providing measurable buffering. We found that latitude had little influence on mean daytime low-tide temperatures, whereas local-scale factors had pronounced effects. Lower tidal position, reduced solar exposure, and algal cover each moderated thermal conditions and, in combination, provided an average cooling of approximately 4 {degrees}C. These findings highlight the importance of fine-scale habitat heterogeneity in shaping thermal exposure and identify features that could be incorporated into local climate-adaptation strategies, supporting coastal conservation and restoration efforts.
papers.title: Mitigation of intertidal temperature extremes by algal canopies

papers.abstract: The spatial architecture of neural networks underpins nervous system function, yet dynamic in vivo evidence for their early establishment process remains scarce. Here, using long-term confocal live-cell imaging of transgenic zebrafish, we dissected neural network development across the brain, yolk sac, and spinal cord at single-cell resolution. We reveal that repeated growth cone bifurcation is the fundamental cellular mechanism for network node formation. Despite distinct developmental origins, networks in all three regions exhibit highly conserved dynamics, strictly following Strahler hierarchical ordering and Hack's power-law scaling. Quantitative topological analysis shows that as development progresses, node numbers and clustering coefficients increase, while network density decreases. This reflects a structural optimization strategy balancing high functional efficiency with low wiring cost. These findings suggest that physical and geometric constraints, combined with simple local rules, drive the self-organization of complex neural networks, offering valuable principles for artificial network design.
papers.title: Structural Evolution of Neural Networks during Zebrafish Early Development

papers.abstract: Maladaptive daydreaming is a form of maladaptive repetitive thought characterized by excessive, dysfunctional fantasy engagement, with notable links to psychological distress and poor well-being. Although symptoms can be reliably measured along a continuum, it remains unclear how they manifest in the phenomenological characteristics of everyday thinking, as well as which thought characteristics are unique to maladaptive daydreaming versus shared with trait rumination, a transdiagnostic manifestation of maladaptive repetitive thinking that frequently co-occurs with maladaptive daydreaming. To advance these questions, we conducted a pre-registered study using ecological momentary assessment to track the everyday thoughts of 446 young adults (aged 18 to 34) spanning a range of maladaptive daydreaming symptom severity as assessed with the 16-item Maladaptive Daydreaming Scale. Higher maladaptive daydreaming scores were associated with several poor mental health indicators, including higher trait rumination. Positive associations between maladaptive daydreaming scores and both negatively-valenced and task-unrelated thinking emerged, yet these relationships were accounted for by variance shared with rumination. Beyond rumination, higher maladaptive daydreaming scores were uniquely associated with worse mood, as well as greater internally-oriented attention, more socially-oriented thought, and greater overall thought persistence. Maladaptive daydreaming also uniquely moderated the relationship between internal orientation and social orientation, such that the positive association between internal and social thought content became stronger at higher levels of maladaptive daydreaming. Overall, these findings provide novel evidence that maladaptive daydreaming levels are linked to unique socioemotional features and restricted dynamics, beyond its overlap with general ruminative distress in everyday life. These insights suggest that clinical interventions should target immersive fantasy engagement alongside transdiagnostic maladaptive repetitive thinking.
papers.title: Beyond rumination: an ecological momentary assessment of daily thinking patterns in maladaptive daydreaming

papers.abstract: Elucidating the structures of unknown small molecules remains a major challenge in chemistry, pharmacology, and drug discovery. While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the gold standard for structure elucidation, interpreting spectra remains labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge to navigate the vast space of possible structures. Here, we present an AI system for rapid, automated de novo structure elucidation that combines a molecular generative model with a scientific reasoning agent. Its generative component, ChefNMR2, is an atomic flow-matching model that predicts small-molecule structures from molecular formulae and one-dimensional 1H and 13C NMR spectra. ChefNMR2-Agent augments our generative model with large language models (LLMs) to reason over and refine candidate structures. Across diverse benchmarks, ChefNMR2 substantially outperforms existing tools, offering calibrated confidence estimates and two to three orders of magnitude faster inference than frontier LLMs. We use ChefNMR2-Agent to elucidate the structures of four novel natural products, matching human-chemist accuracy in a fraction of the time. Our work demonstrates how specialized generative models and general-purpose reasoning agents can unite to solve challenging scientific inverse problems and accelerate NMR structure elucidation, thus opening new possibilities for AI-driven small-molecule discovery across diverse disciplines.
papers.title: Small molecule structure elucidation from NMR spectra with generative and reasoning models

papers.abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. While RT-qPCR of the swabs detected no active WNV or AIV infections, ELISA testing identified Orthoflavivirus antibodies in 15 of 164 sera, indicating prior exposure. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing revealed a viral landscape spanning 33 families (29 of which were identified in birds). Within this virome, DNA viruses, predominantly Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and Parvoviridae, dominated in abundance but exhibited low diversity. In contrast, the highly diverse RNA virome primarily reflected the birds dietary habits and the local habitat at the nature reserve. Notably, we report the first detection of Bole tick virus 4 (BoTV4) in Switzerland, identified in several ticks (Rhipicephalus turanicus) associated with long-distance migrants. This member of the newly established Pestiviridae family is already established in parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This study provides the first active surveillance of the wild bird virome in Switzerland. Our findings establish a framework for the early detection of emerging viruses and underscore the role of migratory birds as dispersal vectors for ticks and novel tick-borne viruses.
papers.title: Silent travelers: the potential of migratory birds and their ticks to introduce emerging viruses into Switzerland

papers.abstract: Nuclear DNA viruses colonize host genomes already structured into complex spatial domains, yet whether established spatial boundaries dictate viral progression remains unresolved--in part because sequence composition and transcriptional output are intertwined in animal models. Here, we tracked productive lytic infection of the marine picoeukaryote Ostreococcus tauri by the giant double-stranded DNA prasinovirus OtV5, recording transcription, accessibility, and 3D contact dynamics across parallel time courses. Although total cellular transcript pools collapsed 18-fold by 10 h post-infection, the host transcriptional shutdown, decay of insulation, early chromatin opening, and viral DNA positioning were all bounded by architectural coordinates defined prior to viral arrival. Across two low-GC outlier domains, chromatin accessibility spiked rapidly, spatial insulation eroded, and loci exhibited relative upregulation by 6 hpi, with the smaller outlier region retaining elevated transcript levels per cell compared to the rest of the genome. Unexpectedly, viral DNA was preferentially depleted from these accessible outlier cores, contacting instead the standard-GC telomeric flanks situated immediately beyond the pre-existing spatial boundaries. Domain identity, rather than local accessibility or active host expression, thus governs viral positioning, demonstrating that pre-existing nuclear architecture partitions the physical and transcriptional takeover of the host cell.
papers.title: Pre-existing genome architecture partitions viral takeover in the smallest free-living eukaryote

papers.abstract: Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus (IHNV) is a WOAH-notifiable pathogen responsible for severe acute disease in salmonids at temperatures ranging from 4 to 14{degrees}. At higher water temperatures, the disease is generally associated with reduced mortality and lower viral replication. In the context of climate change, rising water temperatures could favor the emergence of thermotolerant strains while representing a major physiological and metabolic stress potentially altering fish's immune responses.
