Dab2, an endocytic adaptor linking clathrin to scavenger receptors, controls the biogenesis and function of ETs by recruiting unconventional myosin Myo6 and by influencing dynamin activity. Our findings suggest that continuous pinching of vesicles from ETs allows for rapid, high-capacity internalization of dietary protein.
papers.title: Clathrin-coated endocytic tubules mediate rapid and selective protein absorption by lysosome-rich enterocytes

papers.abstract: Understanding the genetic changes that drove the evolution of human-specific traits is a central goal in biology. Changes in gene expression are thought to be a major source of phenotypic innovations, but identifying the underlying changes in cis-regulatory elements (CREs) along the human lineage has been difficult: functional data from great apes are scarce and unobtainable for extinct hominins, and pinpointing causal substitutions requires knowing which sequences determine CRE activity. Here, we used AlphaGenome, a sequence-to-function deep-learning model, to predict the cis-regulatory effects of ~17 million single-nucleotide substitutions specific to the human lineage and traced their consequences for gene expression evolution across 305 tissues and cell types. The 71,345 predicted cis-regulatory gains lie mostly outside human accelerated regions and arose either through creation of new CREs or, more often, through co-option of CREs ancestrally accessible in other tissues. They are also enriched for distal enhancers and for target gene functions characteristic of the corresponding tissues, suggesting that they contributed to the evolution of tissue-specific biology in humans. Genes linked to more gains were more likely to be upregulated in humans, and in silico reversion to ancestral alleles traced such upregulations to individual substitutions creating transcription factor binding motifs. Comparison with Neandertal and Denisovan genomes revealed that nearly all gains now fixed in humans predate the split from archaic hominins, yet a few modern-human-specific gains contribute substantially to gene upregulation. Our study provides a genome-wide, tissue-resolved map of cis-regulatory changes and their contribution to gene expression evolution along the human lineage.
papers.title: Reconstructing human gene regulatory evolution using deep learning

papers.abstract: Mathematical models of mutation processes often assume deterministic population growth, although biological populations are continuously subjected to random fluctuations. Here, we extend a model inspired by the classical Luria-Delbruck framework by introducing stochastic perturbations into population growth while assuming a constant mutation rate. Using Ito calculus, we derive an analytical solution for a stochastic logistic growth model with carrying capacity. By comparing the stochastic model with its deterministic counterpart, we demonstrate that random perturbations can substantially influence population variability, particularly as the population approaches its carrying capacity. While deterministic growth levels off, stochastic fluctuations persist and may become increasingly important relative to the underlying growth dynamics. The magnitude of these effects depends on the relationship between population growth and stochastic volatility. We illustrate the model using real life within-host SARS-CoV-2 infection data and discuss its implications. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic population dynamics when modelling mutation-related processes in capacity-limited microbial populations.
papers.title: Stochastic population growth and its implications for mutation dynamics under carrying capacity constraints

papers.abstract: Introduction: Arginine vasopressin receptor 2 (AVPR2) signaling regulates kidney collecting duct signaling and urinary concentration, but the kidneys cell-type-specific responses to its pharmacological inhibition and their relevance to non-cystic kidney injury remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We examined physiological and transcriptional responses to the AVPR2 antagonist Tolvaptan in uninjured male mice and assessed tissue outcomes after unilateral ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) and repeated cisplatin administration. Analyses included renal tissue osmolality measurements, single nucleus and bulk RNA sequencing of kidney tissues, quantitative PCR, in situ hybridization, and histology. Results: In uninjured kidneys, Tolvaptan reduced urine and medullary tissue osmolality and altered transcription predominantly in medullary collecting-duct populations, including lower expression of selected stress-associated and proinflammatory genes. Following IRI, Tolvaptan-treated mice exhibited attenuated expression of inflammatory and monocyte recruitment genes, reduced macrophage accumulation in the renal medulla, and diminished fibrotic remodeling. In cisplatin-induced kidney injury Tolvaptan reduced tubular injury markers and inflammatory activation in the outer medulla. Conclusions: Tolvaptan attenuates medullary tubular stress responses and post-injury inflammation and fibrosis. These findings extend the effects of pharmacological AVPR2 antagonism beyond water homeostasis to tissue-level responses in non-cystic kidney injury.
papers.title: AVPR2 antagonism with tolvaptan alters medullary cell responses and attenuates kidney injury

papers.abstract: As highly pathogenic human coronaviruses continue to emerge from zoonotic sources, understanding how host intrinsic immune responses control infection is critical for preventing severe disease. The interferon (IFN) pathway induces antiviral effectors, including the interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) Shiftless (SHFL), which restricts -1 programmed ribosomal frameshifting during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Here, we investigate a novel proviral mechanism for SHFL using loss-of-function and gain-of-function approaches. Despite its established antiviral activity, SHFL enhanced infection by SARS-CoV-2 and the seasonal coronavirus HCoV-229E by increasing cellular susceptibility to infection. SHFL further promoted coronavirus infection by reducing cellular sensitivity to IFN, potentially through modulation of JAK/STAT signaling. Finally, we demonstrate that SHFL-mediated enhancement of baseline viral susceptibility is partially dependent on the domain previously implicated in its antiviral inhibition of -1 programmed ribosomal frameshifting. In contrast, SHFL-mediated regulation of IFN signaling is independent of this domain. Together, these findings establish SHFL as a dual-function ISG with distinct proviral and antiviral activities, highlighting the complex roles of innate immune effectors during coronavirus infection.
papers.title: A novel proviral mechanism for the ISG, Shiftless, during human coronavirus infection

papers.abstract: Background Atherosclerotic plaque rupture is the leading cause of fatal atherothrombotic events, including myocardial infarction. Intimal microcalcification is a major determinant of plaque instability, but its pathogenic mechanisms remain poorly understood. The nuclear receptor Rev-erb-alpha regulates lipoprotein metabolism and inflammation. We hypothesized that it modulates atherogenesis by also controlling arterial calcification. Methods To identify regulators of vascular calcification, transcriptomic analysis of CD14+CD16- monocytes from diabetic patients with different calcium scores (ANGIOSAFE cohort) was combined with targeted analysis in calcified and non-calcified atherosclerotic plaques from diabetic and non-diabetic patients (AtheroPortal cohort) and in calcified and non-calcified areas of human endarterectomies isolated by laser capture microdissection (OPAL Cohort). Functional relevance was evaluated in 18-month-old Ldlr-/- mouse and in primary aortic vascular smooth muscle cells after targeting Rev-erb-alpha. Results In ANGIOSAFE (n=668), REV-ERB-alpha expression was lower in classical CD14+CD16- monocytes from diabetic patients with low coronary artery calcium scores. In the AtheroPortal cohort (n=968), REV-ERB-alpha expression was reduced in highly calcified plaques from diabetic patients, and laser capture microdissection confirmed lower expression in calcified compared to non-calcified areas of human endarterectomies. Rev-erb alpha-deficient Ldlr-/- mice displayed accelerated atherogenesis and calcification, with SMCs reprogrammed toward an osteochondroblastic phenotype. In vitro, Rev-erb-alpha preserved SMC identity by repressing IL-1-beta-driven transdifferentiation, notably via Spp1, Osterix and Sox9, and repressed the hyaluronidase Cemip, whose activity degrades hyaluronic acid and promotes intimal calcification. Conclusions Rev-erb-alpha restrains SMC-driven vascular calcification by suppressing osteogenic reprogramming, and may represent a therapeutic target to reduce calcification and cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients.
papers.title: Rev-erb-alpha inhibits vascular calcification by repressing osteogenic reprogramming in atherosclerosis

papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable success of new therapeutic approaches, a considerable number of melanoma patients still relapse on conventional therapies within two years and develop resistance. Alterations in metabolism, including amino acid availability and regulation of metabolic processes, have been implicated in acquired drug resistance. In this study, we developed in vitro and in vivo models of target therapy resistance (TTR) and identified a translational program that supports primary ciliogenesis in drug-resistant BRAF melanoma. We established that drug resistance enhances primary ciliogenesis, which is needed to respond and survive to combination therapy (CT). Mechanistically, impairing cilia formation (IFT88KO) rewires glutamine and aspartate metabolism. Overall, we provide a new molecular mechanism underlying therapy resistance that should be considered to tailored therapeutic strategies.
papers.title: THERAPY RESISTANCE IN MELANOMA DRIVES CILIOGENESIS AND GLUTAMINE/ASPARTATE METABOLISM DEPENDENCY

papers.abstract: Single-cell perturbation profiling is limited by cost and throughput, while computational methods remain constrained by inconsistent evaluation and underperformance relative to simple baselines. Here we present DCAF, a unified framework for single-cell perturbation simulation that that jointly addresses data validity, evaluation validity and predictive modeling. Among its three components, DCAF-data addresses the single-measurement limitation by reconstructing pre- and post-perturbation status using entropy-regularized optimal transport, and is demonstrated on both cell line and multi-cell type datasets. DCAF-criterion evaluates log fold changes in non-silenced genes to improve sensitivity to model error and robustness to zero inflation noise, validated on synthetic datasets. DCAF-model combines JEPA with explicit modeling for regulatory-dynamics modeling for interpretable prediction. Across benchmarks, DCAF outperforms state-of-the-art deep-learning methods, as well as mean and linear baselines in cross-gene, cross-cell-type and cross-region generalization. In adult Mouse brain, DCAF recapitulates known cell-type-specific regulatory heterogeneity of Dgcr8 knockdown at both cell type and gene levels. DCAF thus provides a rigorous and biologically grounded foundation for reliable perturbation simulation across development, disease and therapeutic discovery.
papers.title: DCAF: Unifying Data Validity, Evaluation Validity and Predictive Modeling for Single-cell Perturbation Simulation

papers.abstract: O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is an essential mammalian glycosyltransferase that installs O-GlcNAc onto thousands of cytosolic and nuclear proteins. Dysregulated glycosylation by OGT is associated with disease states, including cancer and neurodegeneration. However, cellular consequences of acute loss of O-GlcNAc remain poorly understood. Here, we employed a cell-permeable small molecule inhibitor of OGT, OSMI-4, coupled with transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses to characterize the effects of O-GlcNAc depletion in human cell lines. Loss of O-GlcNAc led to changes in expression of lipid metabolism genes and remodeling of the lipidome, with unsaturated phosphatidylcholines (PCs), saturated lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) and unsaturated storage lipids accumulating. We also observed increased lipid droplets. Our results suggest that polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) accumulate in the membrane under low O-GlcNAc conditions and that cells buffer this accumulation by removing PUFAs from membrane lipids and sequestering them in lipid droplets. We found that treatment with OSMI-4 sensitizes cells to ferroptosis inducers, likely because accumulated cell membrane PUFAs undergo peroxidation. Taken together, our results highlight lipid remodeling as an important process that mediates the downstream effects of loss of O-GlcNAc. It may be possible to exploit the synergy between OGT inhibitors and ferroptosis inducers for therapeutic benefit.
papers.title: Lipid Changes due to Low O-GlcNAc and the Downstream Consequences

papers.abstract: Mindfulness-based interventions are known to enhance emotion regulation and stress management, yet their neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Effective coping strategies for emotion regulation and stress management would be particularly beneficial for healthcare students, frequently exposed to highly stressful situations. Based on prior work implicating hippocampal-somatomotor dynamics in emotion regulation, we tested whether Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Life (MBCT-L) modulates hippocampal micro-coactivation patterns (CAPs) in healthcare students. In a randomized controlled study including 161 healthcare students, 57 participants (39 females; mean age: 23+/-5 years old) completed resting-state fMRI before and after the 8-weeks intervention and were allocated to MBCT-L (N = 24) or a no-intervention control (N = 33) condition. Hippocampus-seeded CAPs analysis identified six recurrent patterns, including a somatomotor network. MBCT-L improved self-reported mindfulness, but no significant Group*Time interaction for hippocampus-somatomotor coactivation or resting physiological measures was found. In the MBCT-L group, higher hippocampus-somatomotor co-activity was associated with higher perceived importance of the intervention, perceived long-lasting benefits, and post-intervention mindfulness scores. This study suggests that the capacity to up-regulate hippocampus-somatomotor coactivation may index part of the individual benefit derived from mindfulness, supporting its role as a tool for emotion regulation and stress management.
papers.title: Hippocampal-somatomotor coactivation and perceived benefit following Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Life in healthcare students: An exploratory randomized study

papers.abstract: How do plants repeatedly evolve the ability to thrive in saline environments? We analyzed ~10 million protein-coding genes from 232 angiosperm genomes spanning 55 families to identify convergent genomic signatures of halophytism. Across lineages, halophytes exhibit recurrent patterns in salt-response genes, including reduced gene numbers, higher basal expression, and constrained expression variation. We identified distinct evolutionary rate patterns and independent positive selection at the same amino acid sites across halophytes, revealing molecular convergence. Comparisons of crops and their wild halophytic relatives uncover contrasting gene family trajectories in stress-response pathways. These findings challenge the idea that increased gene number is the predominant route to adaptation and reveal recurrent genomic strategies associated with halophytism, advancing understanding of convergent evolution and providing a foundation for developing salt-tolerant crops.
papers.title: Convergent genome evolution reveals shared routes to salt tolerance in flowering plants

papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are significant environmental contaminants that cause a number of adverse human health effects. Studies increasingly link exposure to PFAS with disruptions in osteoblast and osteoclast differentiation and function, reduced bone mineral density (BMD), and negative impacts on skeletal structure. In vivo studies on the effects of PFAS on bone health remain limited, with none investigating the impacts in mice expressing human peroxisome proliferator activated receptor (PPAR). Given PFASs ability to interact with the peroxisome proliferator activated receptor family and their importance in bone health, we present work investigating the effects of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) exposure and PPAR genotype (mouse, human or null) on bone quality across two exposure periods (6 and 14 weeks) in mice fed a human relevant diet. In both exposure scenarios, the serum PFOA concentrations were {approx} 50 {micro}g/mL, similar to a highly exposed fluorochemical worker. We began by establishing the liver phenotype across exposures and genotypes. Across genotypes and exposure timing, PFOA increased liver to body weight ratios, but the contribution of increased triglycerides was reduced at 14 weeks. Exposure to PFOA increased hepatic PPAR-dependent gene expression (Acox) in both sexes and exposure periods, but only in mPPAR mice. The effect of PFOA on hepatic CAR- and PXR-dependent gene expression (Cyp2b10 and Cyp3a11, respectively) was more complex; with sex-, genotype-, and exposure timing-dependent differences. Trabecular and cortical bone parameters were not impacted by PFOA treatment, but genotype was a significant factor across sexes and exposure periods. mPPAR mice had higher trabecular tissue mineral density at 9 and 20 weeks of age than hPPAR mice, but the lower trabecular bone volume evident at 9 weeks of age resolved at 20 weeks of age. mPPAR mice had higher cortical tissue mineral density and bone volume than hPPAR and PPAR null mice. Analysis of serum markers of osteoblast and osteoclast activity following 14 weeks of exposure to PFOA revealed a PPAR-dependent decrease in PINP but no effect on CTX. Our results reveal the importance of PPAR genotype for bone quality parameters and emerging evidence of the effect of PFOA on osteoblast activity. Given the unusual mouse bone quality model (sv/129 background), this work underscores the need for future in vivo research shifts to investigate the effects of PFAS on in bone quality.
papers.title: PPARα genotype impacts bone quality and perfluorooctanoic acid-induced effects

papers.abstract: Visual perception unfolds through sequential eye movements, yet computational models of episodic memory typically assume that event representations already exist. Here, we propose that sequential gaze sampling does not simply supply memory with visual information, but helps construct the representations that are subsequently stored and retrieved. We introduce a computational model in which successive fixation-dependent samples are integrated into an evolving internal representation before one-shot storage in associative memory. Within individual elements, successive samples progressively individuate the representation; across elements, transitions promote relational integration. Crucially, both effects arise from the same history-dependent updating process where each new sample is integrated into a state already shaped by what came before. As a result, sampling history becomes embedded in the memory representation itself. Changing the order of otherwise identical samples alters both the resulting representation and element-specific retrieval, while reinstating the original sampling trajectory facilitates access to the stored memory. Model-neural analysis further show that changes in the model's evolving representations correspond to neural representational dynamics in lateral temporal cortex. Together, these findings support sequential sampling as a candidate computational process for constructing representations available to episodic memory, linking ongoing perceptual sampling to subsequent memory formation and retrieval.
papers.title: Sequential Sampling as a Computational Principle of Episodic Memory

papers.abstract: The tobamovirus Tomato brown rugose fruit virus (ToBRFV) has rapidly emerged as a major threat to tomato production worldwide, overcoming the widely deployed Tm-22-mediated resistance and challenging current strategies for tobamovirus disease control. The tomato coiled-coil nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (CC-NLR) immune receptor HREZ confers resistance to ToBRFV. However, the activation mechanism underlying HREZ recognition of ToBRFV remains unclear. Here, we show that HREZ is activated by the movement protein (MP) of ToBRFV and induces hypersensitive cell death. Upon activation, HREZ assembles into a higher-order oligomeric complex, with AlphaFold 3 modelling supporting a pentameric resistosome model. Phylogenetic analysis places HREZ in a CC-NLR lineage distinct from the canonical tobamovirus resistance receptor Tm-22, consistent with convergent evolution of tobamovirus MP recognition. Comparative analysis of eight MPs from the family Virgaviridae reveals that HREZ and Tm-22 have distinct recognition spectra. Four distinct tobamovirus MPs that activate HREZ also promote its assembly into a higher-order oligomeric complex. Together, these findings show how phylogenetically distinct CC-NLRs can converge on the same viral target while retaining distinct recognition breadth and provide a foundation for developing resistance strategies against current and emerging tobamoviruses.
papers.title: Convergent recognition of tobamovirus movement proteins by phylogenetically distinct NLR immune receptors

papers.abstract: As benchmarks saturate, traditional validation methods fail to capture the probabilistic representations of genomic foundation models. This study probes self-supervised generalists (NTv3 650M, Evo2 40B, Genos 10B) alongside task-specific specialists (SpliceAI, AlphaGenome, Borzoi) using a mechanistically focused paradigm centered on expert-curated single-nucleotide substitutions within the splicing regions of the exon-rich OPA1 gene. Extending this analysis across the broader corpus of OPA1 mutations, variants of uncertain significance (VUS), and an independent 65-gene dataset of spliceogenic mutations demonstrates that foundation models not only match task-specific networks, but also generalize across mutation types. Training data scale, genetic diversity, and evolutionary context are key for capturing RNA splicing syntax, whereas sparse routing may constrain performance. Mechanistically, foundation models exhibit a compute asymmetry: Evo2 40B frontloads compute into massive parameter scale to resolve single-nucleotide variants within a narrow 425-bp context window, whereas the bidirectional NTv3 650M model and the Genos 10B mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture backload compute to inference, requiring spatial logit aggregation and vast context windows of up to 94 kb. Furthermore, accuracy may benefit from locus-specific thresholding rather than mutation-class calibration, exposing representation boundaries of the self-supervised models.
papers.title: Probing Genomic Foundation Models with Splice-Variant Perturbations

papers.abstract: How do psychedelic drugs alter human brain function? Answering this question relies on our ability to understand how information is stored, transferred, and transformed across the cortex. Here, we leverage a precise mathematical framework for multivariate information decomposition to construct the first comprehensive picture of these processes across five compounds: LSD, psilocybin, ketamine, DMT and 5-MeO-DMT (N=80). We provide a formal and empirical explanation of major prior results, revealing sets of competing underlying phenomena masked by extant approaches. We extend this analysis to novel higher-order phenomena, and we demonstrate how all of these observations can emerge from a minimal generative model in which neural populations operate with reduced self-coupling. In sum, our results suggest that the psychedelic brain is one in which cortical populations become alike, but not necessarily together. This has important implications for models of how psychedelics reorganize brain dynamics to alter subjective experience and alleviate mental health conditions.
papers.title: Psychedelics restructure information in the human brain

papers.abstract: Olfactory function declines with age, and olfactory impairment predicts subsequent cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease. Age-related impairments in odor identification and discrimination implicate central olfactory circuits in both mice and humans, but it remains unclear where in the processing hierarchy aging alters neural function. To resolve this, we acquired simultaneous Neuropixels recordings from olfactory bulb (OB) and piriform cortex (PCx) in young and old mice during awake, head-fixed odor presentation, allowing us to examine successive processing stages within individual animals. Our recordings revealed a shift toward greater excitation in both regions and reduced inhibitory neuron activity in PCx. Aging also restructured odor-evoked local field potential (LFP) oscillations within and across regions, with strongly elevated beta power and coherence. Population odor representations were less discriminable in OB but not PCx, constituting the clearest neural analog of previously reported discrimination deficits. Single-unit, LFP, and population measures did not collapse onto a single axis using dimensionality reduction, indicating that several partly independent processes reshape central olfactory dynamics with aging. Together, these findings identify central circuit excitation/inhibition and oscillatory imbalances that parallel age-related olfactory dysfunction despite largely preserved odor responsivity.
papers.title: Aging reshapes odor-evoked dynamics in central olfactory circuits

papers.abstract: Phytoplankton sustain all marine ecosystems and are key components of the carbon cycle being responsible for ~50% of the global primary production. A major hypothesis to explain their coexistence with highly efficient lytic viruses is antiviral resistance. Although intracellular and extracellular mechanisms have been shown to underly such resistance and while its determinism is commonly associated to a genomic polymorphism or a (random or virus induced) phenotypic plasticity, comparisons of the impact of those molecular determinants on phytoplankton-virus population dynamic are genuinely lacking. We combined 12 epidemiological models with an unprecedented set of parameter estimates derived from experimental studies of the ubiquitous species Ostreococcus tauri and its prasinoviruses to provide such comprehensive predictions. We show that 'bet-hedging' strategies corresponding to random phenotypic switches between susceptible and resistant cells provide the strongest barrier to virus emergence. When such resistance is associated to intracellular mechanisms the virus' R0 is at least halved because of the strong 'dilution effect' produced by the 'dead-end' hosts. In addition, once the virus has spread, both random and virus-induced phenotypic plasticity strongly stabilize the otherwise 'boom and bust' phytoplankton-virus dynamics, which is highly consistent with the experimental dynamics observed for such interactions.
papers.title: How do the molecular determinants of antiviral resistance shape the dynamic of phytoplankton-virus interaction?

papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) deep learning models predict genome-wide functional profiles directly from DNA sequences and have significantly advanced our understanding of gene regulation. However, existing S2F models are fundamentally constrained by their initial training datasets, and no single model encompasses the full spectrum of cell types, clinical conditions, and cellular states, while training new models de novo is nontrivial. Here, we develop Kidzoi, a kidney cell-type-specific S2F model obtained by transfer learning from the pretrained model Borzoi using single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from human kidney tissue. Kidzoi accurately predicts cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility and improves regulatory variant effect prediction in proximal tubule cells by up to 23% in terms of AUROC over existing models. Furthermore, Kidzoi effectively prioritizes genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapped causal variants associated with kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate based on both creatinine and cystatin C; eGFRcr-cys) while resolving their cell-type specificity. Systematic ablation of flanking sequence indicates that a local context of 32-64kbp, representing only 6-12% of the full model input, captures most of the information needed for variant effect prediction. Finally, we show that a multi-task model achieves comparable performance to single-task models at a substantially reduced computational cost.
papers.title: Kidzoi Enables Cell-Type-Specific Regulatory Activity and Variant Effect Prediction in Kidney

papers.abstract: To increase perceptual precision, the brain is hypothesized to perform Bayesian inference, evaluating sensory input within the context of the statistical structure of the environment. The cerebellum is a strong candidate for this computation in interval timing: its integrity is essential for precise timing and supports encoding temporal statistics in animals. However, how the sensory input is combined with prior knowledge within this circuit remains unknown. To examine this, we tested patients with cerebellar degeneration and matched controls on duration reproduction tasks with varying prior distributions. Patients showed the signatures of Bayesian inference, but with greater timing variability, stronger regression toward the mean, and slower updating of the prior. We developed a model of the cerebellar microcircuit in which Purkinje cell plasticity over a granule cell temporal basis set provides a shared substrate for learning the prior and performing the inference. Simulations of cerebellar degeneration showed an output approximated a Bayesian observer with an intact prior and a noisier likelihood. This model provided a good fit of the patients' behavior over a wide range of parameter space. These results suggest a critical role for the human cerebellum in Bayesian inference, supporting optimally timed behavior even under extensive neuropathology.
papers.title: Impaired representation of temporal statistics in cerebellar degeneration

papers.abstract: Biobank-scale genomic analyses are increasingly constrained by computational costs, as hundreds of thousands to millions of samples and variants must be analyzed together. The genotype representation graph (GRG) compactly encodes population genetic variation to accelerate computation, but its graph-traversal implementation does not exploit modern accelerators. This work introduces Mikado, a methodology that expresses GRG-based computation using sparse linear algebra primitives. Under a reverse topological ordering, the GRG adjacency matrix is strictly block-lower-triangular, and the genotype matrix-vector product becomes a sparse triangular solve, decomposed into a pipelined sequence of blocked sparse matrix-vector multiplies. Because GRGs are shallow by construction, the solve completes in only a few sequential stages, exposing fine-grained parallelism and enabling vendor-optimized sparse primitives on GPUs. On the full All of Us cohort, Mikado computes principal components in minutes, where PLINK2 cannot complete one chromosome in 72 hours, and runs genome-wide BOLT-LMM-inf in under 19 minutes on one GPU, where the official BOLT-LMM analysis would be impractical. Our two-stage reformulation is independent of the hardware: the same code runs unchanged across GPU architectures and, on CPUs, gives a 1.8x single-threaded speedup over the existing GRG library together with multi-threaded scaling, providing a scalable, portable approach for population genetics as biobanks continue to grow.
papers.title: Sparse Linear Algebra Accelerates Genotype Representation Graph Computation at Biobank Scale

papers.abstract: For datasets with thousands of neurons and images, vision transformers have proven successful at predicting neural responses to stimuli. However, they are expected to underperform in low-data regimes, where CNNs and Gaussian processes are considered more effective. We ask whether transformers can be made competitive for small-scale neural prediction, and show that underperformance in this regime can be overturned with the right inductive bias. We equip a vision transformer with a differentiable per-neuron circular crop in feature space. The crop is centered on each neuron's receptive field, with a radius selected per neuron, so the model only sees the small image region that drives that neuron instead of the whole image. This makes the cost of attention scale with the size of the receptive field rather than with the size of the image. A single transformer stack is shared across all neurons: each neuron's specificity resides in the crop, not in the architecture. We call this model circular receptive-field vision transformer (CiRF-ViT). We evaluate it on small multi-electrode-array recordings of mouse and salamander retinas: a mouse preparation of 41 ganglion cells and two salamander preparations totaling 49 ganglion cells, each with only a few thousand stimulus-response pairs, two orders of magnitude below the scale at which transformers are typically trained. Against CNN and Gaussian-process baselines, CiRF-ViT reaches the highest mean explained variance on both datasets (0.94 on mouse, 0.95 on salamander). Probed with the local spike-triggered average (LSTA), a zero-shot test of context-dependent, nonlinear stimulus sensitivity, CiRF-ViT reproduces the qualitative polarity inversion that a linear model cannot capture by construction. A biologically grounded, per-neuron locality prior is therefore enough to make transformers competitive for neural prediction well below their usual data scale, while matching the reference models on an established functional signature of the retina's nonlinear computation.
papers.title: Biologically grounded locality priors close the data gap for vision transformers in neural prediction

papers.abstract: Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) offers a wearable, movement-tolerant alternative to conventional cryogenic MEG, placing sensors closer to the scalp and, in principle, improving sensitivity to deep sources. This is advantageous for examining subcortical structures that are affected by ageing, disorders and disease, such as the hippocampus. However, it remains unclear whether well-established activity (such as the attenuation of theta oscillations during the imagination of novel scenes) can be recovered from the medial temporal lobe (MTL) with OPM-MEG, and whether an individual structural MRI is required. Here, fifteen adults completed a scene imagination task. Initially we applied a 12-parameter template warping coregistration pipeline to the full sample. Following source reconstruction, we recovered the expected attenuation of theta (4-8 Hz) power during scene imagination compared to a counting baseline, with a significant cluster of activity peaking in the left parahippocampal gyrus. The clusters centre of mass was localised to the left hippocampus (t = -3.55, p = 0.048, whole-brain FWE-corrected) and was mostly confined to the left medial temporal lobe. We further supported our findings by using an individual T1-weighted MRI reconstruction pipeline in six participants who had these scans available. The two approaches produced similar whole-brain topographies and localised the peak MTL theta effect to left hippocampus, with temporal-lobe conjunction centroids 3-mm apart. These findings provide evidence that the theta attenuation of the scene construction network can be recovered at the group level with OPM-MEG, without an individual MRI.
papers.title: MRI-free OPM-MEG recovers medial temporal lobe theta during scene imagination

papers.abstract: The DUP240 gene family in Saccharomyces cerevisiae encodes ten proteins containing two transmembrane domains (TMDs). Despite decades of interest driven by their high sequence similarity, little functional information exists regarding whether Dup240 family members share redundant or distinct roles. In this study, we combined computational modelling, subcellular localisation, and functional assays across the family to identify shared and unique features. Computational modelling revealed that the Dup240 member Ktd1 possesses a unique structural element adjacent to its TMD region. Out of six successfully localised family members, Ktd1 was the only protein predominantly targeted to the vacuolar membrane and the sole Dup240 required for defence against the K28 killer toxin. Computational predictions further indicated that Ktd1 undergoes extensive post-translational regulation, containing multiple validated phosphorylation sites. Screening potential regulatory kinases and phosphatases identified several enzymes required for K28 defence, which were independently validated using liquid-based toxin sensitivity assays. A multicopy suppressor screen demonstrated that KTD1 overexpression rescued K28 sensitivity across most enzyme mutant backgrounds, confirming Ktd1 acts downstream or in parallel to many factors. However, the phosphatase Sit4 and the kinase Hog1 scored as most likely co-factors in Ktd1 mediated defence. Live-cell fluorescence imaging of these two enzymes revealed no dramatic spatial re-localisation during K28 exposure, suggesting that phospho-dependent regulation of Ktd1-mediated defence may occur through transient signalling events. Together, these findings identify Ktd1 as the central effector of the Dup240 family in toxin defence and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding Dup240 regulation.
papers.title: Ktd1 is a phospho-regulated member of the Dup240 family that mediates defence against killer toxin K28

papers.abstract: Protein dimerization networks can implement biochemical logic, but their practical realization has largely relied on designing or optimizing protein-protein interaction affinities, creating a major barrier to experimental implementation. Here, we ask whether computation can instead be extracted from interaction networks already generated by evolution. We repurpose experimentally characterized basic leucine zipper (bZIP) interactomes from Nematostella vectensis, Ciona intestinalis, and Homo sapiens as programmable biochemical logic substrates while keeping all measured binding affinities fixed. Using mass-action equilibrium modeling coupled with genetic optimization, we identify accessory monomer concentrations and output dimers that reconfigure these natural networks to perform Boolean operations. Unengineered bZIP clusters computed up to 15 of the 16 possible two-input Boolean functions, including nonlinearly separable XOR and XNOR operations, and up to 13 functions within a 17-gate three-input benchmark. Computational versatility depended on network architecture and input selection, revealing design constraints inherent to natural interactomes. Stochastic perturbation analysis further showed that many optimized configurations preserve logic-state separation under substantial concentration variability. Finally, a nondimensional scaling framework provides a route for translating simulated concentration regimes toward cell-free implementation. Together, these results demonstrate computationally that natural protein interaction networks contain latent, evolutionarily encoded computational capacity that can be accessed through concentration tuning rather than de novo protein engineering.
papers.title: Programmable Biochemical Logic Computation Through Repurposing Natural bZIP Protein Interaction Networks

papers.abstract: In muscle cells, desmin intermediate filaments form a cytoskeletal network that maintains the structural integrity and mechanical coupling of myofibrils. Dominant missense mutations in desmin cause myopathies characterized by intracellular protein aggregation. To explore the process of aggregate formation, we investigate the assembly kinetics of wild-type desmin and four disease-associated variants (N342D, L345P, R350P, and R406W) using dual-wavelength stopped-flow spectroscopy, complemented by atomic force microscopy and molecular dynamics simulations. At low ionic strength, all proteins form uniform tetramers. Increasing the ionic strength initiates assembly by rapid lateral association of tetramers into unit-length filaments (ULFs), followed by longitudinal elongation and radial filament compaction. R406W forms ULFs with wild-type-like kinetics, whereas N342D, L345P, and R350P exhibit delayed lateral assembly. After short filaments have formed, all four mutants diverge from productive filament maturation, but through distinct pathways. Quantitative analysis of atomic force microscopy images together with kinetic modelling of the spectroscopic data shows that wild-type filaments elongate continuously, whereas R406W filaments progressively associate into fibrillar clusters and cease elongating. By contrast, N342D, L345P, and R350P rapidly collapse into globular complexes that subsequently coalesce into larger aggregates. Molecular dynamics simulations indicate that the mutations differentially destabilize coil 2, which leads to local structural perturbations and mutation-specific assembly defects. Together, these findings identify early filament maturation - when elongating ULF-derived filaments would normally undergo radial compaction to form stable, mature filaments - as a critical time point in desmin assembly. At this stage, pathogenic mutations redirect the internal reorganization of the filament from productive stabilization toward mutation-specific structural collapse and aggregation.
papers.title: Desmin Mutations Disrupt Filament Elongation and Drive Polymorphic Aggregation

papers.abstract: Blood-based DNA methylation is widely used as a molecular surrogate for traits ranging from circulating protein and metabolite levels to biological aging, but whether the CpGs driving these models reflect genuine gene regulation or statistical convenience is unresolved. Training elastic-net models using the expression of 77 T cell genes across 333 matched T-cell enriched blood samples, we show that predictability is governed by regulatory mode: genes associated with differentiation and lineage-identity are strongly predictable, whereas dynamically regulated genes encoding cytokines and immune checkpoint ligands are not. The predictive CpGs are neither at the gene promoter nor at master-regulator binding sites; instead, the signal is carried by gene-specific sets of distal CpGs enriched within T-cell enhancer chromatin states distributed throughout the genome. Methylation-predicted gene expression validated against directly measured NanoString values in an independent 228-sample cancer cohort, remaining highly concordant for lineage genes but only weakly concordant for stimulus-responsive checkpoint ligands, confirming the lineage-versus-stimulus divide independently of the training cohort. In short, how far methylation can substitute for direct measurement depends on a genes regulatory biology rather than modeling choices; the on-gene control and chromatin-state audit introduced here offer a general way to test this for any methylation-based biomarker.
papers.title: Regulatory mode and enhancer architecture determine limits of blood DNA methylation as a molecular proxy

papers.abstract: The evolutionary mechanisms leading to nonfunctional trait loss are not well understood. Some Arabidopsis thaliana populations display incomplete loss of short stamens, floral organs that do not contribute significantly to seed set in this species. In nature, short stamen number is correlated with ovule number and flowering time, suggesting that tight linkage or pleiotropy with these traits could drive stamen number evolution. To investigate the role of colocalized QTLs in short stamen number evolution and the repeatability of QTL co-localization between replicate mapping populations, we performed QTL mapping of stamen number, ovule number, and flowering time for two sets of recombinant inbred lines (RILs), Belm-12 x Roda-47 and Tsu-1 x Kas-1. All three traits were correlated in Belm-12 x Roda-47 RILs, but none were correlated in Tsu-1 x Kas-1 RILs. For both stamen and ovule number, some QTLs were unique to each RIL set and others were shared. Notably, for Belm-12 x Roda-47 RILs, we mapped QTLs affecting ovule and short stamen number to a region of chromosome 5 that also affects flowering time. For Tsu-1 x Kas-1 RILs, we identified the same chromosome 5 region as a short stamen number QTL, but ovule number and flowering time QTLs map to other genomic regions. Tests for pleiotropy revealed that the flowering time and short stamen number QTLs on chromosome 5 in Belm-12 x Roda-47 are likely separate QTLs, linked but not pleiotropic, but each may have pleiotropic effects on ovule number. Thus, the large-effect stamen number QTL on chromosome 5 was consistent between crosses, but only in Belm-12 x Roda-47 does this QTL co-localize with the other two traits.
papers.title: Shared QTLs underlie loss of a conserved trait in replicate mapping populations of Arabidopsis thaliana

papers.abstract: Centrosomes organize microtubules, coordinate ciliogenesis, and support accurate cell division. At the mature mother centriole, distal and subdistal appendages confer specialized functions in ciliary docking, microtubule organization, and intracellular trafficking. Nuclear distribution element 1 (NDE1) is a centrosome-associated regulator of dynein-dependent processes and ciliogenesis, but its nanoscale organization and contribution to centrosome architecture are poorly understood. Here, using expansion microscopy and STED super-resolution imaging, we show that endogenous NDE1 forms a ring-like structure at the subdistal appendages in mouse embryonic fibroblasts and human RPE-1 cells. NDE1 occupies an intermediate radial position between the more centriole-proximal CEP128 layer and the more peripheral NIN (ninein) layer. Depletion of ODF2 or CEP128 reduces centrosomal NDE1, whereas CEP170 depletion has little effect. Conversely, NDE1 depletion impairs NIN centrosomal enrichment, positioning NDE1 downstream of ODF2 and CEP128 and upstream of NIN within the subdistal appendage assembly hierarchy. NDE1 depletion compromises centrosome integrity, reduces the centrosomal enrichment of core centriolar proteins, increases the separation between paired centrioles, and generates ectopic foci containing multiple centriolar markers. Loss of NDE1 also disrupts pericentriolar material organization and impairs the establishment of focused, centrosome-associated microtubule arrays. Together, our findings establish NDE1 as a subdistal appendage-associated factor that supports centrosome architecture and microtubule-organizing activity. More broadly, they support an emerging view of subdistal appendages as a molecularly layered platform in which distinct but cooperating components connect mother centriole maturation to microtubule organization, ciliary regulation, and intracellular trafficking.
papers.title: NDE1 Localizes to the Subdistal Appendages to Maintain Centrosome Integrity and Microtubule Organization

papers.abstract: A changing abiotic environment may affect the fitness and performance of an organism directly by challenging its environmental tolerance (related to its fundamental niche), or indirectly by modifying the abundance of other species it interacts with, and/or the strength of their interactions (related to its realized niche). The strength of an interaction may itself depend on how well each of the involved species performs across environments. However, there is a dearth of studies investigating how the intrinsic fitness of each interacting species covaries with the intensity of their interaction across an abiotic environmental gradient. We addressed this question in a hypersaline consumer-resource system: the microalga Dunaliella spp. grazed by the brine shrimp Artemia franciscana. We exposed four Dunaliella strains to a range of salinities, from just below to much above seawater, with or without brine shrimps. We tracked their population sizes over time and the survival of their grazers, to estimate basic parameters of a Lotka-Volterra model. We found that the intrinsic growth rate of algae, the survival rate of grazers, and the per-capita grazing rate, all varied with salinity and algal strain. Significant interactions between strain and salinity further revealed that these ecological responses to salinity are evolvable. Together with correlations between demographic parameters across salinity, this suggests that predation may influence the evolution of salinity tolerance curves, blurring the line between the fundamental and realized niches.
papers.title: Linking the fundamental and realized niches in ahypersaline consumer-resource system

papers.abstract: Defects in lysosomal lipid handling provoke fatal disorders presenting neurovisceral symptoms with variable onset and life spans. A prime example is Niemann-Pick type C disease (NPCD), where export of cholesterol and other lipids from the endosomal-lysosomal system is impaired due to variants of either NPC intracellular cholesterol transporter 1 (NPC1) or NPC intracellular cholesterol transporter 2 (NPC2). Therapeutic options for NPCD are limited to palliative care and disease-modifying drugs, and there is an unmet need for new treatments. Based on positive effects in patient-derived fibroblasts in vitro, we explored here how inhibition of bromodomain and extra-terminal domain (BET) proteins, a family of histone acetylation readers, affects a well-established mouse model bearing the frequent I1061T variant of NPC1. To this end, we used employed intraperitoneal administration of the blood-brain-barrier penetrating drug JQ1 or vehicle (dimethylsulfoxide), and gauged drug effects based on weight, biomarker levels and quantitative assessment of motor coordination.Treatment of mice with JQ1 induced beneficial effects on some outcome measures, notably a transient increase in weight, reduction of liver cholesterol, and improvements in the footprint test, but these effects occurred only in male but not in female mice. Our results indicate bromodomain proteins as potential therapeutic drug target for NPCD and reveal sex-dependent BET protein signaling in mice.
papers.title: Effects of bromodomain protein inhibition in a mouse model of Niemann-Pick type C disease

papers.abstract: How do leader and follower roles shape the brain mechanisms that support coordinated action between people? This question has therapeutic relevance for conditions such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder, where the capacity for reciprocal social coordination is a defining vulnerability. Here, we propose a tetradic framework and examine sensorimotor coordination in 16 healthy adult pairs (15 included in EEG analyses) using dual-brain EEG hyperscanning and a 2x2 within-subject design crossing Role (Leader/Follower) and Condition (Mirroring/Matching). Mirroring required resonance with a partner's movement; Matching required its controlled transformation. This contrast was designed to dissociate automatic from controlled coordination. Behaviourally, Mirroring produced a robust Follower reaction-time advantage: pooling an independent behavioural-only cohort (combined N=64) revealed a smaller Leader advantage, consistent with role-dependent attention-inhibition gating. At the neural level, tonic power and significant phasic condition clusters were greater during Matching than Mirroring, while role-dependent phasic clusters suggested an anticipatory sequence around Leader responses and post-response gating and rebound around Follower responses. Information-theoretic decomposition identified Leader-unique predictive information in superior temporal regions and a separate frontal-pole interaction, Follower-unique predictive information in insular and superior frontal regions, sparse Synergy in the right rostral anterior cingulate cortex, and Redundancy spanning multiple cortical regions. These findings characterize tetradic coordination within dyads as a multiscale, role-asymmetric architecture in which top-down predictive control and bottom-up adaptive regulation are functionally dissociable. The tetradic framework provides a scaffold for this dissociation, and the role-specific signatures it reveals may offer candidate biomarkers for clinical populations in whom interpersonal coordination is disrupted.
papers.title: Tetradic Dynamics of Dyadic Sensorimotor Coordination: A Multiscale EEG Hyperscanning Study

papers.abstract: Food webs become progressively sparser as species richness increases, yet the number of interactions grows faster than linearly, placing communities between the limiting expectations of constant degree and constant connectance. Similar scaling has also been documented in other interaction networks, but whether they share a common architectural regime, and what general principle could generate it, remain unresolved. Here, we show that 1,533 ecological networks spanning different interaction types broadly converge on an intermediate link--species scaling regime, with an overall exponent of 1.43. We interpret this pattern through a thermodynamic trade-off in which increasing network connectivity enhances signal propagation while reducing the diversity of independent modes contributing to the network's response to perturbations. Optimizing this trade-off yields a scaling exponent of 1.45, closely matching the empirical estimate, while randomly adding or removing interactions generally reduces thermodynamic efficiency in empirical networks. These results support a propagation--response-diversity trade-off as a plausible systems-level principle underlying how ecological network complexity grows with diversity.
papers.title: Ecological networks balance connectivity with flexibility to perturbations

papers.abstract: Conventional pipelines for differential expression analysis in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data first cluster individual cells and then test for differentially expressed genes between the resulting clusters. Using the same data for clustering and testing, however, poses a selective inference problem and can result in overconfidence in differences that may not reflect true biological variation. We introduce StabCell, a stability selection framework which integrates clustering and detection of differentially expressed marker genes. By repeatedly performing clustering and differential expression analysis on complementary pairs of random subsamples, StabCell assesses clustering and marker stability, yielding a stable clustering, cell-specific stability scores, and sets of stable marker genes. In simulations, we demonstrate that StabCell generally maintains empirical per-family error rate (PFER) below prespecified thresholds, selecting fewer false positive marker genes than the conventional approach, especially in cases with low signal-to-noise ratio and low sequencing depth. Simultaneously, StabCell provides competitive marker detection performance compared to alternative approaches. An application to a cell differentiation dataset from induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs) to cardiomyocytes illustrates that StabCell can reduce overclustering and prioritize biologically meaningful marker genes, improving the robustness and interpretability of scRNA-seq analyses.
papers.title: StabCell: Stability selection for clustering and marker detection in single-cell RNA sequencing

papers.abstract: The classic psychedelic psilocybin elicits long-lasting neural plasticity and behavioral effects, but prior studies largely examined stress-naive animals. Using longitudinal imaging, we show that psilocybin increases dendritic spine density in frontal cortical neurons and facilitates fear extinction after chronic restraint stress, demonstrating psilocybin's effects in a translationally relevant mouse model.
papers.title: Structural plasticity and enhanced fear extinction following psilocybin in chronically stressed mice

papers.abstract: Auditory-motor learning is critical for mastering the production of complex sounds, such as speaking and playing music. It is anchored upon internal models of interactions between actions and their sensory consequences, which are fine-tuned by minimizing the errors between the predicted and received sound. Here, we investigated the neural dynamics of sensorimotor learning by manipulating sensorimotor surprisal, with high surprisal defined as unexpected changes in the mapping between actions and their auditory outcomes. Participants performed a piano-playing task in which the key-to-pitch mapping switched unpredictably among three configurations, creating a dynamic sensorimotor environment that required ongoing adaptation. At the change boundaries, a signature of violated motor-to-auditory predictions was found in the auditory evoked responses at N100, which could not be attributed to either purely auditory surprisals or motor execution errors. This prediction error is modulated by short-term context, with greater error responses following longer periods of no map change, indicating that the brain continuously tracks short-term map contexts and rapidly adapts to them. In contrast, 30 minutes of extended goal-directed training on a single key-pitch map modulated P50 amplitude only for the trained map, a modulation that can be explained by a slow, training-driven update of the sensorimotor map. Hence, while auditory predictions from motor actions can be implicitly learned within short-term contexts for rapid adaptation, the complementary process of building a reliable sensorimotor map requires targeted training sustained over time. Our approach of studying auditory-motor surprisal in time-varying sequences reveals that auditory-motor learning is fast, context-sensitive, and shaped by both short- and long-term experience.
papers.title: Auditory-motor interactions are sensitive to adaptation and learning on multiple timescales

papers.abstract: Cognitive training often aims to improve cognitive skills, but improvements in cognitive performance have been variable. One factor that has been found to predict training outcomes is the degree of modularity of functional brain networks, defined as the extent to which brain regions are more strongly connected to regions within the same functional subnetwork than to regions outside of the subnetwork. Specifically, more modular organization of functional brain networks at baseline has been associated with greater benefits from cognitive training in adults. During childhood, cognitive development is marked by a slow progression towards network integration and segregation, which together contribute to increasing modularity. Thus, network modularity might also be an important predictor of training outcomes in children. To investigate whether individual differences in network modularity predict outcomes of task-switching training in children, we examined 87 children aged 8 to 11 years who completed nine weeks of varying amounts of task-switching training. Prior to training, children showed lower network modularity than adults, in line with previously reported developmental changes in network configuration. More modular organization of functional brain networks before training was associated with higher overall accuracy during task switching and with faster improvements in integrated speed-accuracy scores, especially at the beginning of training. These results suggest that more modular functional networks might allow for faster adaptation to training demands in children and thus faster improvements with training.
papers.title: Modular functional brain network organization contributes to training-related changes in task switching in children

papers.abstract: Quantifying individual protein behavior in living mammalian tissues remains challenging. Here we introduce intravital single-molecule microscopy (iSiMM), an imaging and analysis framework that combines instant structured illumination microscopy guided tissue navigation with highly inclined and laminated optical sheet illumination. In live mice, iSiMM enables single-emitter detection and tracking of endogenously expressed fluorescently tagged proteins at 30 ms per frame. Trajectory-based modeling quantifies diffusion coefficients and model-defined bound and free fractions, while localization-density reconstructions map molecular organization. We illustrate the approach using the actomyosin cytoskeleton, resolving isoform-specific mobility and responses to physiological stimulation and genetic perturbation. Single-molecule detection in pancreas and skeletal muscle, including after in vivo transfection, further demonstrates feasibility across additional tissues and labeling strategies. iSiMM provides a framework for investigating molecular behavior in the physiological context of living mammalian tissues.
papers.title: Intravital single-molecule microscopy reveals protein kinetics in live mammalian tissues

papers.abstract: Transcription is modulated by interactions among transcription regulatory elements (TREs), including promoters and enhancers, but their underlying interaction specificities remain opaque. Here, we develop a Chromatin-Integrated, landing-pad-based Enhancer Reporter Assay, CIERA-seq, that interrogates regulatory interactions between target promoters and distal TREs (dTREs) in a controlled genomic and chromatin context. We found both promoter-derived (pdTREs) and enhancer-derived-dTREs (edTREs) exhibit enhancer activities on target promoters with a specificity that depends on factors that dTREs recruit. pdTREs are generally enriched for factors involved in the core transcription process, whereas edTREs are enriched for pioneer factors, SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers, and histone acetyltransferase EP300. To further leverage the chromatin integration system, we applied deaminase-based footprinting to profile chromatin accessibility across individual fibers containing distinct target promoter-dTRE pairs. We found that different target promoters and dTREs exhibited distinct accessibility profiles, and that dTREs could modulate the accessibility of their cognate target promoters in a transcription factor and cofactor-dependent manner. Moreover, promoter accessibility was positively associated with transcriptional activity, linking dTRE-mediated changes in local chromatin accessibility to functional transcriptional output. Overall, our CIERA-seq assays and deamination-based footprinting assays support a model where dTREs activate target promoters constrained at different rate limiting steps in transcription by supplying complementary components of the transcription regulatory machinery.
papers.title: Molecular features underlying functional and structural interactions between diverse transcription regulatory elements in a chromosomal context

papers.abstract: Recent advances in spatial omics enable high-resolution, multiplexed imaging of RNA and protein expression, but cell annotation remains challenging, particularly in complex tissues with numerous markers or rare cell types. Here, we present QuantCell, a machine learning framework that leverages quantitative imaging data to improve annotation derived from qualitative profiles. QuantCell evaluates multiple models and applies a user-defined false discovery rate to ensure high-confidence annotation. Using PhenoCycler imaging of mouse bone marrow, QuantCell increased annotated cells from 33.1% to 90.2% at 5% FDR, achieving 96.5% accuracy. QuantCell supports diverse imaging platforms and robustly detects rare cell populations.
papers.title: QuantCell: machine learning based cell annotation integrating qualitative and quantitative imaging profiles

papers.abstract: The integration of electroencephalography (EEG) and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) can be used to characterize temporal and spatial components of neural activity during unfolding mental experience. Here we introduce a multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with measures of continuous behavior and spontaneous mental experience. Data components, organized in Brain Imaging Dataset Structure (BIDS) format, include fMRI, EEG with carbon wire loop sensors for artifact removal, continuous performance task responses, experience sampling ratings, and mental health surveys, from 24 healthy adults. Tasks included the gradual-onset continuous performance task and resting state with intermittent experience sampling of 13 unique thought dimensions (36 repetitions, including 468 total ratings, per participant). The same protocol was completed on two different days, yielding approximately 1.33 hours of simultaneous EEG-fMRI data per individual. The dataset may be used to explore the behavioral and experiential relevance of brain activity during the wakeful resting state. The dataset also provides a means to study the reliability of relationships between fMRI and EEG features across sessions within individuals.
papers.title: A multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with repeated experience sampling

papers.abstract: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. OAC and its precursor, Barrett oesophagus (BO), are defined by substantial early heterogeneity, complicating prevention and treatment of OAC. This diversity is poorly recapitulated by current in vitro and animal model systems. We have generated 91 patient- and healthy donor- derived organoids (PDOs) spanning normal oesophagogastric tissue (n=29), BO (n=13), dysplasia (n=8) and OAC (n=41). These PDOs capture population heterogeneity and recapitulate phenotypic, genomic and transcriptomic features of their respective disease stages. We develop a single cell-derived clonal organoid (sc-organoid) approach, with which we isolate 28 additional organoid lines representing subclonal populations that are difficult to discern and maintain in bulk PDO cultures, and which may represent clones at high risk of progression. Using this platform, we demonstrate functional utility across the pre-malignant to invasive disease spectrum, including recapitulation of step-wise disease progression, subclonal phylogenetic structure, and diverse responses of OAC to systemic anti-cancer therapies and radiotherapy.
authors: Oesophageal Cancer Clinical and Molecular Stratification (OCCAMS) Consortium,
papers.title: Polyclonal and clonal organoid models of Barrett oesophagus and oesophageal adenocarcinoma reveal heterogeneity in progression and therapy response

papers.abstract: Complex environments with simultaneous change in multiple stressors is the new norm in ecosystems worldwide, and adaptive evolution will be critical for population persistence under these combined environmental challenges. Yet, how the selective complexity imposed by such stressor combinations affects the pace of evolution remains poorly understood. Using a coordinated experiment, we exposed 14 species, from bacteria to unicellular eukaryotes and plants, to single stressors versus their pairwise combinations over multiple generations, while keeping the overall stress level comparable. We find that populations evolving under combined stressors tended to have lower fitness increase, and a shallower relation between initial maladaptation and fitness gain, than populations evolving under single stressors, although this direct response depended strongly on stressor type. When assayed in the control, benign conditions, lines evolved under combined stressors had higher fitness reductions than those evolved under single stressors, with higher consistency between species than for direct evolutionary responses. Our unique coordinated experimental evolution approach provides new insights into how environmental complexity can impact the pace of evolution, together with revealing the diversity of these responses. It further highlights the importance of incorporating evolutionary dynamics into the combined-stressor research agenda.
papers.title: Adaptation to complex environments is associated with higher fitness costs under benign conditions

papers.abstract: Eph-Ephrin are powerful signaling molecules that form dimers, tetramers, and tetramer superclusters. The tetramerization mechanism - central to how these receptor-ligand molecules become activated - remains poorly understood. We find EphrinB2 is a proteinaceous chelator that binds to two juxtaposed arginine-rich electropositive pockets on the surface of EphB1 and EphB2 receptors when presented as two precisely aligned EphB-EphrinB2 dimers. This snaps the two low-affinity dimers into a high-affinity circular tetramer. We show EphrinB2 binds copper, consistent with ancestry to Cupredoxins, explaining why metal chelators such as EDTA, EGTA, and 8-hydroxyquinoline are potent tetramer inhibitors: they bind the EphB arginine-rich, copper-like pocket to compete with EphrinB2. Our findings reveal how small molecules, pH, salts, and copper dynamically modulate the kinetics of Eph-Ephrin binding and provide a mechanistic framework for therapeutic targeting of the tetramer.
papers.title: Proteinaceous Metal-Binding Eph-Ephrin Tetramerization is Modulated by Copper and Chelators

papers.abstract: Ephs and Ephrins are a large group of interacting membrane-anchored receptor-ligand molecules that form dimers, tetramers, and tetramer superclusters to become activated and signal upon cell-cell contact. While most noted for bidirectional phosphotyrosine signals in development, Ephs/Ephrins also become overexpressed and participate in chronic pathologies, including EphB1 in pain and EphB2 in fibrosis. We searched for small molecules that disrupt EphB-EphrinB receptor-ligand interactions and discovered a large set of 8-hydroxyquinoline compounds that target tetramer-driven EphB1-EphrinB2 and EphB2-EphrinB2 interactions, with less action toward the more dimer-driven EphB4-EphrinB2 interaction. The compounds are orally available, reduce EphB forward signaling and EphrinB reverse signaling, and act to blunt inflammatory pain and opioid withdrawal. Our data indicates 8-hydroxyquinolines, which are known metal-binding compounds, effectively target the high-affinity circular tetramer structure needed for bidirectional signaling.
papers.title: Eph-Ephrin Tetramerization Inhibitors Target Bidirectional Signaling to Combat Pain and Addiction

papers.abstract: An organism's survival depends on the rapid classification of sensory events as either harmful or beneficial. In mammals, this computation is partially performed by neurons in the amygdala that respond to signals with negative or positive valence. The larval zebrafish pallium is thought to contain homologs of the mammalian amygdala, isocortex, and hippocampus; however, the signals encoded by pallial neurons remain largely uncharacterized. Using two photon light sheet microscopy to image 7 to 9 day old zebrafish that express pan-neuronal GCaMP6s, we recorded calcium dynamics throughout the brain while presenting a panel of strongly aversive stimuli including infrared heat, electric shock, and a whole field looming shadow, together with milder threats including vibration, loud sound, light transitions, and a partial looming stimulus. A compact cluster of neurons in the rostrolateral dorsal pallium (Rl) responded vigorously to strongly noxious and fully looming stimuli, but not to the milder cues. In contrast, neurons in the ventromedial pallium and habenula responded to all stimuli tested. Rl neurons are characterized by high Tiam2a expression, suggesting they can be genetically accessed. Thus, our results identify a locus of negative valence neurons in the teleost pallium.
papers.title: Negative-Valence Neurons in the Larval Zebrafish Pallium

papers.abstract: Strong repeated stimulation of a neuron triggers an increase in local protein synthesis along with a change in localization of proteins, allowing the neuron to rapidly adjust its proteome in response to activity. One of these proteins, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), is involved in mediating structural and functional changes after activity. While postsynaptic CaMKII translation has been studied, very little is known about presynaptic synthesis, including its mechanisms and the functional consequences. We utilized the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) as a model to study the molecular requirements for activity-dependent synthesis along with the localization of CaMKII protein. Presynaptic-specific tagging of endogenous CaMKII demonstrates that spaced stimulation rapidly increases presynaptic CaMKII through local translation of pre-existing mRNA, independently of somatic factors. This activity-dependent synthesis requires the distal 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of the CaMKII mRNA, which is also necessary for steady-state synaptic accumulation. Additionally, we show that activity-dependent synthesis requires CaMKII T287 autophosphorylation-induced activation of the PI3K/Akt/mTor pathway. While activity-dependent redistribution of CaMKII has been previously identified, very little is known about how local synthesis and translocation may interact to define different pools of protein that may have distinct functions. We demonstrate that CaMKII with a T287D phosphomimetic mutant localizes to the synaptic membrane and pulse-chase experiments show that the localization of newly-synthesized CaMKII differs from pre-existing CaMKII, indicating neuronal activity generates spatially distinct, and likely functionally distinct, CaMKII populations which may underlie long-lasting plasticity.
papers.title: Activity drives local CaMKII synthesis and subcellular localization via autophosphorylation-dependent pathways

papers.abstract: Dysregulation of cellular metabolism is a hallmark of cancer, which remains poorly understood in adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC). Here, we dissected ACC metabolism by integrating transcriptional profiling from human and mouse ACC, targeted tissue metabolomics from a mouse ACC model, and untargeted serum metabolomics from a large patient cohort, providing cross-species validation of metabolic rewiring in ACC. This study revealed global metabolic dysregulation, involving glutamine-dependent pathways such as amino-acid and hexosamine biosynthesis, nucleotide metabolism, and glutathione biosynthesis, suggesting glutamine catabolism is a critical metabolic vulnerability in ACC. Treatment with glutamine antagonists 6-Diazo-5-Oxo-L-Norleucine (DON) and JHU-083 elicited robust anti-tumor responses. Mechanistic studies revealed DON's anti-tumor effect was primarily driven by selective inhibition of glutamine-fueled de novo nucleotide biosynthesis. Additionally, DON led to DNA damage, which yielded potent synergism with inhibition of the DNA damage response pathway. Collectively, this work highlights glutamine metabolism as a central metabolic dependency and therapeutic target in ACC.
papers.title: Glutamine antagonism suppresses tumor growth in adrenocortical carcinoma through inhibition of de novo nucleotide biosynthesis

papers.abstract: The primary cilium acts as a specialized signaling compartment that coordinates multiple developmental pathways, yet its role in regulating signaling activity during human brain development remains poorly understood. Biallelic mutations in ciliary genes cause neurodevelopmental ciliopathies such as Joubert syndrome, which are characterized by cerebellar hypoplasia and dysplasia. Here, we generated human cerebellar organoids carrying null or patient-derived mutations in RPGRIP1L, a ciliary transition zone gene associated with Joubert syndrome, to investigate how ciliary dysfunction alters human cerebellar neurogenesis. While control organoids robustly express markers of cerebellar glutamatergic and GABAergic lineages including Purkinje cells, RPGRIP1L-deficient organoids display a consistent and severe reduction in Purkinje cell markers, accompanied by impaired neurogenesis and increased progenitor proliferation. These defects coincide with prolonged overactivation of the FGF/MAPK signaling pathway. We further show that the MAPK effector pMEK1/2 localizes at the base of primary cilia, where its levels are significantly increased in RPGRIP1L-deficient cerebellar progenitors. Pharmacological inhibition of FGF receptors reduces pMEK1/2 activation at cilia base and rescues both the proliferation-neurogenesis imbalance and Purkinje lineage defects, without restoring the underlying ciliary abnormalities. Together, our findings identify the primary cilium as a compartment that refines FGF/MAPK signaling in human cerebellar progenitors, and support a model in which RPGRIP1L restrains FGF pathway activity to promote neurogenesis. These results provide a mechanism linking ciliary dysfunction to altered cerebellar development and provide new insight into the developmental origin of cerebellar impairment in neurodevelopmental ciliopathies
papers.title: Regulation of FGF/MAPK signaling at the primary cilium base controls the proliferation-neurogenesis balance in human cerebellar organoids

papers.abstract: Chlamydiosis, a sexually transmitted infection induced by Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), increases local inflammation (cytokine production, recruitment of neutrophils). Vaginal microbiota (VM) is involved in the regulation of local immune responses and STI acquisition where Lactobacillus spp are associated with protection. In this study, the VM of cynomolgus macaques was enriched with Lactobacillus crispatus after local metronidazole treatment followed by repeated intravaginal inoculations of CT. Metronidazole treatment induced drastic VM modifications (decrease abundance of several anaerobes and increase of natural Lactobacillus spp ). After CT exposure, a non-persisting CT infection and no association between Lactobacillus crispatus enrichment and a lower CT susceptibility were detected. However, serum specific anti-CT IgG production was higher in treated animals. High concentration of blood cytokines after CT infection was observed in untreated animals, whereas treated animals exhibited an increased production of cervicovaginal cytokines. Blood neutrophils were more mature and activated after CT infection in both groups. These results suggest an efficient local immune response associated with a controlled systemic inflammation (low cytokine production and higher anti-CT IgG titer) upon CT infection in Lactobacillus crispatus treated animals. This study confirmed that VM composition can be a powerful tool to modulate local immune responses to STIs.
papers.title: The vaginal microbiota shape local and systemic inflammation during Chlamydia trachomatis infection in non-human primate.

papers.abstract: Background: Multiple sequence alignment of full viral genomes can be challenging due to factors such as long sequences, large insertions/deletions (spanning several 100 nucleotides), large number of sequences, sequence divergence, and high computational complexity in particular when computing alignments based on RNA secondary structures.
