papers.abstract: Motor skill-learning increases spatio-temporal consistency in neuronal activity in primary motor cortex (M1), and Somatostatin-expressing (SST) interneurons are causally involved in these learning-related activity changes. Yet, how SST-excitatory interactions shape population level activity changes during motor skill acquisition is still unknown. Here, we imaged large populations of excitatory neurons and identified SST or parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons across successive days as mice learned a dexterous, persistently M1-dependent reach-to-grasp task. Sparse, temporally coordinated, trial-resolved, and rate-controlled functional interactions between SST neurons and skill-modulated excitatory neurons emerged with learning and were stronger than those in excitatory-excitatory or PV-excitatory pairs. Interactions strengthened as neurons were recruited to the skill-modulated ensemble and weakened when skill modulation was lost. SST activity also became temporally reliable earlier than excitatory or PV activity, and SST consistency was significantly associated with behavioral performance even after controlling for training session number. Additionally, SST neurons carried more information about movement kinematics than randomly selected subsets of excitatory neurons. Overall, SST neurons became selectively coordinated with behaviorally relevant excitatory populations, revealing a cell-type-specific functional architecture for dexterous motor learning.
papers.title: Somatostatin-excitatory coordination emerges with dexterous motor skill learning

papers.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the leading delivery vehicles for RNA-based therapies, with pH-dependent mesophase transitions of their ionizable lipids proposed to play a crucial role in LNP function and endosomal escape. However, a consistent quantitative framework linking molecular lipid properties to the thermodynamics of these transitions is still lacking. Here, we establish such a framework by combining X-ray scattering, fluorescence spectroscopy, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, and continuum modeling. Using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and Laurdan fluorescence spectroscopy, we characterize the pH- and temperature-dependent phase behavior of both bulk lipid systems and LNPs containing the ionisable lipids MC3 or ALC-0315. Laurdan fluorescence measurements reveal the same pH- and temperature-dependent transitions in bulk and LNP systems, which closely follow the inverse micellar (LII) - inverse hexagonal (HII) transitions identified by SAXS, establishing Laurdan as a reporter of these mesophase transitions in LNPs. We combine experimental and simulation data to parameterize a continuum model of the LII - HII transition, providing a quantitative description of mesophase stability. The model reveals that geometric frustration arising from packing constraints is a key determinant of mesophase stability. By combining experimental and simulation data with theoretical analysis, we determine the relevant membrane parameters, including mean and Gaussian curvature bending rigidities, and identify the parameter ranges that govern phase stability. Together, these results establish a quantitative continuum theory for pH-dependent mesophase transitions of ionisable lipid and suggest metastable states in response to pH changes as an inherent feature of LNP core phase.
papers.title: Thermodynamic Model and Experiments Indicate Kinetically Trapped States in Ionisable Lipid Nanoparticles

papers.abstract: Human organoids represent promising models for studies of significance to the biology and medical communities. Of the existing approaches for monitoring organoids, none offers the ability to apply programmable mechanical forces while simultaneously recording multi-modal physiological responses, of relevance to phenomena spanning from traumatic brain injuries to cardiac rhythm disorders. Here, we present a mesoscale soft robotic organoid interface that enables programmable delivery of forces to organoids of diverse shapes, and to map electrophysiological activity and mechanical responses. The platform combines actuation elements with integrated sensors for quantitative measurement and control. Studies using this technology reveal that spheroidal cortical organoids exhibit distinct responses to mechanical trauma, including silencing, recovery, and changes in neuronal firing patterns. Additional experiments on cardiac ring tissues demonstrate that sustained stretching induces beat-to-beat rhythm variability and altered conduction. The results establish a framework for investigating force-triggered transitions between physiological and disease-like states in human tissue models.
papers.title: Mesoscale Soft Robotics for Mechanically Perturbing and Functionally Monitoring Responses in Human Organoids

papers.abstract: Cellular contractile forces regulate VE-cadherin dynamics, adhesion, and endothelial junction integrity. RhoA controls these forces through two parallel effector kinases: ROCK, which activates non-muscle myosin II motors, and SLK/LOK, which promote actin-membrane attachment through phosphorylation of ezrin, radixin, moesin proteins (ERM). How these two RhoA effector pathways differentially affect VE-cadherin dynamics at junctions is not known. Using single-molecule tracking of Halo-tagged VE-cadherin, we obtained a detailed characterization of VE-cadherin diffusive behavior inside and outside junctional regions in cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC). VE-cadherin was substantially less mobile and more confined within junctions than in non-junctional membrane. Inhibiting ROCK with Y-27632 increased VE-cadherin mobility both inside and outside junctions, consistent with RhoA/ROCK-driven contractility restraining cadherin diffusion globally. Unexpectedly, inhibiting SLK/LOK produced the opposite effect, selectively reducing VE-cadherin mobility within junctions with no comparable change outside them. This effect was accompanied by an increase in reticular junctions, suggesting that SLK/LOK inhibition alters VE-cadherin mobility indirectly, through a change in junctional architecture, rather than through a direct effect of actin-membrane coupling on VE-cadherin itself. These findings identify SLK/LOK as a regulator of VE-cadherin dynamics acting in parallel to ROCK downstream of RhoA and point to junctional architecture as a previously unappreciated determinant of VE-cadherin mobility at endothelial cell-cell contacts.
papers.title: RhoA effectors ROCK and SLK/LOK oppositely regulate VE-cadherin mobility at endothelial junctions

papers.abstract: His Domain Protein Tyrosine Phosphatase (HD-PTP) is required for multivesicular body (MVB) formation and endosome maturation, with Rab5-GTP levels raised upon HD-PTP depletion (Parkinson et al., 2021. doi: 10/1242/jcs.259192). Mass Spectrometry-based interactomics revealed that HD-PTP depletion increased association of Rabaptin5, a component of the early endosome Rabex5-Rabaptin5 Rab5-GEF, with multiple components of STRIPAK (striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase). Native IPs and co-expression studies confirmed association between STRIPAK and Rabex5-Rabaptin5, including Strip1-Rabex5 and SLMAP-Rabaptin5 interactions. Consistent with functional Rabaptin5-STRIPAK links, co-depletion of Strip1 or Rabaptin5 with HD-PTP restored normal early endosome positioning and Rab5 distribution. Strip1 depletion impaired formation of central, Rab5-positive early endosomes, reduced cellular Rab5-GTP levels, and prevented the accumulation of internalised EGF-EGFR into centrally located endosomes. SLMAP depletion accentuated the central clustering of early endosomes and other endosomal compartments while also retarding the generation of new, EGFR-containing endosomes and EGFR lysosomal transport. We conclude that STRIPAK is a novel co-assembly factor of Rabex5-Rabaptin5, exerting subunit-specific effects on early endosomes.
papers.title: STRIPAK associates with Rabex5-Rabaptin5 to promote Rab5-dependent early endosome formation and EGFR transport

papers.abstract: Epigenetic memory, reinforced by redundant heterochromatic networks, is a major barrier to somatic cell reprogramming. In cattle, single-agent chromatin-modifying treatments show inconsistent efficacy, likely due to compensatory crosstalk among repressive marks. Here, we evaluated a multi-target small-molecule cocktail, GUSTC, combining GSK343 (EZH2 inhibitor), UNC0638 (G9a/GLP inhibitor), Sodium Butyrate (HDAC inhibitor), Trichostatin A (HDAC inhibitor), and Chaetocin (SUV39H1 inhibitor) to simultaneously target facultative and constitutive heterochromatin in bovine fibroblasts. At optimized, non-cytotoxic concentrations, GUSTC treatment reduced H3K9me2, H3K9me3, H3K27me3, and HP1-alpha levels while increasing H3K9 acetylation by immunofluorescence. Using GUSTC-treated fibroblasts as donor cells for somatic cell nuclear transfer did not significantly change cleavage (83.6% vs. 92.2%; p = 0.15), blastocyst rate (28.4% vs. 39.0%; p = 0.20), bovine embryonic stem cell line derivation efficiency (26.3% vs. 33.3% of seeded blastocysts; p = 0.57), or the core pluripotency marker profile (OCT4, NANOG, SOX2) of the resulting lines. In a separate, serum-free, pluripotency-permissive culture system, GUSTC-treated cells adopted a colony-like morphology and showed increased POU5F1 and NANOG expression, along with increased DNMT1, EHMT2, HDAC1, HDAC2, and SUV39H1 transcripts. GUSTC thus reduces repressive heterochromatin marks in donor fibroblasts and is associated with a potentially more reprogramming-permissive state, without detectable improvement in preimplantation developmental competence. It provides a starting point for chemical reprogramming strategies in cattle.
papers.title: Epigenetic Remodeling Increases Plasticity of Bovine Fibroblasts Without Improving Embryo and Stem Cell Development

papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which whole genome duplication contributes to expression divergence of duplicate genes, which can impact the evolution of form and function, has been a long-standing question in evolutionary biology. We compared expression patterns of paralogs derived from the most recent Solanaceae-specific genome triplication event across 23 tissues and inferred ancestral expression states to investigate patterns of expression evolution. While the partitioning of ancestral expression states is traditionally considered the second most common (after the gene loss) trajectory of duplicate expression evolution, we found that the ancestral expression states tended to be retained by most (~66%) duplicates, with ~6% of gene lineages experiencing expression gain events and ~20% experiencing expression losses. The genes that gained expression in fruit tissues are significantly enriched with functions associated with fruit quality. Notably, asymmetrical expression divergence is prevalent among duplicates, especially when ancestral genes were either not expressed or were highly expressed. Our study demonstrates the utility of integrating paralog expression comparisons with phylogenetic analyses to document the potential evolutionary history of spatial expression patterns and gain insight into how expression divergence contributes to the evolution of function across tissues.
papers.title: Spatial expression evolution of duplicated genes post-whole genome duplication in cultivated tomato

papers.abstract: The human mammary gland arises through sequential lineage restrictions from surface ectoderm to hormone-responsive bilayered epithelium, yet a tractable in vitro model that captures these events has remained elusive. Here, we established a stepwise differentiation protocol that directs human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) into mammary organoids (MGOs) by sequential induction of non-neural ectoderm, mammary placodes, and lineage maturation in a defined medium. The resulting MGOs reproducibly formed polarized basal (KRT14+, TP63+) and luminal (KRT8+, GATA3+) layers, with ~25% of luminal cells expressing oestrogen receptor (ER). MGOs accumulated lipids, expressed {beta}-casein upon prolactin stimulation, and retained lineage fidelity after serial passaging. Upon transplantation into cleared mouse mammary fat pads, MGOs generated branched mammary ductal networks. Single-cell transcriptomics confirmed the emergence of basal, luminal hormone-sensing, luminal secretory, and stromal populations, transcriptionally aligned with adult human breast epithelium and responsive to endocrine disruption. These findings demonstrate that hiPSCs can be reprogrammed into functional mammary epithelium, providing a platform to dissect development, endocrine signalling, and breast cancer pathogenesis.
papers.title: Functional Mammary Gland Organoids From Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells

papers.abstract: Solid-state nanopores enable single-molecule detection and characterization through ionic-current measurements, but rapid translocation can limit the resolution of molecular features. Here, we investigated the translocation of 7.2 kb dsDNA and 3.3 kb RNA:DNA hybrids at LiCl concentrations extending to 7 mol/L. Both constructs exhibited a substantial increase of {gtrsim} 500% in mean translocation time when increasing LiCl concentration from 2--3 M to 7 M . We also observed a decrease in translocation frequency at increasing LiCl concentration. Both observations indicate a reduction in the effective electric driving force. Further analysis indicates a substantial decrease in the relative width of secondary peaks induced by labels on the molecule. Our results show that increasing salt concentration beyond 4 mol/L is an accessible way for increasing translocation time in solid-state nanopore sensing, with possible implications for barcode sensing resolution.
papers.title: Extreme Slowdown of dsDNA and RNA:DNA Hybrids in Solid-state Nanopores for LiCl concentrations above 4 mol/L

papers.abstract: Managing biological invasions requires deciding where, when, and how to act while populations continue to grow and spread. Invasive species threaten ecosystems and livelihoods, but limited management resources mean that managers cannot treat every affected area. This study asks how control efforts can be directed across a landscape to slow an invasion while keeping costs low. We develop a reinforcement-learning framework that can use broader spatial context to control biological invasions, using the spongy moth as a case study. The stochastic simulator captures host-dependent growth, short- and long-distance dispersal, density-dependent mating, and the effects of multiple treatments. The reinforcement-learning strategies are compared with benchmarks that are based on local treatment rules. We find that reinforcement learning achieves the lowest mean cost, with its advantage widening as management complexity increases, such as with simultaneous advancing-front control, nascent-colony management, and established-colony containment on heterogeneous-host landscapes. The reinforcement-learning strategies exhibit highly context-dependent treatment behavior, adjusting treatment choices as invasion dynamics evolve and coordinating interventions across long distances, all of which is learned from scratch.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Reveals Spatial Strategies for Slowing Biological Invasions

papers.abstract: Phase separation of biomolecules, including intrinsically disordered proteins, is an underlying physical process behind cellular condensate formation. To increase mechanistic understanding of its initial stages, we demonstrate the application of charge detection mass spectrometry to characterise the mass dispersion of protein nanoclusters that represent intermediates in this important biophysical process. We detect polydisperse clusters of 1-280 protein molecules (64 kDa-18.4 MDa), that are currently invisible to most analytical techniques.
papers.title: Mass spectrometric detection of protein nanoclusters: the invisible intermediates of phase separation

papers.abstract: Background: Rare genetic epilepsies are often difficult to diagnose and treat. They can arise from changes in many different genes, and the molecular basis linking these changes to epilepsy remains poorly understood. This complexity makes it difficult to select effective treatments and develop new therapies, leaving many patients with poorly controlled seizures and reduced quality of life Methods: To address this gap, we first identified epilepsy-associated genes and conducted a network-based analysis of biomolecular interactions in genetic epilepsy to identify converging pathways with high translational relevance and potential therapeutic targets. To run the analysis, we constructed a human brain-specific molecular interaction network by integrating all human pathways from the WikiPathways database. HotNet2 was then applied to identify highly perturbed clusters through evidence-based weight diffusion of EAGs in the human brain network. Results: We identified 2,496 epilepsy-associated genes (EAGs) from multiple resources. These genes encode coding for metabolite interconversion enzymes (20%), transporters (15%), and protein-modifying enzymes (11%). Furthermore, the network analysis identified 19 subnetworks with more than two nodes and 125 unique genes. Gene enrichment analysis revealed convergence of processes including action potential, synaptic function, nervous system development, TOR signaling, cilium organization, DNA repair, and cell fate specification. We identified 44 first-order neighbors connecting the subnetworks. By integrating drug-target interactions from DrugBank using CyTargetLinker, we highlighted potential therapeutic targets within the S4 subnetwork, associated with cerebral cortex development, as well as CREB1, a connector between subnetworks. Conclusion: Network analysis organized heterogeneous epilepsy-associated genes into biologically related subnetworks and generated hypotheses for further research.
papers.title: Network analysis reveals converging molecular mechanisms in genetic epilepsies

papers.abstract: Oxygen is the archetypal agent of photooxidative damage, and it is generally countered by removing its reactive products or by regulated, energy-costly responses. We show that in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, oxygen also drives a rapid, reversible photoprotective switch. Using a new bulk fluorescence method that separates reversible dark states from irreversible photobleaching, together with single-molecule spectroscopy, we find that illumination and oxygen generate a reversible, protein-stabilized charge-separated state comprising oxidized chlorophyll and superoxide. Access to this state increasingly outcompetes irreversible photodamage as excitation intensity falls to physiological levels and is strongly accelerated by ascorbic acid in native thylakoid membranes. These findings identify a constitutive oxygen-dependent photoprotective pathway and suggest that redox-state recovery can determine whether oxygen-associated chemistry protects or damages photoactive systems.
papers.title: Oxygen drives a rapid, reversible photoprotective switch in photosynthetic antennae

papers.abstract: Bacterial pathogens deploy sophisticated nanomachines such as the Type III Secretion System (T3SS) to inject effector proteins directly into host cells, thereby subverting cellular defenses and promoting infection. Central to this machinery is a conserved homo-oligomeric ATPase that fuels substrate unfolding and translocation. Despite extensive structural and biochemical studies, the precise mechanism of T3SS ATPase oligomer assembly and regulation remains incompletely understood, events crucial for the overall functionality of the T3SS. Here, we report high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Yersinia enterocolitica T3SS ATPase YsaN, captured in two previously uncharacterized oligomeric states, a dodecamer (12-mer) at 3.51 [A] and a tetradecamer (14-mer) at 3.80 [A] resolution. Both assemblies exhibit helical-like symmetry and conformational heterogeneity. A conserved longitudinal fissure interrupts the helical lattice and appears to mediate interconversion between the two states, while an N-terminal interface stabilized by inter-tier disulfide bonds and an extensive non-covalent network locks the assembly together. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that ATP hydrolysis drives a global, correlated compaction upon transition to the ADP-bound state. Together, these structural, biochemical, and MD simulation data establish T3SS ATPases as dynamic, oligomerically plastic molecular motors and provide a mechanistic framework for chaperone-effector dissociation and substrate translocation.
papers.title: Cryo-EM structures of the YsaN ATPase reveal dodecameric and tetradecameric assemblies in the Yersinia enterocolitica T3SS

papers.abstract: Whole genome duplication, or polyploidy, increases cell size and nuclear volume, yet how cells maintain cytonuclear balance and metabolic fitness following ploidy expansion remains unclear. Using isogenic series of Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains ranging from haploid (1N) to tetraploid (4N), and isogenic human diploid and tetraploid cell lines, we investigated the impact of polyploidy on mitochondrial homeostasis and metabolic adaptation. Quantitative proteomics uncovered a sub-linear scaling of mitochondrial proteins with increasing ploidy, with pronounced depletion of respiratory chain components, mitochondrial DNA maintenance factors, and redox homeostasis proteins. These changes were highly conserved, indicating a conserved consequence of genome expansion. Impaired mitochondrial scaling reduced respiratory growth, membrane potential and oxygen consumption, and elevated oxidative stress. In budding yeast, the mitochondrial dysfunction triggered reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and an unconventional activation of stress-responsive signaling pathways, including the Hog1 and cell integrity MAPK networks, which converged on Rtg2-dependent retrograde signaling to promote mitochondrial metabolism despite chronic dysfunction. Our findings identify defective mitochondrial scaling as a key consequence of polyploidy and establish ROS- and stress signaling-dependent retrograde response as a key adaptive mechanism linking genome duplication to mitochondrial homeostasis and cellular fitness.
papers.title: Whole genome duplication uncouples cell volume scaling from mitochondrial homeostasis

papers.abstract: Neovascular tufts (NVTs) are a defining feature of proliferative retinopathies such as diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity, in which they compromise retinal integrity and vision. Excessive endothelial cell (EC) sprouting underlies their formation, yet the cellular and mechanical mechanisms that shape NVTs, and the contribution of pericytes (PCs) to this process, remain unclear. In this work, we investigated the role of actomyosin contractility in ECs and PCs during pathological angiogenesis and NVT formation. We identified non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA) and phosphorylated myosin light chains (MLCs) as a key signature of PCs and ECs in retinopathy and NVTs. Using inducible deletion of Myh9 in the oxygen-induced retinopathy mouse model, we uncover distinct and opposing roles for NMIIA in the two cell types. Endothelial NMIIA promotes neovascularisation and prevents enlargement of NVTs, whilst PC NMIIA drives neovascular tuft formation. Mechanistically, we identify platelet-derived growth factor D (PDGFD), but not PDGFB, as a driver of pathological PC actomyosin contractility through Rho-associated coiled-coil kinase (ROCK). Genetic deletion of Pdgfd partially phenocopies the loss of NMIIA in PCs, reducing NVT formation and lowering NMIIA and phosphorylated MLC levels within NVTs. Our findings establish cell-type-specific actomyosin contractility as a determinant of NVT pathogenesis and identify PDGFD-ROCK-NMIIA signalling in PCs as a therapeutic target in proliferative retinopathies.
papers.title: PDGFD-induced pericyte contractility drives pathological neoangiogenesis

papers.abstract: Insights into the genetic basis of lifespan evolution can link evolutionary theory with an understanding of health, disease and adaptation. We leverage the power of >200 generations of experimental evolution in a seed beetle to unveil the genomic architecture of lifespan evolution. Replicated populations evolved under regimes favoring either a short or long life, resulting in a near doubling of lifespan. Whole genome re-sequencing revealed that short- and long-lived lines were strongly differentiated (global FST = 0.41) and more than 700 genes showed consistent signs of divergent selection. Remarkably, short- and long-lived lines were consistently divergent in a large number of regions harboring copy-number variants (CNVs), involving >600 genes. The evolution of a long life involved many distinct biological processes, such as DNA fidelity, mitotic integrity, reproduction, metabolism, immunity and stress response. A pedigree-based genome scan for quantitative trait loci (QTLs) uncovered several QTLs with large effects on lifespan, but the genetic basis of a long life was dominated by a very large number of regions with medium and small effects. The genome-wide spatial association with QTL effects was, if anything, stronger for CNVs than for sequence variants. The genetic effects of QTLs on lifespan were positively correlated overall between the sexes, but four regions showed pronounced sex-differences. Our results show that structural variants play a significant role in the evolution of an extended lifespan and the highly polygenic genomic architecture is to some extent sex-specific, consistent with differences in physiology and life history tradeoffs between the sexes.
papers.title: Experimental evolution unveils a role for structural variants and sex-specificity in the genetic architecture of lifespan

papers.abstract: Screening plant extracts and other complex natural matrices for antibacterial activity is complicated by optical interference and population averaging in conventional bulk assays. Droplet-based assays mitigate interference while enabling high-throughput assessment of bacterial subpopulations. However, analyzing the resulting image data involves difficult image processing, classification, and interpretation. Here, we present a democratized workflow for antimicrobial screening in complex matrices that combines a polydisperse droplet-based assay with EasyFlow 2.0 (EF2), our updated droplet image analysis platform. EF2 offers stable containerized deployment, expanded polydisperse droplet support, automated thresholding and MIC estimation, LLM-assisted data exploration, and import of other software outputs such as CellProfiler (CP) measurements and CellProfiler Analyst (CPA) classification models. As proof of concept, we applied this workflow to assess the antibacterial and aggregation-modulating effects of chemically distinct extracts of Taraxacum officinale, Rhodiola rosea, and Lonicera caerulea against Escherichia coli. Extracts were chemically characterized by HPLC-MS and evaluated using both standard 96-well plate microdilution and droplet-based assays. In total, 27,059 droplets were segmented in CP, classified into four growth phenotypes using a CPA random forest model, and analyzed in EF2. The droplet-based assay reached minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) at lower extract concentrations than 96-well plate microdilution and revealed extract-specific aggregation effects: L. caerulea reduced E. coli aggregation, whereas T. officinale did not. R. rosea reduced growth in the 96-well plate microdilution assay, but high concentrations caused droplet gelation that prevented droplet-based analysis, showing that sample components must be checked for compatibility with droplet formation. These results illustrate that the EF2-centered workflow supports rapid, automated MIC estimation through unsupervised thresholding when labels are unavailable, and four-class aggregation phenotyping when a CPA model is supplied. This workflow offers flexible, scalable screening, potentially extendable beyond plant extracts to other complex sample matrices.
papers.title: A droplet-to-data workflow for antimicrobial screening of complex matrices

papers.abstract: The composition of host communities in host-pathogen systems is changing through the loss and introduction of host species. Prior studies have shown that these changes can increase or decrease disease levels. However, it remains unclear what transient dynamics occur while host community composition changes, and how the traits of added or lost hosts affect those disease dynamics. In this study, we analyze a two-host model with an environmentally transmitted pathogen, where infection prevalence (proportion of infected individuals) in the focal host species changes as the second (alternative) host species is lost from the system. We use global sensitivity analysis to determine which and when alternative host traits have the strongest effects on the focal host dynamics. We find focal host infection prevalence increased or decreased monotonically when the alternative host has sufficiently higher or lower abilities to spread disease, respectively, than the focal host, but can change nonmonotonically when hosts have similar abilities to spread disease and the alternative host is a sufficiently strong competitor. Additionally, we identify that the alternative host's shedding and uptake rates of pathogen propagules, birth rate, and interspecific competitive ability almost always have strong influence on the magnitude and rate of change in focal host infection prevalence. In contrast, The alternative host's transmission rate, recovery rate, and disease mortality rate are only strongly influential in limited circumstances. Our study yields insight into how host traits influence the transient disease dynamics that occur following host losses in multi-host communities.
papers.title: Host traits predict the transient disease dynamics that occur during the loss of an alternative host

papers.abstract: Dynamic full-field optical coherence tomography (D-FFOCT) enables label-free visualization of tissue microarchitecture and endogenous intracellular dynamics. Here, we establish a volumetric atlas of ten fresh mouse organs using a mobile D-FFOCT imaging platform. The system enables large-area imaging of approximately 1 cm2 within 15 min with 1,024 frames per field of view, achieving 0.75-{micro}m lateral resolution and imaging depths of up to 200 {micro}m. Large-area mosaics, three-dimensional reconstructions, and comparisons with conventional histology reveal diverse organ-specific tissue architectures. Beyond morphological characterization, quantitative analysis of dynamic intensity and mean fluctuation frequency across nine organs reveals distinct dynamic signatures and tissue heterogeneity. Longitudinal imaging of brain, liver, and intestinal tissues further demonstrates organ-dependent temporal changes in endogenous dynamics following excision. Finally, we publicly release raw D-FFOCT imaging datasets from all ten organs, providing an open resource for quantitative tissue characterization, algorithm development, and reproducible research. Together, this study provides a comprehensive, openly accessible optical atlas of fresh mouse organs, establishing a foundation for systematic tissue characterization and advancing the broader application of D-FFOCT in biomedical research.
papers.title: Label-free volumetric dynamic atlas of fresh mouse organs using dynamic full-field optical coherence tomography

papers.abstract: Aim: Biofilms are complex ecosystems formed by phototrophic and heterotrophic organisms, such as bacteria and fungi. Biofilms are hotspots for microbial activity and crucial for the functioning of all aquatic ecosystems, but they are overlooked and poorly studied, especially along large environmental gradients. We aimed at resolving the responses of bacterial and fungal communities to environmental variation along a gradient with strong variation in environmental factors, especially salinity. We also investigated whether the diversity of biofilm-forming bacteria and fungi follows the pattern predicted by the Remane curve, which posits that species diversity is lowest at intermediate salinity. Location: 2300-km-long spatial gradient in the Baltic Sea, Northern Europe Time period: August 2018 Major taxa studied: Biofilm-forming bacteria and fungi Methods: We investigated the composition and diversity of bacteria and fungi by collecting biofilm samples from 42 shallow benthic ecosystems. We also characterized key environmental variables, such as salinity, nutrient concentrations, wind exposure, and climatic conditions. Bacterial and fungal communities in biofilm samples were identified using Illumina MiSeq sequencing. Results: We found that bacteria and fungi responded differently to environmental variation. Bacterial communities were mainly controlled by salinity, and their diversity was lowest in the intermediate salinity. Bacterial communities were also dominated by different bacterial orders in high, intermediate, and low salinity. Fungal communities, instead, were jointly controlled by several environmental variables, i.e., salinity, water temperature, wind exposure, and nutrients, and their diversity or composition did not show a clear pattern along the salinity gradient. Main conclusions: To our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to investigate the biofilm-forming communities, especially fungal communities, along large environmental gradients. Our results highlight the role of biofilms as complex ecosystems where organisms ecological requirements are unique and variable.
papers.title: Differing patterns in community composition and diversity of biofilm-forming bacteria and fungi along a large salinity gradient

papers.abstract: Vector-borne zoonotic diseases pose a substantive risk to public health worldwide, yet predicting outbreaks at scales useful for public health response remains a critical challenge. Transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, West Nile virus is the leading cause of arboviral disease in the United States, progressing to neuroinvasive disease in approximately 1% of infections. Arizona's record-breaking 2021 outbreak, with 1,715 reported human cases and 127 deaths exemplifies this growing burden. Using a decade of mosquito surveillance data coupled with time-lagged weather patterns in a random forest framework, we developed spatial models predicting Culex abundance and West Nile virus occurrence across Arizona at weekly temporal and fine spatial resolution. Our weighted models classified viral occurrence with 98.9% accuracy and explained 65.3% of weekly variation in county-level human cases, with human cases lagging modeled activity by one week. Neither mosquito abundance nor viral occurrence declined at the extreme temperatures characteristic of Arizona summers, suggesting that thermal refugia sustain transmission. Drought-monsoon cycling, rather than temperature alone, emerged as the primary driver of West Nile activity, and projections through 2100 indicate intensifying activity under all climate change scenarios.
papers.title: Climate change and extreme weather events to intensify West Nile virus activity

papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics has become an important technology in biomedical research by preserving the spatial context of gene expression in tissues and enabling the study of cellular states and interactions in situ. However, most existing methods provide only static snapshots of individual tissue specimens, requiring inference of the molecular dynamics underlying development, disease progression, and therapeutic response from different specimens rather than direct tracking in the same living tissue. Here, we introduce Live Spatial Transcriptomics (Live-ST), a technology that enables longitudinal, transcriptome-wide profiling of living tissue. Live-ST combines electroporation-based intracellular sampling and spatial barcoding to enable repeated, spatially resolved mRNA measurements in intact living tissue through next-generation sequencing. We demonstrate its capabilities by (i) benchmarking spatial mRNA capture in patterned two-dimensional cell systems, (ii) spatially profiling transcriptomes in intact, patient-derived living melanoma tissues while preserving tissue viability, and (iii) longitudinally tracking drug-response dynamics within the tumor microenvironment. Together, Live-ST enables repeated, non-destructive measurements of spatial gene expression, providing a new framework for studying dynamic tissue biology in native physiological and pathological contexts.
papers.title: Live Spatial Transcriptomics Enables Longitudinal Tissue Mapping

papers.abstract: The eukaryotic nucleus has a hierarchical organization that permits genomic regulation. The genome is packaged as chromatin, which is silenced conditionally as facultative heterochromatin, or more stably silenced as constitutive heterochromatin. The smaller fractions of the genome that contain gene-rich sequences are organized into open chromatin conformations known as euchromatin. The inactive X (Xi) chromosome territory presents a uniquely powerful model system to investigate chromosome-scale gene silencing, as the entire chromosome undergoes coordinated epigenetic repression. The unique chromosome-wide silencing event provides a tractable system for investigating how molecular mechanisms of gene repression are translated into mesoscale structural features. This work builds on previous structural studies of the Xi that have leveraged conventional electron microscopy (EM) and cryo-EM, which have led to remarkable insights into the structural underpinnings of genome silencing. These approaches, however, are unable to directly distinguish chromatin from RNA and protein features. To resolve the molecular composition of the Xi chromosome territory and to provide a model of the structural organization of the chromatin, RNA and protein we analyzed the Xi using Electron Spectroscopic Imaging (ESI). We are able to resolve structural features without the use of contrast enhancing stains, using the distinct elemental signatures of chromatin, RNA and protein and combining them into composite images. By coupling ESI and electron tomography, we can circumvent the projection limitation of EM and provide an unprecedented view of the spatial organization of chromatin fibres in relation to structural features including RNA and proteins in 3D. Additionally, we employed correlative light-microscopy with ESI in physical serial sections and computationally assembled a structural model of the entire Xi chromosome territory revealing an intricate spatial network with distinct chromatin domains, distributed RNA-protein clusters, and identified a large, and previously uncharacterized mesoscale non-chromatin structure. Together, these observations provide new insights into the architecture of the Xi chromosome territory and shed electrons on the structural basis of chromosome-scale genome organization.
papers.title: The Structural Basis of Genome Silencing: The Inactive X Chromosome Resolved by Electron Spectroscopic Imaging

papers.abstract: In situ electron cryo-tomography (cryo-ET) is a powerful tool for visualising biology inside cells at the molecular scale. The routine application of cryo-ET in tissue samples promises biological insight beyond single cells, but is currently limited by the technical challenge of preparing high quality, electron-transparent specimens from thick (>100 m) biopsies efficiently. Here, we demonstrate that cryogenic femtosecond pulsed laser ablation (cryo-fs-PLA) can accelerate the preparation of vitreous specimens of mammalian brain tissue for cryo-ET. Using cryogenic fluorescence microscopy, regions of interest within high-pressure frozen tissue can be specifically targeted, and cryo-fs-PLA can be employed as a preparative step for serial cryogenic lift-out experiments. We define cryo-fs-PLA parameters and determine ablation rates for two different laser wavelengths, and demonstrate that tilt series collected on lamellae fabricated from sites exposed to cryo-fs-PLA largely maintain their vitrification state. Incorporating cryo-fs-PLA into existing cryo-ET workflows has the potential to unlock the sample preparation of tissues at the throughput necessary for routine in situ cell biology of multicellular samples.
papers.title: Femtosecond pulsed laser ablation for in-tissue electron cryo-tomography

papers.abstract: Gene therapies utilizing hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) have curative potential across hematologic diseases, but manual manufacturing workflows are costly and difficult to scale, limiting patient access. Here, we demonstrated automation of an HSPC gene knock-in protocol on a high-throughput manufacturing platform designed for clinical-scale production. The platform executed all steps, from post-thaw HSPC inoculation through Cas9 electroporation, AAV6 transduction, and harvest, producing gene-edited HSPCs (geHSPCs) carrying an anti-HIV antibody transgene at the CCR5 locus with high purity, preserved differentiation potential, and editing efficiencies comparable to small-scale processing. Following transplantation into mice, geHSPCs engrafted and reconstituted multiple hematopoietic lineages, demonstrating that repopulation capacity was preserved. This work shows that clinical-scale doses of geHSPCs meeting release criteria can be produced on an automated, high-throughput platform, while preserving key product attributes and in vivo function, providing a path toward scalable and cost-effective manufacturing that could broaden access to HSPC gene therapies.
papers.title: End-To-End, Fully Automated Manufacturing of Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cell Therapy Via CCR5-Targeted Integration

papers.abstract: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) remains a significant global public health threat, yet antiviral discovery is limited by experimental systems that provide little mechanistic resolution and rely heavily on transformed cell lines of uncertain physiological relevance. Here, we developed complementary live-cell CHIKV reporter systems comprising a dual-fluorescent subgenomic replicon and fluorescent infectious viruses that enable real-time monitoring of distinct stages of the viral replication cycle. By coupling an nsP3-tagged reporter to genomic RNA translation and replication with a subgenomic reporter of structural gene expression, we achieved temporal resolution of early and late replication events in living cells. Functional validation using replication-defective and subgenomic RNA-deficient mutants confirmed that the system distinguishes between viral RNA replication and downstream structural gene expression. Application of these reporters revealed distinct antiviral responses across transformed and physiologically relevant human cell models. Ribavirin and the nsP2 inhibitor RA-0002034 potently inhibited CHIKV replication in transformed cell lines. Unexpectedly, ribavirin activity was markedly diminished in primary human skeletal muscle myoblasts and dermal fibroblasts, despite robust antiviral effects in commonly used screening cell lines. Mechanistic studies showed that ribavirin-mediated inhibition was rescued by guanosine but not inosine supplementation and was recapitulated by mycophenolic acid, consistent with guanine nucleotide depletion as the predominant antiviral mechanism under the conditions tested. Notably, inhibition through this pathway was substantially less effective in primary human cells. Together, these findings establish versatile live-cell CHIKV reporter systems for mechanistic studies of viral replication and reveal striking cell-type-dependent differences in response to guanine nucleotide depletion. Our results demonstrate that host-cell context can profoundly influence both CHIKV replication and antiviral susceptibility, highlighting the importance of physiologically relevant models for understanding virus-host interactions and antiviral mechanism.
papers.title: Chikungunya virus live-cell reporter systems reveal cell-type-dependent antiviral responses to ribavirin

papers.abstract: Neuroimaging studies often derive and discuss structural covariance (SC) as a representation of underlying brain circuitry that reflects coordinated maturation, anatomical connectivity, transcriptional similarity, and shared genetic influences. These associations motivate its use to study brain organization across development, aging, and disease. However, the algorithms used to derive SC networks impose constraints that may shape their biological interpretation. To understand the impact of algorithm choice, we used the thalamocortical system as an example and compared five common representations of voxelwise SC, namely, principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), orthogonal projective NMF (OPNMF), and \textit{k}-means clustering, in 755 participants aged 8--22 years from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC). SC networks derived from deformation-based morphometry (DBM) were evaluated against three complementary biological benchmarks: age-related individual differences, fractional-anisotropy (FA)-based microstructural connectivity of regionally-specific thalamocortical connections, and Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression. Each algorithm demonstrated underlying sensitivity to differing aspects of neurobiology: PCA and OPNMF showed the strongest associations between participant-level component weights and age. NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means showed greater spatial overlap between positive cortical SC and tractography-derived projections. ICA and PCA showed stronger correspondence between thalamic and cortical gene-expression profiles across the transcriptome, whereas NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means more often identified thalamic components with relatively high core-matrix gene expression. This study emphasizes that algorithmic constraints effectively act as biological priors and decomposition methods do not provide neutral compression of the data. We conclude that it is critical to consider whether the algorithmic objective matches the representational geometry of the neurobiology being studied. Overall, our findings suggest that SC studies should select and justify algorithms according to the biological question, explicitly considering whether their constraints favour distributed gradients, overlapping regional parts, or discrete clusters. Meanwhile, interpretations of SC findings could also be informed by the specific algorithmic constraints used to derive them.
papers.title: Algorithmic Geometry Shapes the Biological Meaning of Thalamocortical Structural Covariance

papers.abstract: Neuroligins are conserved postsynaptic adhesion proteins involved in synaptic function and behaviour. In Drosophila melanogaster, Neuroligin 3 (Nlg3) regulates social behaviour, sleep and synaptic architecture. We now report, through analysis of publicly available transcriptomics data, confirmed with RT-qPCR data, that loss-of-function of the nlg3 gene downregulates the expression of longevity-associated genes foxo, hsp70s, and hsp68. Graded genetic manipulation of the Drosophila melanogaster neuroligin 3 (nlg3) gene indeed modulates both social spacing and lifespan. Specifically, reduced nlg3 expression (via heterozygous deletion, or transposable-element insertion) extends lifespan in both sexes, while overexpression or complete deletion shortens it. In contrast, overexpression or complete loss of nlg3 leads the flies to be further apart (increased social distance, or social space), as does RNAi knockdown, while heterozygous reduction of nlg3 expression either lowers or does not alter the flies social space. This work identifies a previously unrecognized link between a conserved synaptic gene, social behaviour, and organismal longevity.
papers.title: A novel function of neuroligin 3: Beyond sociality, Regulating lifespan in Drosophila

papers.abstract: Background: Patients with multiple myeloma (MM) are at increased risk for light chain cardiac amyloidosis (CA) due to high circulating levels of light chains. ALCA is a clinical diagnosis based on biopsy, cardiac imaging findings of restrictive cardiomyopathy, and serum monoclonal proteins. To overcome these challenges, we have developed machine learning models that accurately predict ALCA status while identifying key diagnostic features based on routine laboratory measurements and using limited data. Methods: Utilizing electronic medical data (EMR) data, we built support vector machine models (SVMs) using the MISTIC framework. Data including diagnosis history, treatment, and laboratory values for patients with MM or monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS) were collected as a retrospective cohort study at Moffit Cancer Center and Research Institute between 2014 and 2019. To utilize the wealth of information in longitudinal EMR data, we fit regression models to the EMR data and used the parameters and characteristics of the fits as features for our SVMs. We tested three different sets of features: descriptive statistics alone, parameters and characteristics of fit only, and both the descriptive statistics and parameters of fit (DescFits). A classifier using raw data at a timepoint proximal to the date of ALCA diagnostic imaging (EchoAdj), as well as analogous random forest and XGBoost models were used for comparison. Findings: SVM classifiers trained on the DescFits feature set (AUC= 1.0) outperformed blind model predictions of the EchoAdj model (AUC = 0.36) and other conventional machine learning approaches in identifying which patients were diagnosed with ALCA. The DescFits model selected features describing the temporal relationship of physiologic parameters including hematologic state, and cardiac and renal function. Interpretation: We demonstrated that the MISTIC SVM framework and the shape of EMR data can aid in identifying patients with cardiac amyloidosis without cardiac biopsy or imaging.
papers.title: Computational alternative to cardiac biopsy in multiple myeloma: utilizing the shape of routine laboratory data for the classification of AL cardiac amyloidosis

papers.abstract: Rescoring docked ligands with molecular dynamics (MD) and end point free energy methods such as MM/GBSA is widely used, but its benefit over docking for series of close analogs is uncertain. We compared AutoDock Vina scores with Md based MM/GBSA energies for 29 neutral p38 kinase inhibitors (PDB 3FLY) from the Open Force Field protein-ligand benchmark, whose IC50 values from a single publication span 3.8 kcal/mol in estimate {Delta}G. Each ligand was docked with three random seeds and simulated in two independent 20 ns replicas started from the benchmark pose (AMBER99SB-ILDN, GAFF2, TIP3L; GROMACS). MM/GBSA energies were calculated from 251 frames per trajectory without an entropy term. All 58 simulations remained stable with the ligand bound. Vina scores correlated weakly with experimental {Delta}G (Spearman {rho} = 0.28 98% CI -0.15 to 0.62), as did replica averaged MM/GBSA energies ({rho} = 0.24 -0.18 to 0.62). The difference was -0.03 (-0.50 to 0.43), so the methods were not distinguishable. Independent replicas of the same ligand differed by 3.3 kcal/mol on average, comparable to the experimental range. Raising the interior dielectric constant from 1 to 2 gave a nearly identical ranking ({rho} = 0.96 between the two sets of scores; {rho} = 0.37 against experiment, -0.04 to 0.69). In an exploratory analysis, ligands size alone correlated with affinity ({rho} = 0.60, 0.28 to 0.82), whereas neither computed score tracked size. For this narrow range series, short MD rescoring gave no measurable improvement over docking, and replica variability limited its resolution.
papers.title: Does Short Molecular Dynamics Rescoring Improve the Ranking of p38α Inhibitors over Docking? A Replicate Benchmark

papers.abstract: Light-oxygen-voltage (LOV) domains are blue-light sensors that make fused effector proteins optically controllable. The AsLOV2-Rac1 fusion (PA-Rac1) is one of the most widely used of these tools, yet the structural basis of its activation has been inferred largely from cryogenic structures and from solution studies, mostly of the isolated AsLOV2 domain. Here, room-temperature dark and light-state structures of AsLOV2-Rac1 at 1.8 [A] resolution are reported, determined by serial femtosecond crystallography at the SwissFEL Cristallina beamline with sheet-on-sheet (SOS) chip sample delivery. Repeated 450 nm pump-laser excitation during chip rastering accumulated the FMN-cysteine adduct in about 80 % of the molecules, giving strong Fourier difference maps. To our knowledge, this is the first light-state structure of PA-Rac1 or of any AsLOV2 fusion and the first AsLOV2 light state in which the thioether adduct is not compromised by X-ray radiolysis. Apart from the N-terminal residue and one marginal Rac1 loop residue, C displacements above 0.3 [A] between dark and light models recorded at the same temperature are confined to the chromophore environment, the D helix and the G{beta}-H{beta} and H{beta}-I{beta} loops of AsLOV2. These changes, including the Ile445 rotamer switch, are also seen in light-state structures of the isolated AsLOV2 domain, but the Asn414 rotation reported there is absent in the fusion. Comparison with the cryogenic dark-state structure also shows temperature-dependent differences that exaggerate the apparent changes. In the crystal, the GTP, the Mg2+ site and the switch regions of Rac1 show no detectable light-induced change and the J helix does not unfold, although transient or low-population states cannot be excluded. This modest response is consistent with the small difference in effector affinity between dark- and lit-state mutants in solution, with lattice contacts and an interdomain Ca2+ ion as possible further contributions.
papers.title: Room-temperature light-state structure of the AsLOV2-Rac1 optogenetic actuator by sheet-on-sheet serial femtosecond crystallography

papers.abstract: Expansions of the pathogenic (AAGGG)n repeat within the RFC1 gene cause the hereditary disease CANVAS. We have shown that this repeat impedes DNA replication both in vitro and in vivo. Here, we investigated the mechanisms of replication fork stalling and reversal at (AAGGG)n repeats within an SV40-based episome in human cells. A comprehensive 2-dimensional electrophoretic analysis of replication intermediates revealed a strict orientation dependence of the replication block, evident only when the homopurine sequence was in the lagging-strand template. Fork accumulation was further increased in the presence of the G4-DNA stabilizer pyridostatin, implicating G4-DNA in the process. This stalling was followed by an accumulation of reversed forks and further analysis revealed roles for SMARCAL1 and RAD51 in this process. Biochemical studies showed that SMARCAL1, with assistance from RPA, efficiently remodels a fork carrying the G4-forming AAGGG repeat in the ssDNA gap, but not a substrate carrying the repeat in triplex conformation. We conclude that stalling results from G4-DNA formation by the repeat, which then triggers SMARCAL1-mediated fork reversal at the repeat. Given the mirror symmetry of the sequence, the nascent strands at the reversed forks likely adopt a triplex conformation, leading to a thorough accumulation of branched structures.
papers.title: Mechanisms of fork stalling and reversal at pathogenic CANVAS (AAGGG)n repeats

papers.abstract: Olfactory stimuli (odorants) are represented by combinatorial patterns of olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) activation that are translated into spatially-organized glomerular maps at their input to the CNS. How glomerular maps relate to odorant features - including chemical structure and concentration - remains a key question in understanding the neural mechanisms of odor coding. Here, we compared glomerular response maps for the same 59 odorants across three concentration regimes, using GCaMP6 imaging from OSN axon terminals in the olfactory bulb (OB) of the anesthetized mouse. At the lowest regime, in which concentrations were chosen to distinguish the most sensitive glomeruli for each odorant, glomeruli were exceptionally narrowly tuned and responses across glomeruli were extremely sparse. We then compared responses at two higher-concentration regimes, 'low' and 'high', differing by 25-fold from each other and 2 - 5 log units higher than the 'most-sensitive' regime. Increasing concentration broadened tuning of OSN inputs; this broadening was heterogeneous across chemical space and was well-described by classifying glomeruli into several subpopulations with distinct consensus tuning profiles. Each subpopulation was selectively tuned to one or a few odorant chemical classes and spatially clustered in a manner consistent with the projection patterns of receptor-defined OSN classes. Glomerular subpopulations retained distinct tuning and spatial localization even at the highest concentrations. OSN subpopulations thus sample chemical space nonuniformly across a large concentration range. These results suggest a lower-dimensional structure in the representation of odorant information that largely reflects OSN subpopulations which, in turn, map to olfactory receptor subfamilies. This organization may enable distinct odor coding strategies for different OSN classes and for parts of chemical feature space with distinct ethological relevance.
papers.title: Odor representations are structured by heterogeneous tuning and concentration-dependence of functionally distinct olfactory sensory neuron subpopulations.

papers.abstract: Aggregation of the microtubule-stabilizing protein Tau into insoluble deposits is characteristic for several neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease. While phosphorylated Tau (pTau) appears as a normal post-translational modification, the accumulation of hyperphosphorylated Tau aggregates represents a hallmark of these disorders. The molecular mechanisms involved in the conversion from functional Tau into pathological assemblies are still not elucidated. Here, we identified the role of phosphorylation levels on the phase separation and aggregation behavior of Tau, and how these processes can be counteracted by the molecular chaperone-like Bri2 BRICHOS domain. We found that the phosphorylation pattern modulates Tau fibrillation and enhances its droplet-formation propensity. Remarkably, Bri2 BRICHOS generally shifts Tau phase boundaries, counteracting the dense state, and inhibits Tau fibril formation, irrespectively of the degree of phosphorylation. Solution NMR results pinpointed the binding site of Bri2 BRICHOS on pTau, both in the dilute phase and droplet state, revealing an effect on specific regions and phosphorylated residues, which appear to be crucial for the formation and maintenance of the droplet state. Taken together, this study uncovered the opposing regulatory roles of phosphorylation and the anti-amyloid chaperone Bri2 BRICHOS on biomolecular condensation and fibrillation of Tau, providing detailed insights into the molecular mechanisms involved in tauopathies, which may facilitate future treatment strategies using chaperone-based inhibitors.
papers.title: Opposing Regulation of Tau Condensation by Phosphorylation Levels and Molecular Chaperone Interactions

papers.abstract: Motivation: Functional regulatory variants are important determinants of heritable diversity, yet their systematic identification requires both genome-wide maps of transcription factor (TF) occupancy and suitable genome sequences for mapping. While chromosome-scale assemblies remain costly for large association panels, short-read sequencing data are widely available. We investigated whether draft genomes reconstructed from short reads are sufficient for comparative MOA-seq analyses of TF occupancy. Results: We generated genome-wide TF footprint maps for the barley cultivars Bowman, Morex, and Golden Promise, identifying approximately 240,000 loci per genotype. Roughly half of all footprints occurred in intergenic regions. Footprints conserved between genotypes were depleted for sequence variation and located closer to genes. Meanwhile, genotype-specific footprints were enriched for SNP-containing and gene-distal regions, highlighting the extensive diversity of regulatory landscapes among barley cultivars. We further compared two short-read-based draft genome assembly strategies: i) a SNP-replacement and ii) a Practical Haplotype Graph (PHG)-based composite genome approach, to enable MOA-seq analyses without chromosome-scale genome assemblies. Compared to the SNP-replacement strategy, the composite genome displayed 2.3-fold higher local sequence concordance for SNPs/INDELs relative to the published reference. Both draft genomes accurately reproduced MOA-seq profiles, recovering approximately 80 % of reference peak bases with per-base coverage correlations of 0.79-0.90 relative to the assembled reference. While the composite genome performed best across the genome overall, the simpler SNP-replacement strategy more accurately recovered TF occupancy within regulatory peaks due to fewer structural alignment artefacts. Availability: Pipelines consist of existing open-source tools, Bash, GAWK and Java, and are available at [zenodo; tbd].
papers.title: A composited genome approach to analyse cistrome diversity in barley

papers.abstract: Diet has been a major selective force throughout human evolution, yet dietary adaptation is often studied through individual loci rather than as interconnected systems of traits. Here, we integrated genome-wide association data for 58 diet-related phenotypes with genomes from 938 ancient Europeans spanning the last 10,000 years to reconstruct the evolution of dietary endophenotypes. We identified four major systems encompassing adiposity and metabolism, body composition, fatty-acid metabolism and food-related behaviours. Multiple endophenotypes showed significant temporal shifts during the Holocene departing from the expected under neutrality, including coordinated decreases in genetic architectures associated with adiposity, insulin regulation and lipid metabolism, alongside increases in traits related to docosahexaenoic acid metabolism. Moreover, these patterns showed marked geographic heterogeneity across Europe. Our results indicate that dietary adaptation proceeded through coordinated evolutionary changes across interconnected physiological systems, providing a systems-level perspective on how cultural and subsistence transitions reshaped human biology.
papers.title: Beyond single-trait analysis: ancient genomes reveal coordinated evolution of dietary endophenotypes in Holocene Europe

papers.abstract: Mental health is crucially linked to social behavior. Healthy social behavior involves learning to adapt emotional responses to social cues, for example learning to suppress anxiety through social familiarity, or social familiarity-induced anxiolysis (SoFiA). SoFiA is well documented and forms the basis for interpersonal therapy, however, the neural mechanisms of SoFiA are unclear. SoFiA is modeled in rats by employing the social interaction habituation (SI-hab) protocol. Using SI-hab protocol, it has been determined that SoFiA represents social safety learning, which requires both anxiogenic stimulus and social familiarity during training sessions (5-6 daily SI sessions), and SoFiA expression is dependent on infralimbic subdivision (IL) of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the basolateral amygdala (BLA). Here we investigated the role of IL in SoFiA acquisition and expression, using chemogenetics to inhibit IL neurons. Male Wistar rats received bilateral viral injections targeting the IL or BLA and left undisturbed for 5-7 weeks to allow for viral expression. We chemogenetically inhibited via low doses of ip. clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) either the IL, the BLA, or the projections neurons from the IL to the BLA during expression of SoFiA in rats. We found that projection neurons from IL to the BLA are critical for the recovery SI behavior from the attenuation caused by the bright light (expression of SoFiA). Furthermore, CNO inhibited IL neurons with projections to the BLA and there were no off target effects of CNO on the behavioral measures. These results suggest an essential role of the IL-BLA pathway in social safety learning.
papers.title: Projection Neurons from Infralimbic (IL) to the Basolateral Amygdala (BLA) are Critical for the Expression of Social Familiarity induced Anxiolysis (SoFiA) in rats

papers.abstract: Inflammatory responses are heterogeneous, even among cells exposed to a common insult, yet the regulatory mechanisms that distinguish these inflammatory states remain poorly understood. Here, we leveraged inflammatory state heterogeneity to identify a conserved Foxp1-Pde4d regulatory relationship and uncover a role for this axis in preserving inflammatory responsiveness. Genotoxic stress in adipocyte progenitors generated heterogeneous engagement of type-I interferon (IFN) and NF{kappa}B transcriptional programmes, and transcriptome-wide analysis independently identified Foxp1 and the cAMP phosphodiesterase Pde4d among genes associated with lower IFN- and higher NF{kappa}B-associated transcription. ChIP-seq revealed selective loss of Foxp1 occupancy at a Pde4d-associated regulatory element following genotoxic stress, while Foxp1 gain- and loss-of-function established Foxp1 as a positive regulator of Pde4d expression. Remarkably, coupling of Foxp1-Pde4d expression was broadly conserved across vertebrate tissues and damage models. In vivo, Foxp1 loss in zebrafish revealed a striking dissociation between inflammatory state and response capacity: basal NF{kappa}B activity was elevated, yet injury-induced NF{kappa}B activation was markedly blunted and macrophage recruitment impaired. Adenylyl cyclase inhibition restored macrophage recruitment in Foxp1-deficient zebrafish, functionally linking the Foxp1 phenotype to cAMP signalling and supporting a model in which Foxp1-Pde4d regulation preserves inflammatory responsiveness through control of cAMP. Together, these findings show how inflammatory-state heterogeneity can reveal conserved regulatory mechanisms linking basal cellular state to subsequent response capacity.
papers.title: A conserved Foxp1-Pde4d axis regulates inflammatory responsiveness

papers.abstract: Toxoplasma gondii is a widespread zoonotic pathogen of major One Health concern, capable of causing congenital toxoplasmosis in both humans and sheep. Despite its impact, early host-parasite molecular interactions during acute infection in pregnant hosts remain largely unexplored. In this study, we characterized the transcriptomic responses of key tissues involved in early infection (the small intestine, mesenteric lymph nodes, and placenta) in pregnant ewes experimentally infected with T. gondii strain TgShSp1. RNA-seq analysis revealed pronounced, tissue-specific transcriptional changes at 6 days post-infection (dpi), particularly in the mesenteric lymph nodes, characterized by activation of interferon- and cytokine-mediated immune pathways. In contrast, transcriptional responses at 3 dpi were limited, consistent with a silent phase of parasite dissemination. Despite the absence of detectable parasite DNA, placentomes showed modest interferon-associated responses and upregulation of DNA repair and cellular stress pathways. These changes coincided with marked suppression of cell-cycle progression and extracellular matrix remodeling alongside inhibition of angiogenesis and hypoxia pathways. Altogether, early disruption of placental vascular function and tissue remodeling may contribute to fetal loss. In summary, these findings provide new insights into early host responses to T. gondii infection in a pregnant host and identify molecular mechanisms that may predispose to early fetal death during ovine congenital toxoplasmosis.
papers.title: Tissue-specific transcriptomic responses to early Toxoplasma gondii infection in sheep during congenital toxoplasmosis

papers.abstract: Nearly every computational account of hierarchical cortex rests on assumptions about the influence of direct cortico-cortical inputs and which neurons they act upon. Yet, disentangling their direct functional contributions from indirect, multisynaptic influences remains difficult. We examined how feedforward (FF) and feedback (FB) pathways between mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and posteromedial cortex (PM) modulate visual responses, combining retrograde labelling, multi-area two-photon imaging and optogenetic perturbations. High or low activity in either pathway was associated with both excitation and inhibition of neurons in the targeted areas. FF activity was associated with stronger additive changes, while FB activity was related to stronger multiplicative modulations and improvements in visual decoding. Optogenetic manipulations causally confirmed these asymmetries. Both pathways preferentially modulated reciprocating "looped" neurons, with FF exciting them and FB either exciting or inhibiting them. These findings demonstrate that feedforward and feedback pathways serve distinct functional roles within recurrent cortical loops.
papers.title: Direct cortical feedforward and feedback pathways differentially shape visual responses and selectively engage looped circuits

papers.abstract: Phase-separated protein condensates organize biochemical processes in cells. ATP-driven enzymatic reactions can change the physical properties and even trigger the dissolution of such condensates. Here we use molecular simulations to show how ATP-driven kinase and phosphatase reactions modulate the organization of TDP-43 low complexity domain (LCD) condensates. TDP-43 phosphorylation is enhanced by condensation, as CK1{delta} preferentially binds to and acts in TDP-43 LCD condensates, whereas dephosphorylation by the phosphatase calcineurin occurs predominantly in the dilute phase. This differential recruitment of kinases and phosphatases, together with the slow redistribution of kinases into newly formed condensates, triggers oscillatory appearance and disappearance of TDP-43 LCD condensates. The oscillations are self-sustained, persisting at constant chemical driving, showing that an antagonistic kinase-phosphatase pair can endow a condensate with autonomous dynamics rather than only setting its structure.
papers.title: Kinase-phosphatase cycles drive self-sustained oscillations of protein condensates

papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in cytoplasmic FMR1-interacting protein 2 (CYFIP2) cause neurodevelopmental disorders, with hotspot substitutions at arginine 87 (Arg87) associated with particularly severe symptoms. CYFIP2 functions both as a component of the WAVE (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein family verprolin-homologous protein) regulatory complex (WRC), regulating the actin cytoskeleton, and as an interactor of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) involved in mRNA processing/translation. Although Arg87 variants reduce CYFIP2 protein stability, heterozygous knock-in mice carrying Arg87Cys (Cyfip2+/R87C) show markedly more severe phenotypes than heterozygous knockout (Cyfip2+/-) mice, supporting a toxic gain-of-function mechanism. However, how the dual roles of CYFIP2 contribute to this mechanism remains unclear. To address this, we examined Cyfip2+/R87C mice at postnatal week 7, before overt neuronal loss and gliosis, focusing on the progressive dispersion of hippocampal cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) pyramidal neurons, a phenotype absent in Cyfip2+/- mice. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing suggested candidate alterations related to translation and cell adhesion/migration in CA1 pyramidal neurons. Complementarily, human embryonic kidney 293T cells expressing CYFIP2 Arg87Cys showed defects in proliferation and morphology, accompanied by altered expression of cell adhesion-related genes. Quantitative proteomic analysis of the CA1 region uncovered an imbalance between CYFIP2-associated protein networks, characterized by increased RBPs and reduced WRC components. Phosphoproteomic analysis further revealed altered phosphorylation of synaptic and translational regulators. Consistently, whole-cell recordings and biocytin-based morphological analyses showed increased frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents and altered dendritic morphology in Cyfip2+/R87C CA1 pyramidal neurons, most prominently in the more severely dispersed deep-layer neurons. Moreover, the cell adhesion molecule Eph receptor A3 was reduced, possibly as a result of RBP dysregulation. Together, these findings suggest that an imbalance between RBP- and WRC-associated pathways underlies the gain-of-function effects of CYFIP2 Arg87Cys and contributes to early neuronal phenotypes, most notably CA1 layer dispersion. This mechanism, distinct from CYFIP2 haploinsufficiency, supports allele-specific therapeutic strategies for Arg87 variants.
papers.title: Imbalance between RNA-binding proteins and the WAVE regulatory complex underlies the toxic gain-of-function effects of the CYFIP2 Arg87Cys variant in neurodevelopmental disorders

papers.abstract: Andrographolide, a labdane diterpenoid isolated from A. paniculata has been investigated for activity in a broad panel of biological contexts, including its anti-inflammatory, antiviral, and anticancer properties. Previously, A-ring analogs of andrographolide bearing silyl and trityl ethers at C19 have demonstrated improved in vitro anticancer activity in human cancer cell lines, with putative activity through the Wnt1/{beta}-catenin signaling axis. In order to investigate the activity of this series of C19 andrographolide analogs, alongside a cyclic A-ring acetonide analog, as anticancer agents in murine cancer cell models, we evaluated antiproliferative activity of these compounds in B16F10 melanoma, CT26 colorectal adenocarcinoma, Neuro2a neuroblastoma, and 4T1 mammary ductal carcinoma cell lines, and found that most compounds exhibited potent micromolar level anticancer activity. Among these, all trityl ethers exhibited nearly indistinguishable IC50 values of 4-20 M, and generally exhibited greater potency compared to C19 silyl ether analogs. This anticancer activity was further validated through apoptosis flow cytometry, wherein we concluded that our compounds induced apoptosis to a greater extent than the parent compound, andrographolide. Further, we examine the role of modulation of canonical Wnt1/{beta}-catenin signaling in a series of co-delivery assays with CHIR-99021, a selective GSK-3{beta} kinase inhibitor, and MSAB, a selective {beta}-catenin degrader. Finally, we demonstrate that a selection of silyl ether analogs of andrographolide elicit cell cycle arrest by flow cytometry in a manner that is decoupled to in vitro potency trends. Altogether, we report the first in vitro evaluation of trityl and silyl ether analogs of andrographolide within murine adherent cancer cells.
papers.title: C19 trityl and silyl andrographolide analogs exhibit in vitro anticancer activity in murine cancer models

papers.abstract: The Congo rainforest was the heartland of the Bantu Expansion, yet its demographic history remains partially understood. We inferred past population dynamics using genomes from 960 sub-Saharan Africans, including four newly sequenced ancient individuals from Iroungou cave and 176 present-day individuals from Gabon. Bantu-speaking populations began differentiating ~4,000 years ago, preceding explosive population growth by a millennium. Distinct southward dispersals contributed to the ancestry of Bantu speakers in Gabon and elsewhere in sub-Saharan Africa, with the ~700-year-old Iroungou individuals providing the closest genetic proxies for the latter. Both Bantu speakers and hunter-gatherers from the Congo rainforest experienced a major demographic crisis ~1,500 years ago, coinciding with an archaeological hiatus. These findings illuminate early Bantu dispersals and the subsequent, unexplained collapse of rainforest populations.
papers.title: A 4,000-year genomic history of Bantu speakers from the Congo rainforest

papers.abstract: Orienting coordinates movements of the eyes, whiskers, nose, and other effectors, but how the superior colliculus (SC) recruits these components over time remains unclear. We combined unilateral optogenetic activation of SC GABAergic neurons with high-speed tracking of facial movements and Neuropixels recordings to examine SC-evoked orienting in head-fixed mice. Stimulation recruited movements of the whiskers, nose, eyes, and pupil. Horizontal eye and nose movements were directed contralateral to the stimulated hemisphere, whereas vertical eye movements, pupil dilation, and whisker protraction did not differ significantly between stimulation sides. Nose and whisker movements generally preceded eye movements, followed by slower pupil dilation, revealing a temporally organized response. Recordings from the SC contralateral to the stimulated hemisphere revealed heterogeneous neuronal responses comprising short-latency excitation and delayed excitation or inhibition. Short-latency excitation was similar on trials with and without evoked movements, whereas delayed excitation was greater on trials that evoked eye or nose movements. Neurons modulated during spontaneous nose movements showed corresponding optogenetically evoked responses, linking stimulation-induced activity to endogenous movement-related activity. Thus, activation of SC GABAergic neurons initiates evolving population activity that recruits a coordinated sequence of orienting movements.
papers.title: Coordinated orienting behavior emerges following unilateral optogenetic activation of Superior Colliculus GABAergic neurons

papers.abstract: This study establishes a unified pipeline for generating human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons (iMNs) with defined hindbrain, cervical, and lumbar identities to support anatomically resolved studies of motor neuron development and degeneration. Conventional differentiation methods can efficiently produce iMNs but provide limited control over rostrocaudal identity and frequently generate populations with heterogeneous HOX profiles. We addressed this limitation by optimizing developmental morphogen combinations and treatment windows, establishing three complementary protocols that reproducibly generated hindbrain/rhombomere-associated motor neurons (RiMNs), cervical motor neurons (CiMNs), and lumbar motor neurons (LiMNs) across iPSC lines from six non-diseased donors balanced by sex. Transcriptomic and protein analyses demonstrated graded rostrocaudal specification from RiMNs through CiMNs to LiMNs, together with region-appropriate motor neuron subtype features. These identities showed the expected relationships to human week 9 fetal rostrocaudal HOX programs. High-density multielectrode array analysis further revealed synchronized network firing, electrically active neurite networks, and enhanced axonal signal propagation in the regional iMN populations compared with conventionally differentiated iMNs. Spike-sorted recordings additionally revealed protocol-associated differences in single-neuron electrophysiological profiles.
