We define optimality as the stability of thermal niche estimates derived from empirical data, rather than as an agreement with a known true distribution. The framework integrates two complementary approaches. The Last Stable Thinning Parameterization (LS-TP) identifies the largest thinning intensity that preserves the stability of species-specific niche descriptors. Biogeographic-size Dependent Thinning Parameterization (BD-TP) links thinning intensity to species' geographic range size and scales spatial filtering across taxa with different distributional properties. Using seagrasses as a model system, we evaluated the framework across a global compilation of more than 100,000 occurrence records. Our results showed that optimal thinning parameters varied systematically with species range size and that uniform thinning approaches led to either excessive information loss or reduction of spatial clustering. Furthermore, the framework identified species for which available data did not support stable niche characterization, as these species failed to meet stability criteria even at the smallest thinning parameters. We recommend explicitly acknowledging this limitation in future studies and prioritizing increased sampling effort for such undersampled taxa. Our approaches provide a first step toward explicit, data-driven spatial thinning parameterization, with direct implications for ecological niche modelling, biodiversity assessment, and climate-driven distribution analyses.
papers.title: Stop guessing thinning distances: a data-driven framework for spatial thinning parametrization for ecological modelling

papers.abstract: An unusually divergent Plasmodium vivax parasite was reported in a Swedish patient with recent travel. Using whole-genome sequencing, we show that the infection was caused by a strain of ape P. vivax-like, providing evidence of the zoonotic potential of these parasites that infect wild gorillas and chimpanzees in central Africa.
papers.title: Human infection with an ape Plasmodium vivax-like parasite

papers.abstract: We introduce a multimodal microscope that combines quantitative oblique back-illumination microscopy (qOBM) with wide-field epi-fluorescence deconvolution microscopy to acquire intrinsically co-registered phase and fluorescence volumes of fresh, bulk tissue. Using paired qOBM phase and DAPI fluorescence images of fresh ex vivo mouse brain tissue, we train a supervised conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to predict DAPI-like nuclear contrast from the structural information encoded in the phase images. Results not only demonstrate high-fidelity image translation but also show improved imaging depth and more homogeneous staining. Additionally, we combine the qOBM phase contrast with captured or virtual fluorescence nuclear images to produce volumetric pseudo-H&E representations of fresh tissue, enabling a supervised approach for achieving robust virtual histological staining. This work paves the way for virtual fluorescence imaging of many more structural targets and supervised virtual histological staining of thick, unaltered, bulk tissues ex vivo and potentially in vivo. Such capabilities could have significant implications for biological research as well as for point-of-care, intraoperative, and other clinical applications.
papers.title: Multimodal epi-mode 3D quantitative phase and fluorescence microscopy enables supervised volumetric virtual fluorescence in bulk tissue

papers.abstract: MyD88 is a universal adaptor that connects to Toll-like receptors and interleukin-1 receptors through its Toll/IL-1R homology (TIR) domain and activates inflammatory signaling via its death domain (DD). However, how MyD88TIR serves as the platform for these functions and if it has additional functions remain unclear. Here, we report cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of MyD88TIR and its cancer-specific mutant L252P (previously L265P) mainly in ring and spiral forms, respectively. Both assemblies are formed by antiparallel double-filaments, using canonical TIR interfaces within each strand but unique surfaces between the strands, and position MyD88DD at the same sides of the assemblies for self-oligomerization and pathway activation. Surprisingly, these WT or L252P filaments are bound to dsDNA using the concave sides of the rings and the spirals. In vitro assays and cellular studies establish that MyD88 directly binds dsDNA and promotes inflammatory cytokine expression, particularly pro-IL-1{beta}, following dsDNA transfection or viral infection. Notably, these responses are unaffected by deficiency of UNC93B1, the essential chaperone required for trafficking endosomal nucleic acid-sensing TLRs. Structure-guide MyD88 mutant that disrupts dsDNA binding specifically compromises dsDNA-induced transcriptional program while maintaining TLR signaling. RNA-seq further reveals that MyD88 plays a crucial role in inducing gene expression upon dsDNA sensing and that about half of cGAS-dependent genes are also MyD88-dependent. Together, our structural, biochemical and genetic data support the findings that MyD88 directly engages with cytosolic dsDNA and cooperates with cGAS to promote the full innate immune transcriptional response.
papers.title: Structures of MyD88 and its oncogenic mutant reveal DNA binding with implications for cytosolic DNA sensing

papers.abstract: Short tandem repeats (STRs) are highly mutable, multiallelic variants with distinctive mutation dynamics and have been associated with phenotypic variation across diverse species. However, genome-wide STR variation remains poorly characterized in olive, and the large number of naturally occurring alleles creates a challenge for variant interpretation. Genomic language models offer a potential way to assess how STR length changes alter learned sequence representations, but their responses to natural multiallelic STR series have not been systematically evaluated. Here, we identified 117,119 polymorphic STRs across 212 Iranian and Mediterranean olive accessions. STRs recovered the major SNP-defined ancestry axes while resolving additional geographically structured subcomponents. We then quantified STR-induced embedding perturbation using three plant genomic language models: AgroNT, PlantCAD2, and GPN. Across all three models, embedding distance generally increased with repeat-length difference from the reference allele, and 7,417 loci were embedding-sensitive in all three models. These signals were robust to fixed-length input construction and exceeded those of matched nonrepetitive indels at most tested loci. Integration with oil-composition associations prioritized four exploratory loci supported by all three models. Overall, we provide a genome-wide olive STR resource and show that plant genomic language models capture reproducible responses to natural STR length variation. Combining cross-model embedding evidence with phenotype association provides a potential framework for prioritizing candidate STRs for further investigation.
papers.title: Interpreting Short Tandem Repeat Variations with Genomic Foundation Models in Olive

papers.abstract: Accurate bacterial promoter prediction supports genome annotation, but many models use fixed-length promoter windows anchored to transcription start sites (TSSs) rather than promoter-element boundaries. We developed the General Bacterial Promoter Predictor (GBactPro), a convolutional neural network-bidirectional long short-term memory (CNN-BiLSTM) framework using promoter sequences resolved by the Promoter Architecture Scanner. Using Escherichia coli-trained models evaluated across 43 bacterial species, we compared eight input designs and identified the contiguous -35/spacer/-10 core as optimal (mean AUROC = 0.9859). Species-specific models showed broad transfer in a 43 x 43 evaluation. Joint training on all 43 species achieved a mean AUROC of 0.9943 across their held-out test sets and outperformed four established predictors under matched-length benchmarks. In genome-wide E. coli scanning, GBactPro achieved AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.979 and 0.160 under stringent full-containment matching (0-bp tolerance), increasing to 0.997 and 0.323 under a 100-bp tolerance. False-positive predictions overlapped H-NS binding regions more frequently than true positives (24.4% versus 18.8%), and predictions also overlapped promoters derepressed in an H-NS-knockout dataset. Prediction precision varied across four TSS classes. These findings demonstrate that element-resolved promoter definitions improve cross-species prediction and support genome-wide identification of candidate bacterial promoters.
papers.title: GBactPro: cross-species bacterial promoter prediction using element-resolved promoter definitions

papers.abstract: Black alder (Alnus glutinosa) is a native tree species in the British Isles, which it colonised after the last glaciation from continental refugia. It is now a widespread pioneer species, thriving on wetlands and riverbanks. We present whole genome sequence data for 324 alder seedlings grown from seed collected from 44 populations across the UK. Among these we found two triploids and one sample with trisomy at chromosome five. Removing these, we found little population genetic structure apart from diverging northern populations with lower diversity. Using Latent-Factor Mixed Models (LFMM) analyses we identified 1,364 loci whose allele frequencies were significantly associated with environmental variables. Of these loci, 93% were associated with the number of snow days. In contrast, the greatest total genomic signal (variance in SNP effect sizes of 7.38 million SNP loci) was observed for mean temperature of the wettest quarter and annual number of frost days. Estimates of maladaptation using 1.49 million SNPs, predicted that northern populations are worst adapted to present and future worst-case climates. Our results suggest that similarity of source-site temperature variables should be prioritised when choosing seed sources for new planting, and northern populations could benefit from assisted gene flow from the south.
papers.title: Genomic signals of local adaptation in UK black alder populations (Alnus glutinosa)

papers.abstract: Cardiac damage in the aftermath of myocardial ischemia / reperfusion (MI/R) compromises both electrical and mechanical function, predisposing patients to arrhythmia and heart failure. Microvascular obstruction (MVO) is increasingly recognized as a sequela of MI/R and a contributor to proarrhythmic cardiac remodeling. While transvalvular unloading (TVU) using a percutaneously delivered pump is garnering appreciation as a means of limiting infarct size and preserving mechanical function following percutaneous coronary intervention, its benefits for arrhythmia prevention remain unclear. We used a porcine model to test the hypothesis that cardiac unloading prior to and through reperfusion mitigates MVO, preserves cardiomyocyte nanostructure, and alleviates arrhythmias following MI/R. Anesthetized domestic swine undergoing acute ischemia (LAD occlusion, 90 mins) and reperfusion (120 mins) were randomized to TVU (n=5) and no treatment (control; n=6) treatments. Thioflavin-S was infused into the mid-LAD to assess coronary microcirculation and quantify MVO. Arrhythmia burden was assessed by in vivo electrocardiography using 3 lead EKG. Cardiac tissues were preserved for histology and optical microscopy studies. Compared to no treatment controls, TVU hearts evidenced significantly reduced infarct area (48 +/- 5 % vs. 59 +/- 11 % p = 0.03) and MVO (19 +/- 4 % vs. 27 +/- 5% , p = 0.03) normalized to area at risk and a higher myocardial salvage index (52 +/- 5 % vs. 41 +/- 11% p = 0.03). Extensive perivascular edema, and neutrophil infiltration observed in controls was markedly reduced in TVU hearts. Confocal microscopy and spatial pattern analysis revealed significantly mitigated disruption of gap junctions and NaV1.5 dissociation from N-cadherin in TVU hearts compared to controls. Importantly, severity-adjusted arrhythmia burden during reperfusion was significantly lower in TV-P hearts (8+/-8 vs. 12+/-5 episodes lasting greater than 5seconds in controls). Our results demonstrate that TVU effectively prevents arrhythmias during reperfusion by preserving coronary microvasculature and cardiomyocyte nanostructure.
papers.title: Cardiac unloading via a transvalvular pump prevents arrhythmias following myocardial ischemia / reperfusion by preserving coronary microcirculation and cardiomyocyte nanostructure

papers.abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) control post-transcriptional gene expression by regulating RNA processing, localization, stability, and translation. However, our understanding of RNA regulation remains limited by the resolution, scale, and uniformity of available RBP binding maps. Here we introduce eclair CLIP (ecCLIP), a high-throughput CLIP-seq platform that combines endogenous protein tagging for uniform affinity capture with ligation-free library preparation to generate high-resolution RNA-protein binding profiles. We applied ecCLIP to 67 endogenously tagged RBPs in HEK293T cells, generating a high-quality transcriptome-scale atlas that recovered known binding preferences and captured post-transcriptional regulons linked to RNA half-life. To test the utility of the atlas, we incorporated ecCLIP into Borzuki, a Borzoi-derived sequence-to-function model trained on complementary RNA degradation, expression, CLIP, and Perturb-seq data. Inclusion of ecCLIP data improved RNA half-life prediction and assessment of 3' UTR variant effects on RNA stability, demonstrating that our atlas helps capture RNA dynamics. To directly model the cis-regulatory grammar underlying these RBP-RNA interactions, we developed Pythia, a structure-aware neural network architecture that incorporates context-free grammar-inspired fixed convolutions to explicitly encode RNA base-pairing features. Pythia predicted RBP binding from sequence and structural context and decomposed predictions into sequence- and structure-dependent components. We tested this decomposition for five RBPs using massively parallel reporter CLIP (MPRC) binding assays in cells, using synthetic RNA libraries containing mutations designed to preserve or disrupt predicted RNA structures across nominated binding sites. We used the same MPRC strategy to confirm allele-specific binding effects for variants prioritized by Pythia. Together, ecCLIP and Pythia provide a resource for structure-aware decoding of RNA-protein interaction grammar and interpretation of post-transcriptional regulatory variation.
papers.title: A high-resolution protein-RNA binding atlas for structure-aware interaction prediction and post-transcriptional regulatory modeling

papers.abstract: Transcription factors are critical regulators of homeostasis, and disruption of their function is a common underlying mechanism in cancer. The homeobox Myeloid Ecotropic Integration site-1 (Meis1) and its binding partner Homeobox A9 (HoxA9) are among the most highly dysregulated transcription factors in cancer, particularly in Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). Upregulation of HoxA9 is observed in more than 50% of AML cases and is a predictor of poor prognosis. Meis1 forms a cooperative DNA complex with HoxA9 and is required for HoxA9-mediated leukemogenesis. However, the mechanism by which HoxA9 and Meis1 interact and form a complex with DNA is unknown. To study the molecular mechanisms behind the HoxA9-Meis1-DNA complex and support future development of inhibitors, we describe optimized procedures for the recombinant expression and purification of full-length Meis1 and HoxA9. The constructs with an N-terminal His-tag showed degradation, but the addition of a small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO)-fusion tag improved solubility and stability for both proteins. Conditions were optimized for SUMO cleavage to obtain tag-free Meis1 and HoxA9 with high purity. We showed that both purified proteins bound to DNA with nanomolar affinities using a fluorescence polarization (FP) binding assay. The SUMO-fusion HoxA9 showed a distinct binding profile compared to the tag-free HoxA9 and formed a cooperative complex with Meis1. The tag-free HoxA9 appeared to oligomerize under the assay conditions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report to visualize the HoxA9-Meis1 cooperative interaction in a high-throughput assay. Our work establishes a foundation for future studies to decipher the protein-protein interaction of Meis1-HoxA9 and the development of inhibitors.
papers.title: Strategies for Overcoming the Purification Challenges of Meis1 and HoxA9 and Their Functional Characterization

papers.abstract: Background: Head acceleration events (HAEs) are common in contact sports, but season-long exposure and its relationship with cognitive performance in amateur British American football remain poorly characterised. Methods: Thirty male players were recruited from three British amateur American football teams. Selected Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 (SCAT6) components and computerised tasks were assessed across the season. Seasonal analyses included 20 participants, and exposure-linked analyses included 17. Helmet-sensor events were attributed to participants and restricted to participant-assignment and baseline-to-post-season calendar windows. Mixed-effects models assessed seasonal outcomes. Principal component analysis (PCA) summarised standardised baseline-to-post-season changes, and six exposure associations were evaluated. Results: Players recorded a mean of 768 (SD 482) events. Several individual tests improved across the season. The first principal component (PC1) explained 21.9% of change variance and had loadings with opposing signs. Prior seasons had a nominal association with PC1 (slope -0.153, 95% CI -0.305 to -0.00018; r2=0.233; p=0.0498), which did not survive six-test Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) adjustment (p=0.299). No in-season exposure association survived adjustment. Conclusion: Repeated-test performance improved, while exposure associations remained uncertain. The mixed PC1 pattern cannot be interpreted as a uniform measure of global cognitive worsening or improvement.
papers.title: Season-long head acceleration exposure, prior contact-sport history, and cognitive performance in British amateur American football players

papers.abstract: This work presents DSSNA (Define Spatial Structure of Nucleic Acids) v2026, a free and open-source standalone GROMACS module for the automated analysis of nucleic acid structures from atomic coordinates that reproduces the core functionality of X3DNA and DSSR while extending it to the analysis of molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories. The algorithm identifies and classifies canonical and non-canonical base pairs, hydrogen-bond networks, stacking interactions, helices, and other elements of nucleic acid secondary and tertiary structure, using neighbor-search algorithms for efficient analysis of large trajectory datasets and a modular output system that lets users select the structural metrics required for a particular analysis. Application to a 1 s MD trajectory of a GUAA tetraloop mutant of the sarcin--ricin domain of Escherichia coli 23S ribosomal RNA (PDB: 1MSY) showed that persistent canonical base pairs form the structural core that maintains the secondary-structure profile, whereas most non-canonical base pairs and stacking interactions are transient. These results demonstrate that DSSNA enables the characterization of both static nucleic acid structures and the temporal evolution of structural interactions in MD simulations.
papers.title: DSSNA: Automated Nucleic Acid Structure Analysis in Molecular Dynamics

papers.abstract: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) predict checkpoint-inhibition response, and conventional dendritic cells (cDC) are required to build and maintain them. What licenses tumor niches is not fully understood: chemokines recruit cells but do not specify TLS-archetypal DC:CD4+T:CD8+T triad composition. We show that the organizing signal is a matrix fragment. Proteoglycan versican (VCAN) proteolysis releases the matrikine versikine constitutively in CXCL13-replete germinal center light zones. In tumors, versikine is released inducibly within CXCL13-rich stromal niches. Versikine activates CD11b+ cDC, expands cDC1, and suffices for triad assembly. Versikine-conditioned DC engage progenitor-exhausted CD8+ T-cells (Tpex) and Tpex-sustaining, Th1-polarized follicular helper CD4+ T-cells. Excess unproteolyzed VCAN inverts this toward DC-Treg crosstalk and Tpex loss. Versikine (mRNA or recombinant protein) plus anti-PD-L1 eradicated experimental tumors reverse-translated to model adverse-prognosis, VCAN-proteolysis-weak patients from a prospective PD-1 blockade trial in oligometastatic colorectal cancer. The extracellular matrix instructs, rather than merely scaffolds, the multicellular units of antitumor immunity.
papers.title: A matrikine organizes the dendritic cell- T cell triads that build tertiary lymphoid structures

papers.abstract: Neutrophils are among the first immune cells recruited to fractures, yet their contribution to bone repair remains poorly understood. Anti-inflammatory use has been linked to increased risk of non-union fractures, while prolonged neutrophil activity or failed clearance of neutrophil-derived DNA in the form of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), can also impair fracture healing. Using dynamic live imaging and cellular perturbation in adult zebrafish, we show that neutrophils play a key role in shaping the early fracture microenvironment. Neutrophils rapidly accumulated at fractures where they released NETs and exhibited the activation of gene programmes associated with matrix remodelling. Compromising neutrophil recruitment, via ibuprofen treatment or orthogonal genetic and pharmacological perturbations, dramatically increased incidence of fracture non-union and lead to altered callus architecture through delay of osteoblast differentiation and impaired mineralisation. Mechanistically, neutrophils actively interacted with key structural proteins, including laminin, fibronectin, and collagen I, through uptake, recycling and active de novo secretion pathways. Together, our findings reveal that neutrophils establish a provisional emergency fracture matrix that templates subsequent bone repair, providing a mechanistic link between early non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) exposure and impaired skeletal healing.
papers.title: Ibuprofen impairs fracture healing by disrupting neutrophil-mediated tissue repair

papers.abstract: Auxin is a key phytohormone that regulates all aspects of plant growth, development, and environmental responses, making the precise analysis of its distribution and signaling essential for understanding plant adaptation and physiological processes. However, despite the agricultural importance of oilseed rape (Brassica napus), the lack of robust, species-specific molecular tools limits detailed studies of hormone signaling in this crop. Here, we developed and characterized reporter systems for the sensitive visualization and quantification of auxin distribution and signaling in B. napus. The DR5cc auxin signaling reporter and a novel synthetic auxin-responsive reporter, BIP3, assembled from promoter fragments of three oilseed rape Aux/IAA genes, were generated to drive GUS expression. In hairy roots, both reporters showed auxin-responsive expression in the root apical meristem that became broader after auxin treatment. In transgenic seedlings, flowers at anthesis, and 12-day-old embryos, DR5cc exhibited a more defined expression pattern than BIP3. To monitor real-time auxin dynamics under abiotic stress, DR5cc fluorescent reporters were employed in hairy roots. Mannitol and NaCl treatments induced a time-dependent increase in fluorescence, peaking at 6-12 h before returning to basal levels after 24 h. Furthermore, dual-reporter assays enabled simultaneous monitoring of auxin and cytokinin signaling, revealing distinct hormone-specific spatial responses in hairy roots. Finally, we established a quantitative DII (qDII) reporter system using degron domains from B. napus Aux/IAA proteins, providing a quantitative readout of auxin depletion. Together, these reporter systems enable spatial, temporal, and quantitative analyses of auxin dynamics during development and stress adaptation in oilseed rape.
papers.title: Development of auxin reporters in oilseed rape (Brassica napus)

papers.abstract: Cellular heterogeneity is a major confounder in bulk DNA methylation data for epigenome-wide association studies. Existing reference-based DNAm deconvolution methods often ignore hierarchies among related cell types and may generalize poorly across datasets due to limited variability in reference profiles. We developed HOMED (Hierarchically Optimized Methylation Deconvolution), a framework that integrates cell-lineage hierarchies, single-cell RNA sequencing-guided deconvolution, and paired bulk RNA-seq/DNAm data for CpG signature optimization. Across simulated and real peripheral blood mononuclear cell, lung, and placental datasets, HOMED consistently yielded the highest PCCs and lowest RMSEs, outperforming existing scRNA-seq-guided DNAm deconvolution methods, improving accuracy, resolution, and cross-tissue generalizability.
papers.title: HOMED enables hierarchical and multimodal optimization of DNA methylation deconvolution across tissues

papers.abstract: Background: The vaginal microbiome is a key determinant of women's health, with Lactobacillus-dominant communities protecting against bacterial vaginosis (BV) and related adverse outcomes. Dysbiosis involves a decline in lactobacilli and overgrowth of anaerobes, with Gardnerella species central to initiating polymicrobial aggregates. However, the genetic determinants of community assembly, biofilm formation, and interspecies interactions remain poorly understood. This study investigated the genomic and functional basis of these traits using an integrated multi-omics approach. Results: Long-read whole-genome sequencing of clinical Gardnerella isolates yielded closed genomes and revealed a pangenomic split correlating with high- versus low-biofilm phenotypes, linked to clade-specific genomic islands and allelic variants. Functional gene modules within these regions distinguished G. vaginalis from G. piotii, contributing to nutrient acquisition, cell wall metabolism, and colonization. Integrated 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and proteomics of all pairwise dual-species co-cultures of five key vaginal bacteria showed that G. vaginalis and L. iners acted as dominant ecological drivers, outcompeting neighbors and triggering asymmetric proteomic remodeling. Differential expression of a gene within a putative operon encoding a conserved type II secretion/Tad pilus system, revealed by integrating the pangenome with the proteome, implicated this system in interspecies interactions. AI-based structural predictions of the complex suggested isoform-specific differences in protein folding between G. vaginalis and G. piotii. In parallel, metagenomic analysis of 93 women showed the operon was more abundant in BV samples than in healthy controls, linking it to dysbiosis. Integrated metabolomics further identified a methyl-{beta}-carboline compound elevated in Prevotella bivia-containing co-cultures that selectively inhibited G. vaginalis and P. bivia while sparing L. crispatus. Several dipeptides influenced growth and biofilm formation of vaginal microbes, and methyl-{beta}-carboline and sphingosine additionally inhibited multidrug-resistant pathogens, suggesting new strategies for managing polymicrobial infections. Conclusions: This work links Gardnerella genomic features to virulence-associated phenotypes and demonstrates how interspecies interactions shape community dynamics and antimicrobial metabolite production. The findings support a model in which biofilm capacity is genetically encoded within an accessory genome, deployed through tailored proteomic responses, and modulated by an interaction-specific metabolic landscape, providing a foundation for identifying bioactive molecules and developing diagnostics and targeted therapeutics to restore and maintain vaginal health.
papers.title: Multi-omics uncover interactions in the vaginal microbiome and a type II secretion/Tad pilus system in Gardnerella species

papers.abstract: Fluorescent biosensors that report protein conformation in vivo have been invaluable for understanding how the spatio-temporal dynamics of signaling controls cells. However, for GTPases these biosensors report the activated conformation using reagents that block the binding of downstream proteins, generating dominant negative effects and altering normal cell physiology. We present here a generalizable design to make GTPase biosensors (AlloRac1 and AlloCdc42), in which a circularly permuted fluorescent protein is inserted into a conserved loop allosterically connected to the effector binding site, generating activity-dependent fluorescence without blocking ligand interactions. The Rac1 biosensor showed that effector interactions led to increased Rac1 activation, indicating an auto-regulatory positive feedback made visible by the new biosensor design. This feedback regulated the kinetics and localization of Rac1 activity, including Rac1 activity gradients that controlled motility. Feedback was generated through Rac1 interaction with the effector Pak1, which led to further activation of Rac1 by the guanine exchange factor {beta}-Pix. The new biosensor approach enables quantitative imaging of previously obscure spatio-temporal dynamics in GTPase regulation.
papers.title: Allosteric Biosensors Unravel GTPase-Effector Feedback

papers.abstract: **Background:** Misfolded alpha-synuclein (alphaSyn), a common co-pathology in Alzheimer's disease, acts synergistically with amyloid and tau in animal models, but its role in the human amyloid-tau-cognition cascade is unclear. We examined whether alphaSyn modifies the amyloid-tau and tau-cognition associations, cross-sectionally and over time. **Methods:** We analyzed 615 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative with a cerebrospinal fluid alphaSyn seed amplification assay (SAA), flortaucipir tau positron emission tomography (PET) in Braak stage regions, and amyloid PET and domain-specific cognitive composites within 1 year of tau PET. Linear models with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors tested alphaSyn x amyloid interactions on regional tau and alphaSyn x tau interactions on cognition; mixed-effects models tested the same interactions on repeated tau PET (n = 341) and cognitive testing (n = 516). **Results:** alphaSyn positivity was present in 117 participants (19.0%). Cross-sectionally, the amyloid-tau association was steeper in alphaSyn SAA+ participants for meta-temporal tau (interaction beta 0.258, 95% CI 0.023 to 0.493; p = 0.032) and Braak I-IV (p <= 0.048); no interaction survived false discovery rate correction (q = 0.072), and clinical-stage adjustment attenuated it (beta 0.114; p = 0.333). Over a median of 3.5 years (n = 341; 68 alphaSyn-positive), no alphaSyn x amyloid x time interaction was detected (meta-temporal beta -0.012, 95% CI -0.046 to 0.023; p = 0.513). No cross-sectional alphaSyn x tau interaction on cognition was detected; at mean tau, alphaSyn positivity was associated with lower executive function (q = 0.032). Longitudinally, tau-related executive decline was less steep in alphaSyn-positive participants (q = 0.042). **Conclusions:** The alphaSyn-associated amyloid-tau interaction was modest, did not withstand multiple-testing correction, and had no detected longitudinal counterpart. alphaSyn positivity was associated with poorer executive function at mean tau; the unexpected longitudinal executive interaction needs replication. These findings do not establish alphaSyn status as a marker for tau-progression enrichment in trials.
papers.title: Alpha-Synuclein Co-Pathology and Amyloid-Tau Coupling in Alzheimer's Disease: Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Analyses Across Braak Stage Regions

papers.abstract: As antibiotic resistance poses a major threat to global health, phage therapy offers an alternative to antibiotic treatments in the face of multidrug-resistant bacteria. However, host resistance to phages is also well-documented. Current computational tools for phage cocktail design do not explicitly address the evolution of phage resistance, let alone through the profiling of bacterial receptors whose variability drives much of phage resistance. We introduce PhagePickr, a computational pipeline for the automated design of phage cocktails intended to reduce the risk of host resistance. Unlike other tools, PhagePickr selects phages based on bacterial surface receptor similarity and prioritizes genomic diversity with the aim of reducing cross-resistance. The tool uses receptor annotations to identify phenotypically similar hosts via a nearest-neighbor algorithm and uses multiple sequence alignments to ensure genomic diversity in the final cocktail. We evaluated the utility of PhagePickr on ESKAPE pathogens and two understudied bacterial species. The cocktails included candidate phages selected using bacterial receptor similarity and phage genomic divergence, comprising both lytic phages with confirmed therapeutic potential and novel candidates from similar species. We demonstrate the tool's utility in generating cocktails and its capacity to scale as current databases are updated. PhagePickr provides a novel bacteria-centric framework for resistance-aware cocktail design by exploring shared phenotypes.
papers.title: PhagePickr: A bacteria-centric computational tool for designing resistance-aware phage cocktails

papers.abstract: Cell division in large embryos is coordinated by spatial waves of Cyclin B-Cdk1 activity that spread through the cytoplasm and drive cortical contractility. However, it remains unclear how cell size and nuclear enrichment of Cyclin B-Cdk1 shape these waves, and how the cytoplasmic signal is transmitted to the cortex. Here we couple established reaction-diffusion models of Cyclin B-Cdk1 signaling and the excitable Rho-actin cortex to ask how cell geometry and elevated nuclear Cyclin B-Cdk1 concentration shape cytoplasmic wave propagation in spherical cells. We find that cytoplasmic waves consist of two distinct parts: an activation front that propagates in a manner consistent with trigger-wave behavior, and a wave back controlled by concentration gradients in the cell cycle oscillator. Because these parts are generated by different mechanisms, they can move at different speeds or even in opposite directions, depending on nuclear size and effective cell size. This yields a simple geometric explanation for why surface contraction waves propagate in opposite directions in starfish oocytes and Xenopus embryos, without invoking system-specific cortical mechanisms. Coupling the Cdk1 signal to the cortex further shows how cytoplasmic waveforms regulate Rho-actin dynamics through inhibition of the Rho GEF Ect2. Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework linking localized nuclear activation, cytoplasmic Cdk1 waves, and cortical responses in large embryonic cells.
papers.title: Geometry shapes cytoplasmic Cdk1 waves that drive cortical dynamics

papers.abstract: Historically, neural variability observed during task was interpreted as noise, assumed to obscure meaningful signal and thus something to be minimized both analytically by researchers and functionally by the brain. Changes to this signal-to-noise ratio have been proposed as a possible neural mechanism behind the increased reaction-time variability (RTV) in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, not all variability is the same - in some cases, variability can have some underlying statistical structure that can be beneficial to information processing. The challenge lies in distinguishing meaningful variability from random noise. The edge-of-synchrony critical point, which describes a system poised between synchronous and asynchronous regimes, could be a good theoretical framework to study these different types of neural variability. In this study, we investigate whether changes in criticality and oscillatory dynamics preceded slower behavioral responses during a bimodal continuous performance task in ADHD. We find evidence that, prior to slower responses, neural dynamics shift toward criticality in both ADHD and control groups, suggesting that increase variability in ADHD and during attention lapses are related to structured variability and not necessarily random noise. Notably, these findings run counter predictions based on the proposed model and previous literature on neural noise in this population, challenging predictions of edge-of-synchrony criticality as a unifying account of neural variability and behavioral performance. Furthermore, this effect did not emerge at the between-subject level, underscoring the limitations of relying on between-subject correlations to infer neural mechanisms.
papers.title: Beyond Neural Noise: Critical Dynamics Predict Slower Reaction Times in Adults With and Without ADHD

papers.abstract: Background: Schizophrenia is a severe neuropsychiatric disorder. Efforts to describe the underlying biology and establish diagnostic markers through non-invasive neuroimaging methods are ongoing, resulting in a range of theoretical brain-based frameworks. Prominent frameworks for aberrant schizophrenia-associated functional connectivity in resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) include the dysconnectivity hypothesis, theory of cognitive dysmetria, and triple network theory. Although informative, prior work can be improved by increasing sample size, avoiding confirmation bias, and accounting for individual variability and the effects of medication and chronicity. Methods: With these recommendations in mind, we employed a data-driven, whole-brain approach using a large multi-site rsfMRI dataset (N = 2,656; schizophrenia = 1,248). We used reference-guided independent component analysis to generate subject-specific whole-brain functional network connectivity (FNC) and extract imaging markers of similarity to schizophrenia patterns. We modeled the relationship between medication dosage, age of onset, chronicity, symptom severity, and cognitive performance and FNC. Results: Our analysis identified a reliable schizophrenia-FNC signature characterized by aberrantly stronger negative cerebellothalamic and positive thalamocortical connectivity, implicating sensory, motor, and associative cortical circuits. While medication and chronicity were significantly associated with these signatures, the core cerebellothalamic disruptions remained a robust marker of schizophrenia. Conclusions: This work represents the largest schizophrenia-specific rsfMRI study to date, refines existing theoretical frameworks with a more nuanced map of how clinical variables interact with brain connectivity, and provides a high-fidelity template of schizophrenia-related connectivity. We have released this template as an open-access resource to facilitate reproducibility and accelerate the development of reliable rsfMRI-based schizophrenia biomarkers.
papers.title: NeuroMark-SZ: A Holistic Resting-State-fMRI-Based Model for Divergent Functional Circuitry in Schizophrenia

papers.abstract: Background selection (BGS), the indirect effect of purifying selection at linked and unlinked sites, is a key evolutionary process shaping genomic patterns of variation. Calculating the expected diversity at neutral sites experiencing BGS relative to that under strict neutrality (referred to as B-value or simply B) is important for developing null models when performing population genomic inference, in particular, demographic inference and detection of selective sweeps. We extend and integrate previous theory to estimate B-values analytically, assuming no selective interference, with novel expressions to account for gene conversion between proximal sites. Here, we present the B-value calculator, Bvalcalc, an easy-to-use command-line interface written in Python for efficient analytical calculation of expected genome-wide B at single base-pair resolution. Bvalcalc has several modules for calculating diversity as a function of distance from a single selected element or considering the multiplicative effects of all selected elements across the genome, accounting for recombination maps, gene conversion, self-fertilization, single population size changes, and unlinked effects from other chromosomes. We validated the effectiveness of Bvalcalc with comparisons against simulated results, and generated B-maps for the model species Homo sapiens, Drosophila melanogaster and Arabidopsis thaliana as a proof of concept using public data. Bvalcalc is available with documentation at johrilab.github.io/Bvalcalc/.
papers.title: The B-value calculator: expected diversity with background selection

papers.abstract: In the genomics age, enormous volumes of DNA sequencing information are continuously produced and analysed. Pipelines for processing DNA information are widespread and mature. However, tools for rendering sequence and methylation information can be limited, often resulting in authors taking varied, manual approaches to visualising their DNA sequences. ggDNAvis is designed to easily produce high-quality renders of DNA sequence and methylation information, with extensive customisation options. The three core features are visualisation of a single DNA sequence, multiple sequences at once, or methylation of multiple DNA molecules at once. Additionally, ggDNAvis has tools for reading, writing, processing, and organising genetic data from file formats such as FASTQ to extract suitable inputs to the main visualisation functions. Single-sequence visualisation accepts any DNA or RNA sequence of any length from any source, and is thus extremely versatile and useful in a wide range of biological contexts. Multiple-sequence visualisation was conceived in the context of visualising many long-read sequencing (e.g. Nanopore) reads over causative genes of short tandem repeat (STR) expansion diseases such as neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID) caused by NOTCH2NLC, Huntington's disease (HD) caused by HTT, and fragile X syndrome (FXS) caused by FMR1, but is generally applicable for visualising any set of multiple sequences. Methylation visualisation requires read-level methylation data, which is most commonly obtained through modification-capable basecalling of signal-level Nanopore data. ggDNAvis functionality is available as a Shiny web app and an R package on CRAN, with outputs from the latter supporting extension and annotation via the diverse ggplot2 ecosystem.
papers.title: ggDNAvis: a ggplot2-based R package for creating high-quality DNA sequence and modification visualisations

papers.abstract: RNA polymerase II transcripts are capped with N7-methylguanosine (mG), a conserved modification important for mRNA function. Although traditionally viewed as constitutive, we developed a mass spectrometry-based method to demonstrate that in both yeast and mammalian cells, a substantial population of mRNAs lack cap methylation in response to SAM-limiting conditions and other stress conditions, which may be frequently encountered across organisms. Through developing two transcriptome-wide approaches, we found that methylation is enriched on specific transcripts and uncovered an unexpected connection between histone H3K36me3 and cap methylation, with both marks preferentially associated with stress-responsive MAPK signaling pathways. Strikingly, cap-unmethylated mRNAs exhibit features of canonical mRNAs. They are polyadenylated, exported to the cytosol, and translated. Enforced cap methylation reduces cell growth under SAM limitation, suggesting that unmethylated mRNAs confer an adaptive advantage during stress. These findings establish mRNA cap methylation as a modification responsive to metabolic stress and a previously underappreciated layer of gene expression control.
papers.title: Metabolic stress reveals widespread accumulation of cap-unmethylated RNAs

papers.abstract: The animal cell division cycle is initiated by the cyclin-dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6 in complex with D-type cyclins. Cyclin D-CDK4/6 complex formation is promoted by the assembly factors p21 and p27, which bind both subunits. p27 binds the hydrophobic patch on cyclin D that is similar to the patch used by other cell cycle cyclins to dock their substrates. This raised the question as to how cyclin D could find its substrates if its hydrophobic patch were already occupied? Here, we show that D-type cyclins use their A2' helix to dock the retinoblastoma protein Rb, a key substrate regulating cell cycle progression. The specific interface of cyclin D's A2' helix is unique among cyclins and its mutation slows proliferation. Taken together, our work identifies a cyclin D-substrate docking mechanism that can be targeted by novel cancer therapeutics.
papers.title: Identification and inhibition of the Cyclin D Rb-docking interface that drives cell division

papers.abstract: Single-cell genomics requires methods that account for technical variation while preserving biological signals, remain tractable at atlas scale and support analyses beyond visualization, but existing approaches discard the fitted correspondence that could connect these tasks. Here we introduce scBIOT, a biologically informed optimal-transport framework that formulates single-cell alignment as an explicit and inspectable coupling between cells. scBIOT incorporates prior biological knowledge to preserve known cell identities, compresses transport through prototypes for large datasets and quantifies gene-level changes induced by alignment using coupling-derived transport scores. Across transcriptomic and spatial mapping benchmarks, scBIOT balanced biological conservation, batch correction and label-transfer accuracy while distinguishing batch-associated stress responses from biological immune and drug-response programs. Prototype transport scaled coupling-based analysis to approximately 100 million perturbed cells. Because the coupling encodes probabilistic correspondences rather than only corrected coordinates, the same fitted coupling supports state mapping, trajectory inference, perturbation analysis, multimodal comparison and spatiotemporal localization. Applications to cancer, hematopoiesis and embryonic development identified condition-specific cell states, modality-dependent regulatory programs and spatially resolved developmental transitions. Informed, scalable and unified transport couplings therefore link atlas alignment to downstream biological inference within a single framework.
papers.title: Informed, scalable and unified transport couplings for single-cell alignment and downstream inference with scBIOT

papers.abstract: Comparative genomics and synthetic biology require models that can interpret, annotate, and design DNA sequences across species, yet genomic models have not combined these capabilities beyond a few well-characterized organisms. Here we introduce Nucleotide Transformer v3 (NTv3), a long-context cross-kingdom foundation model that provides a common backbone for functional prediction, gene annotation and controllable sequence generation across phylogenetically diverse species. NTv3 is pre-trained on more than 128,000 genomes using sequences up to 1Mb and post-trained on 16,262 functional tracks across 15 animal and plant genomes. NTv3 performs comparably to AlphaGenome on matched human assays and matches or exceeds evaluated published models for functional-track prediction across 19 species spanning mammals, birds, fish, plants, fungi and protists. Ablation experiments show that both genome pre-training and expanding functional supervision from human and mouse to 15 species improve track prediction. Leveraging these learned functional representations, NTv3 outperforms leading ab initio gene predictors across mammals, plants and insects, with fewer spurious gene models and improved recovery and reduced fragmentation of long genes. Finally, the same representations can be used with discrete diffusion to design regulatory DNA sequences with specific activity levels. We demonstrate this in plant and fly promoters and enhancers, and experimentally validate the activity and promoter selectivity of the generated fly enhancers. Together, NTv3 unifies genome interpretation, gene annotation and regulatory sequence design across the animal and plant kingdoms, with direct relevance to agriculture, biodiversity research and biotechnology.
papers.title: A multispecies foundation model for genome function prediction, gene annotation and sequence design

papers.abstract: The authors have withdrawn this manuscript because of concerns regarding the reliability of the data. Therefore, the authors do not wish this work to be cited as reference for the project. If you have any questions, please contact the corresponding author.
papers.title: WITHDRAWN: PD-L2 Regulates Natural Antibody and IL-10 Secretion by B-1 cells

papers.abstract: Computational models of genomic responses to environmental perturbations identify genes underlying physiological adaptation, but their utility requires further evaluation. Often, gene activity reflects both adaptive mechanisms and noise. Here, we develop a framework that leverages public databases to support the subselection of biologically supported model genes involved in temperature responses. We test our framework on a model that identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and categorized some into Key-Response, Treatment-Specific, Noisy, and Support groups based on inter-individual gene expression variability before and after treatment. The first three groups were hypothesized to constitute a Principal Response. To validate these groupings, we constructed protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks using the Human Protein Atlas and STRING. The main contribution of this work is the implementation of second-order connections restricted to those made via DEGs, ensuring connectivity reflects condition-specific responses rather than generic hubs. We show applying our DEG filter to second-order connections can change the conclusions drawn from the same selected gene sets. Support Group genes also showed strong interconnectivity and overlap with housekeeping genes. STRING confirmed PPI enrichment but produced less stable results. By emphasizing DEG-restricted second-order protein interactions, we address limitations of context-free enrichment methods and strengthen biological evaluation of computational models of differential gene expression. Our framework is designed to support the prioritization of subsets of DEGs for experimental follow up but not to predict exactly how an environmental input produces a physiological output.
papers.title: A Condition-Informed Framework for Evaluating Temperature-Responsive Gene Sets Using Protein Interaction Data

papers.abstract: Litter management plays a critical role in broiler production, affecting bird health, performance, and environmental impact. This preliminary study evaluated the effects of IndigoLT, a biological amendment, in combination with a 40% sodium bisulfate (NaHSO) regimen on litter microbiome composition, compared to a standard NaHSO-only treatment. Litter samples (n = 18) were collected from three commercial broiler houses following flock removal: one control (NaHSO-only), one treated with IndigoLT for a single flock, and one treated for two consecutive flocks. The V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was sequenced to assess prokaryotic community composition. Alpha diversity metrics (Faith's phylogenetic diversity, observed ASVs, Pielou's evenness, Shannon diversity) did not differ significantly across treatments (ANOVA, p > 0.05). In contrast, PERMANOVA analyses of Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, Weighted and Unweighted UniFrac distances revealed significant shifts in {beta} diversity between IndigoLT-amended and control groups (q < 0.05), with no significant differences between the one- and two-flock IndigoLT treatments. Core microbiome and differential abundance analyses suggested that IndigoLT, when paired with reduced NaHSO input, may accelerate organic matter decomposition, promote nitrogen retention, and suppress potentially pathogenic taxa. Although limited by the absence of baseline sampling and biological replication, these findings suggest that IndigoLT influences litter microbial succession. Future work should aim to optimize inclusion rates most complementary between NaHSO and IndigoLT to enhance litter quality, reduce NH volatilization, and support bird health.
papers.title: Poultry Litter Microbiome Shifts in Commercial Broiler Houses Following a Biotic-Based Litter Treatment

papers.abstract: Apico-basal polarity is essential for maintaining cytoskeletal organization and regulating transport and secretory functions in the intestinal epithelium. The opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa exploits the interactions between cell polarity and cytoskeletal networks to promote infection. However, most mechanistic insights into these processes have come from in-vitro epithelial monolayers, which do not fully capture the complexity of multicellular tissues. Here, we show that heat-labile factor/s secreted by P. aeruginosa disrupt apical polarity in Caenorhabditis elegans enterocytes through a PI3K-AKT-dependent mechanism. This disruption is accompanied by apical enrichment of PI(3,4,5)P3, fragmentation of ARP-2/3 organization, localized disruption of apical F-actin, release of F-actin-rich vesicles into the intestinal lumen, and pronounced deformation of the apical surface. Perturbing CDC-42-ARP-2/3-dependent actin assembly, PI3K-AKT signalling, or the endotube regulators, IFB-2 and IFO-1 suppressed intestinal deformation and significantly extend host survival following P. aeruginosa exposure. Notably, these changes occured without detectable loss of epithelial tissue integrity. Together, our findings identify epithelial polarity disruption as a mechanism through which extracellular P. aeruginosa remodels the host cytoskeleton and alters tissue mechanics during infection.
papers.title: P. aeruginosa disrupts ARP-2/3 mediated apical F-actin organization to induce intestinal deformation in C. elegans

papers.abstract: Understanding the processes leading to the emergence of new lineages is one of the major tasks of macroevolution as a scientific field. Multiple commonly used models and metrics allow to estimate the rates of species diversification at the tips of phylogenetic trees, and are thus potentially useful for predicting future evolutionary success of individual extant lineages. However, the predictive performance of these methods has never been tested with real-world data. Here we use a new approach to quantify the relationship between predictor tip rates and subsequent diversification rates derived from a probability distribution of numbers of daughter species. We explore if and how well the tip-rate methods predict near-future diversification using temporal slices across large fossil and extant tetrapod phylogenies. We find that tip rate estimates from these methods do predict diversification in all four extant and one out of three fossil phylogenies. The quality of these predictions varies across the tested methods, with the model-free approach being more robust overall but likelihood-based models delivering correctly scaled diversification rates. Our results suggest that future cladogenesis can be predicted using existing tip rate methods, but only moderately well and likely dependant on factors that are difficult to evaluate in practical applications.
papers.title: Phylogenies can be used to predict future diversification but with limited success

papers.abstract: Latent inhibition (LI) refers to the reduced ability to learn or express learning about a stimulus following prior exposure to it without consequence. It has been extensively studied to investigate associative learning and memory as well as the aberrant attribution of salience to irrelevant stimuli in both humans and animals, a process which is thought to underpin hallucinations and delusions in psychosis. Despite sex differences observed in numerous aspects of psychosis, few studies have attempted to characterise sex differences in LI. This systematic review outlines the current evidence of sex differences in LI in both human and rodent studies, showing predominantly inconclusive and conflicting evidence for sex differences. However, the majority of cases in which sex differences were found were in studies that assessed the impact of additional factors on LI such as drug administration, juvenile handling, and oestrous phase, and demonstrated interactions between sex and these additional factors. Hence, there is stronger evidence for sex differences in vulnerability to perturbations in LI. Furthermore, we present data demonstrating sex differences in latent inhibition of contextual fear conditioning and associated gene expression in the hippocampus in rodents, suggesting sex differences in hippocampal processing underpinning latent inhibition at both the behavioural and neurobiological levels. Although there have been relatively few studies demonstrating sex differences in LI identified by the systematic review, the data suggest that in hippocampally dependent forms of LI, sex differences may be more apparent, which may be of relevance in relation to sex differences in the presentation of psychosis.
papers.title: Sex differences in latent inhibition and their implications for psychotic disorders

papers.abstract: E. coli curli, an archetypical bacterial amyloid, is a critical biofilm scaffold comprised mainly of the CsgA protein. CsgA is highly aggregation prone, confounding high-resolution studies of its structure and amyloid formation mechanism. Ensemble studies show that monomeric CsgA is intrinsically disordered, while structure predictions show a well-folded {beta}-solenoid. Here, single-molecule force spectroscopy with optical tweezers is used to define the conformational dynamics in single CsgA molecules. CsgA monomer shows unfolding/refolding consistent with fully folded, partially folded and collapsed molten globule conformations, indicating that CsgA exists in metastable folded states in equilibrium with disordered states. These folded states are likely highly aggregation prone and thus have avoided characterization at the ensemble level. Steered molecular dynamics simulations reveal unfolding patterns consistent with the experimental data. These studies help us better understand curli amyloid formation that is important both as a novel antimicrobial drug target and engineered biomaterial.
papers.title: Single molecule studies of the bacterial curli protein CsgA reveal a structurally dynamic monomeric structure

papers.abstract: RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by hierarchical structure, making structural information important for pre-training. Existing approaches often depend on noisy annotations or task-specific objectives that can limit generalizability. Here we present structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model pre-trained on 21 million RNA sequence--structure pairs by integrating base-pairing interactions into masked language modelling through a pair-matching operation. We also introduce MUSES, a multi-source ensemble of secondary structures designed to mitigate predictor bias, and a dynamic masking ratio that balances structure-guided and nucleotide-level masking. structRFM learns joint sequence and structure representations as sequence-level, nucleotide-level and pairwise features for broad downstream adaptation. It ranks among the leading models in zero-shot homology classification and establishes new benchmarks for secondary-structure prediction. Its tertiary-structure adaptation, Zfold, consistently improves both three-dimensional predictions and their extracted secondary structures, with performance comparable to AlphaFold3 across CASP15-natural, CASP16 and RNA-Puzzles. structRFM also improves performance on function-prediction tasks and generalizes to newly released RNA families and long non-coding RNAs. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight multimodal RNA language models for robust structural and functional inference. The complete 21-million-pair dataset, model weights and source code are openly available to support multimodal RNA foundation-model development.
papers.title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction

papers.abstract: Recent years have seen rapid growth in sequence-to-function (S2F) models that predict diverse molecular readouts from DNA sequence alone. However, these models have faced criticism for their limited accuracy in predicting individual-level gene expression. AlphaGenome, a state-of-the-art S2F model, excels across a range of sequence-based prediction tasks, but its utility for personal expression prediction remains incompletely assessed. Here, we evaluate AlphaGenome's ability to predict tissue-specific, personal gene expression and find that it significantly outperforms its predecessor, Enformer. Across 1,000 genes and 11,471 eligible gene-tissue pairs, AlphaGenome significantly outperforms Enformer for 3,103 pairs, whereas Enformer significantly outperforms AlphaGenome for 828 pairs, yielding a win ratio of 3.75. This imbalance is supported by a global permutation test (P = 2.0e-4), with a median correlation difference of 0.046. Nevertheless, pretrained AlphaGenome substantially underperforms Elastic Net and Random Forest trained on individual-level data. These findings demonstrate that AlphaGenome better captures individual-specific gene expression variation than Enformer, while highlighting substantial room for improvement in sequence-based prediction of personal gene expression.
papers.title: AlphaGenome Enhances Personal Gene Expression Prediction but Retains Key Limitations

papers.abstract: In the natural world, genetic isolation between closely related species is often maintained by direct F1 hybrid sterility or hybrid breakdown in subsequent generations. This phenomenon is also observed in microorganisms within species of the Saccharomyces clade, including the model organism Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Members of Saccharomyces intermate and historical hybridization events have left genomic footprints, but these hybrids are themselves sterile and produce very few viable offspring. Previous work suggests a main cause of F1 hybrid sterility is the action of mismatch repair machinery. The sequence divergence between two parent Saccharomyces species--from ~10% to ~20%--is recognized by the cell as an aberrant attempt to recombine nonhomologous chromosomes during meiosis I, leading to massive nondisjunction and aneuploidy. Deletion of mismatch repair machinery improves fertility in hybrids of S. cerevisiae and its sister species S. paradoxus but leads to increased mutation accumulation during normal mitotic growth. To overcome this drawback, conditional alleles that specifically repress expression of mismatch repair machinery during meiosis have been applied in S. cerevisiae x S. paradoxus hybrids with success. Here, we describe the application of the meiotic null system to a different hybrid: S. cerevisiae x S. uvarum. The system does not increase hybrid fertility likely due to increased sequence divergence and chromosomal translocations, but mass spore recovery and flow cytometry enable the recovery of near-haploid offspring which inherit an assortment of parental chromosomes. These populations of mixed hybrid genomes can be leveraged in phenotypic studies to further understand the effects of hybrid genomes on organismal fitness.
papers.title: Meiotic null MSH2 and SGS1 alleles in S. cerevisiae x S. uvarum hybrids result in near-haploid offspring with mixed parental chromosomal inheritance

papers.abstract: The use of levodopa to manage Parkinsons disease (PD) symptoms leads to levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) and other motor fluctuations, which worsen with disease progression and repeated treatment. Aberrant activity of striatal D1- and D2-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-/D2-MSNs) underlies LID, but the mechanisms driving its progression remain unclear. Using the 6-OHDA mouse model of PD/LID, we combined in vivo and ex vivo recordings to isolate the effect of repeated treatment in LID worsening and other changes in the motor response to levodopa. We found that LID worsening is linked to potentiation of levodopa-evoked responses in both D1-/D2-MSNs, independent of changes in dopamine release or MSN intrinsic excitability. Instead, strengthening of glutamatergic synapses onto D1-MSNs emerged as a key signature. Moreover, we found changes in D2-MSN activity are associated with LID duration, which paralleled a reduction in D2R sensitivity. These findings reveal striatal adaptations contributing to worsening of levodopa-related complications.
papers.title: Repetitive Levodopa Treatment Drives Cell Type-Specific Striatal Adaptations Associated With Progressive Dyskinesia in Parkinsonian Mice

papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques have received increasing interest for their potential to enhance memory function, a fundamental cognitive aspect of daily life. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the efficacy of transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) in enhancing memory function in healthy adults, following the pre-registered strategy at PROSPERO (CRD42022353630). A total of 113 articles (193 trials, 7,299 participants) examining tES were identified. Meta- analysis revealed a significant overall effect of tES on memory function compared with sham stimulation (standardised mean difference [95% confidence interval] = 0.19 [0.12, 0.25]). A positive pooled effect was also observed in the subgroup receiving frontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). Stimulation was associated with positive pooled effects for working- and declarative-memory task performance. Significant pooled effects were observed within 1 day after stimulation; longer-term estimates were imprecise. Regarding adverse events, tingling and itching sensations on the scalp occurred more frequently in the active group than in the sham group, but no serious adverse events were reported. Limitations, including small- study effects, heterogeneity, and uneven coverage of memory domains, were noted, emphasising the need for improved experimental rigour and diversification of memory tasks. These findings suggest that tES is associated with small improvements in memory-task performance and was generally well tolerated under the studied protocols. Heterogeneity, small- study effects, and limited adverse-event reporting constrain conclusions about efficacy, durability, and safety
papers.title: Transcranial electrical stimulation for memory enhancement: A systematic review and meta-analysis

papers.abstract: In addition to its role in episodic memory and spatial navigation, the hippocampus has also been found to influence mood-related disorders such as anxiety and depression. These seemingly distinct roles are consistent with a functional dissociation between the two anatomical poles of the hippocampus: whereas the dorsal portion of the hippocampus in rodents is necessary for spatial tasks, the ventral portion controls affective behaviors. We have recently found that neurons in the ventral, but not dorsal, CA1 area of mice encode anxiety-related information (i.e. are "anxiety cells") in diverse defensive and exploratory behaviors. Still it is unclear how general threat-related information is computed within the hippocampal circuit. In this work, we have examined how distinct hippocampal subregions and cell types encode anxiety-related information by imaging calcium activity in large populations of genetically-defined neurons in the ventral hippocampus while mice explore the elevated plus maze (EPM), a conflict-based anxiety test. We compared the neural encoding of task-related features within the ventral CA1 (vCA1) and ventral dentate gyrus (vDG) regions in order to examine the emergence of anxiety-related activity through the hippocampal circuit. We found that granule cells (vGCs) of the vDG represented similar valence information to neurons in vCA1 in the form of arm-type specific encoding in the EPM, which suggests that encoding of anxiety-related features is already present at this first stage of hippocampal processing. When compared with ventral granule cells (vGCs), ventral mossy cells (vMCs) underlying the DG had stronger spatial encoding and less valence encoding, suggesting that they may be more functionally connected with the highly spatially sensitive dorsal hippocampus. Together these findings will help to understand the encoding of anxiety-related information in the hippocampus and how it relates to neural circuit defects in mood-related disorders.
papers.title: Distinct representations of an anxiogenic environment in different cell types of the ventral hippocampus

papers.abstract: Stem cell-derived {beta}-like cells (SC{beta} cells) are an alternative to cadaveric {beta} cells for replacement therapy in type 1 diabetes. However, SC{beta} cells face a multitude of stresses. Both {beta} cells and SC{beta} cells reside in complex microtissues and are modulated by hundreds of autocrine/paracrine signals. Here, we leveraged multi-omics data from late-stage SC{beta} cells and human islets to map ligand-receptor pairs and generate a prioritized list of ligands for high-content SC{beta} cell survival screening. Our medium-throughput screen tracked cell number, cell death, and INS production over several days using automated, high-content imaging. Members of the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) family significantly prevented cytokine-induced cell death, with the top validated hits being FGF4, FGF5, and FGF8F. With these results, there is the potential to improve SC{beta} cell survival in vitro via readily targetable pathways and to produce a more robust product for translation to the clinic.
papers.title: A prioritized medium-throughput screen identifies fibroblast growth factors as protective for human stem cell derived insulin secreting beta cells

papers.abstract: Epileptogenesis, the process through which the brain becomes seizure-prone, is not well understood. Previous work identified a novel gene in Drosophila, julius seizure (jus), that when mutated or developmentally knocked down, leads to epilepsy in adult Drosophila, providing a useful model for dissecting epileptogenesis. Here we report that when a GFP-tagged Jus was used as bait in a co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assay, a complex of 23 associated proteins was identified that included ATPalpha and Nervana 3, two subunits of the Na+/K+ ATPase. RNAi-mediated knockdown of ATPalpha, Nervana 3, or any of 8 additional complex proteins enhanced seizure susceptibility of jus mutants. The critical period for Jus expression to protect against epileptogenesis was further defined, occurring between pupal stages P4-7; remarkably, the jus seizure phenotype could be rescued by increasing neural activity of jus-expressing neurons during these mid-pupal stages, suggesting that altered neural activity in these neurons may contribute to the seizure phenotype. Our data support a model that, in wild type flies, a protein complex containing Na+/K+ ATPase and Jus prevents epileptogenesis, possibly by regulating neural activity.
papers.title: A Complex Containing the Na+/K+ ATPase Regulates Epileptogenesis in Drosophila melanogaster

papers.abstract: The Ralstonia solanacearum species complex is a group of genetically diverse plant wilt pathogens. We created a database that documents the reported global distribution and host range of Ralstonia clades (e.g. phylotypes and sequevars). In this sixth release, we have cataloged information from 353 sources that report one or more Ralstonia strains isolated from 113 countries or territories. Metadata for nearly 14,000 strains are available as a supplemental table. We continue to maintain this database and the RSSC KBase Narrative. More detailed information regarding specific methods can be found in previous versions of this living pre-print. Recent reports expand the known distribution of several lineages: Ralstonia syzygii subsp. syzygii in Brazil, Ralstonia syzygii subsp. celebesensis (Banana Blood Disease lineage) in continental Asia, and phylotype I in Europe. The interactive Ralstonia Diversity Dashboard https://ralstoniadashboard.shinyapps.io/ RalstoniaWiltDashboard/ ) has been updated with this new version of the dataset. Additionally, this version of the living pre-print has new visualizations.
papers.title: A Meta-analysis of the known Global Distribution and Host Range of the Ralstonia Species Complex

papers.abstract: The two cerebral hemispheres specialize while remaining interconnected. Does greater structural asymmetry imply less connectivity, and does connectivity also relate to how asymmetry changes during development? We addressed these questions in three independent cohorts spanning birth to 22 years, measuring asymmetry as the magnitude of the left-right difference in association tract overlap across 74 homotopic cortical region pairs. The regional pattern of asymmetry was similar across cohorts. In all three cohorts, more asymmetric regions had lower connectional density to cortical and non-cortical targets. However, involvement of the corpus callosum, the major pathway connecting the hemispheres, showed no consistent inverse relationship with regional asymmetry across cohorts. Instead, callosal involvement conditioned the relationship between mean regional asymmetry and its age-related change. In the two older cohorts, greater mean asymmetry accompanied more positive age effects among regions with appreciable callosal overlap, whereas this relationship was weak or negative among regions with little callosal overlap (standardized interactions +0.42 and +0.56). The pattern replicated across the two cohorts at matched ages, and longitudinal region-mean estimates in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development cohort were similar in direction and magnitude. In the youngest cohort, regions converged toward the mean, narrowing the between-region spread by 12%, with no detected callosal moderation. More asymmetric regions have lower overall connectional density, whereas callosal involvement helps explain how regional asymmetry changes with age.
papers.title: Cortical asymmetry and its developmental change have distinct relationships with brain connectivity

papers.abstract: GABAergic interneurons are fundamental to the normal function of neuronal circuits in the neocortex. A growing literature has highlighted the role of somatostatin-expressing interneurons (SST-INs) in regulating cortical activity, and inhibition of SST-INs by other interneurons has emerged as a circuit motif leading to disinhibition of pyramidal neurons. However, the diversity and regulation of GABAergic inputs to SST-INs are only partially understood. Here, we combined widefield and 2-photon optogenetic stimulation of parvalbumin (PV)- and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing interneurons with recordings from fluorescently identified SST-INs in layer 2/3 of primary visual cortex (V1). Our results show that both PV- and VIP-INs form inhibitory inputs onto SST-INs but with varying functional properties. PV-INs evoke strong, fast inhibition onto perisomatic regions of their target cells, while VIP-INs evoke slower inhibition onto target cell dendrites that is partially mediated by alpha subunit-containing GABA receptors. Cholinergic modulation through muscarinic receptors strongly suppresses PV-IN output while adrenergic modulation through beta receptors enhances VIP-IN output. Computational modeling suggests that these parallel inhibitory pathways can differentially regulate circuit gain and network stability across different inputs and arousal conditions. Thus, the diversity of disinhibitory GABAergic circuits in the neocortex provides a mechanism for state-dependent flexibility in circuit function.
papers.title: Cholinergic and adrenergic modulation sculpts parallel inhibition of SST-INs in visual cortex

papers.abstract: Linking genetic variants to their functional consequences at scale remains a major challenge in human genetics. Perturb-seq is limited in the variants it can install, while prime editing has largely been restricted to simpler mechanistic readouts. Here, we introduce prime editing perturb-seq (PEP-seq), which links programmed mutations to transcriptomic states. We designed 2,164 prime editing guides targeting common expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), premature termination codons, and position-matched synonymous controls, generating 749,110 time-resolved single-cell transcriptomes. PEP-seq precisely detected nonsense-mediated decay, while probe-based junction measurements suggested depletion of mature RNAs. For eQTLs, a locus-size-corrected specificity metric showed that the intended target was frequently the most affected transcript within a 1 Mb window, with effects also associated with open chromatin near the edit site. These results establish PEP-seq as a scalable platform for direct, endogenous variant-to-function mapping.
papers.title: Scalable variant-to-function screens using prime editing perturb-seq

papers.abstract: (1) Dissimilarity indices offer an effective way to represent multivariate variability in community composition and to quantify beta diversity and its drivers. However, models that regress dissimilarities against environmental predictors face the challenge of linking site-level predictors to a pairwise response. (2) This mismatch is typically circumvented by regressing dissimilarities against distances in predictor values. But this approach does not reflect how environmental variables act on individual samples, complicates the inclusion of standard modelling features such as random effects, and conflates environmental effects on average composition with effects on compositional dispersion. (3) We propose Reduced-Rank Generalised Dissimilarity Modelling (RRGDM), a framework for model-based ordination that resolves the pair-to-site mismatch by reframing dissimilarity modelling as an ordination problem. RRGDM represents dissimilarities as the outcome of sample positions in a shared, low-dimensional latent space that captures community composition. These positions are in turn modelled as a linear function of predictors and error terms, with an associated dispersion sub-model. (4) Through a simulation study and two empirical examples, we show that RRGDM recovers known environmental effects and represents them as ecologically interpretable outputs. RRGDM enables inference on the relative importance of environmental gradients driving beta diversity and disentangles effects on composition versus dispersion. Although motivated by beta diversity, the approach is applicable to other pairwise dissimilarity data.
papers.title: Reduced-Rank Generalised Dissimilarity Modelling (RRGDM): Model-Based Ordination of Dissimilarity Data
