Here, we evaluated CRISPR-mediated transcriptional activation (CRISPR-ON), based on a dCas9-VPR transcriptional activator, as a strategy to upregulate endogenous Stxbp1 expression in a Stxbp1-haploinsufficient (Stxbp1+/-) mouse model. Screening of guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting the Stxbp1 promoter in Neuro2A cells identified a multiplexed four-gRNA cassette that elevated Stxbp1 mRNA approximately six-fold. AAV-PHP.eB vectors co-expressing this 4xgRNA cassette and Cre recombinase under the EF1a promoter were administered intracerebroventricularly to neonatal Stxbp1+/-/dCas9-VPRfl/+ mice. CRISPR-ON treatment raised brain Stxbp1 mRNA in Stxbp1+/- mice to 1.5-fold the level of wild-type controls, whereas Munc18-1 protein was restored to the wild-type level. In small exploratory cohorts, spike-wave discharge frequency and attack counts tended to be lower in CRISPR-ON-treated than in untreated Stxbp1+/- mice; the discharge data, from two animals per group, were not tested statistically, and the difference in attack counts was not significant, so efficacy cannot be judged from the present data. Locomotor activity was normal in untreated mutants and unaffected by treatment; reduced body weight was not rescued. Together, these findings establish that CRISPR-ON can correct Stxbp1/Munc18-1 expression in vivo, whereas its effect on disease phenotypes remains to be determined.
papers.title: CRISPR-mediated Stxbp1 gene activation restores Munc18-1 levels in Stxbp1-haploinsufficient mice

papers.abstract: Cerebral cortex organoids are powerful in vitro models that recapitulate key features of human development. However, conventional methods produce cortical organoids with spontaneous, spatially disorganized cortical regions due to limited control over morphogen distribution within local environments. Here, we present a spatially engineered hydrogel platform that drives localized formation of posterior signaling centers in cortical organoids through controlled, localized exposure to morphogens. Using a combination of bulk photopolymerization, thermal crosslinking, and digital light processing (DLP) approaches, we fabricated hydrogels with stiffness-controlled layers that preferentially deliver morphogens to one side of the organoid, selectively inducing the expression of posterior markers on the exposed face. We further validated this platform by delivering fluorescently tagged dextran, used as molecular weight-matched model morphogens, to visualize spatiotemporal delivery dynamics at the organoid interface. As a proof of principle, we also demonstrated that DLP fabrication enables the printing of dual morphogen hubs, serving as a model for establishing two opposing gradients within a single organoid. Together, this hydrogel platform enables systematic spatial patterning of cell populations in organoids, more faithfully recapitulating the spatial organization and cellular diversity of native tissues and advancing higher-fidelity models for studying human development and disease.
papers.title: Spatial engineering of posterior signaling centers in cerebral organoids via controlled morphogen exposure within hydrogels

papers.abstract: Surface factors of Staphylococcus aureus have become therapeutic targets, including staphylococcal protein A (SpA), a key contributor to virulence. SpA displays five nearly identical helical ({approx}60 aa) antibody-binding domains on the bacterial surface with high affinity (Kd {approx}0.4-4 nM). Folding free energies have been determined for only domains E and B. Here we used intrinsic fluorescence detected urea denaturation to measure the folding thermodynamics of each domain in isolation and in the native multidomain context (SpA-N, the N-terminal half of the mature protein). Domains D, A, B, and C have identical stabilities in isolation and in SpA-N, confirming independent folding; E domain is stabilized ({approx}1 kcal/mol by its multidomain context. To determine role of the conserved linker between domains D through C we used fluorescence-detected urea denaturation of 1-5 B-domain repeat constructs. Analysis of these data using a nearest-neighbor matrix model demonstrated unambiguously that adjacent domains are thermodynamically uncoupled. We also find a steep N- to Cterminal gradient of increasing domain stability (0.97 {+/-}0.05 to 5.69 {+/-}0.28 kcal/mol), which has not been reported for any repeat protein. We propose this gradient facilitates efficient co-translational secretion of SpA through the SecYEG translocon: the least stable E domain enters the channel first, lowering the energetic barrier to translocation of this highly abundant surface protein.
papers.title: An evolutionary strategy for highly efficient secretion of multidomain Staphylococcal protein A: N- to C-terminal stability gradient

papers.abstract: Mitochondrial density in dendrites adapts synaptic inputs to sustain local ATP and Ca2+ buffering. During long-term depression (LTD), synapse elimination is accompanied by activation of caspase-3 through sublethal mitochondria-derived apoptotic signals. However, upstream signals that link synaptic activity to mitochondrial remodeling remain unknown. Here we show that Na+ influx through NMDA receptors depolarizes mitochondria during chemically induced LTD. This triggers stabilization and activation of PINK1 in a translation-dependent manner, leading to asynchronous mitochondrial fission. Na+ influx and PINK1 are required for cLTD-induced fission, and blocking either prevents caspase-3 activation and spine shrinking in cultured neurons. Together, these findings identify a Na+-PINK1 signaling that couples NMDA receptor activity to mitochondrial fission and caspase-3-dependent synapse elimination during LTD, with implications for the homeostatic regulation of synaptic density
papers.title: A physiological Na+ signal activates mitochondrial PINK1 to couple synaptic depression to caspase-3-dependent spine pruning

papers.abstract: Cancer transcriptomes nominate many disease-associated long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), but functional prioritization remains difficult. Here, we integrated recurrent tumor upregulation, clinical association, co-expression network context, and malignant epithelial detectability across colorectal, gastric, and esophageal cancers, identifying five lncRNAs with convergent clinical and network support. We selected the intergenic lncRNA LINC01094 for functional characterization in colorectal cancer (CRC). Across 52 CRC cell lines, endogenous LINC01094 expression defined a transcriptional state linking higher expression to extracellular matrix, adhesion, and inflammatory programs and lower expression to DNA replication, mitochondrial, and ribosome/RNP programs. Acute CRISPR interference (CRISPRi)-mediated depletion in HCT116 cells produced a nearly inverse transcriptional response; among 764 GO terms significant in both analyses, 748 (97.9%) changed in opposite directions (Pearson r = -0.962). Functionally, LINC01094 depletion impaired cell growth in both HCT116 and Caco-2 cells. In HCT116 cells, depletion reduced DNA synthesis despite induction of replication-associated transcriptional programs and was accompanied by increased {gamma}H2AX, CHK1 Ser345 phosphorylation, and p21 accumulation without detectable apoptotic execution. {gamma}H2AX foci were also elevated within residual EdU-positive nuclei. The predominant LINC01094 transcript in HCT116 cells was nuclear-enriched, whereas SLPI, a reported effector of a cytoplasmic miR-1266-5p/SLPI ceRNA model in CRC, was not reproducibly altered following LINC01094 depletion in either CRC model. These findings link LINC01094 to maintenance of a CRC-associated transcriptional state and show that its acute disruption is accompanied by impaired productive DNA synthesis, replication-associated DNA-damage signaling, and checkpoint activation, supporting a broader, context-dependent role for LINC01094 beyond previously described pathway-specific models.
papers.title: Pan-gastrointestinal prioritization links LINC01094 to a colorectal cancer transcriptional state and replication-associated checkpoint activation

papers.abstract: Metagenomes facilitate Escherichia coli strain-level profiling in human gut microbiomes, informing our understanding of colonisation diversity and the genetic features distinguishing infection from carriage. Among numerous reference-based tools for short-read metagenomic strain-level profiling, the best approach remains unclear. Here, we benchmarked six publicly available tools--PanTax, PathoScope 2.0, StrainGE, Strainify, StrainR2 and StrainScan--for their ability to detect co-existing strains of E. coli and estimate their relative abundance across real and simulated metagenomes of increasing complexity with varying reference database composition. We show that the tools varied substantially in both the number and relative abundance of strains predicted, indicating that despite being designed for the same broad purpose, they produce markedly different representations of strain composition from the same metagenomic samples. StrainR2 achieved the highest F1 score across our experiments (0.995) and successfully distinguished all strains within a complex, 10-strain spike-in mixture containing strains sharing up to 99.9% average nucleotide identity and included in a 304-strain E. coli reference database. However, when ground-truth strains were removed from the reference database to mimic the profiling of samples of unknown strain content PathoScope 2.0 and StrainGE performed strongest: both estimated phylogroup abundances accurately and frequently correctly assigned strain identities to the closest available genomic neighbours to the ground truth. Computational requirements also varied substantially (median runtime: 0.11-68.45 h; peak memory: 2.08-351.53 GiB). Collectively, these results demonstrate that tool selection should reflect the intended application, and we provide practical guidance on the relative strengths and use cases of each approach. These findings will facilitate characterisation of E. coli strain-level diversity within short-read gut metagenomes with greater accuracy than previously possible.
papers.title: Benchmarking strain-level profiling of Escherichia coli in short-read gut metagenomes

papers.abstract: Protein repeats give rise to diverse protein structures and functions, yet their sequence-based detection is often challenging because individual repeat units can diverge substantially in sequence while retaining similar structures. Most sensitive approaches rely on sequence information directly represented by alignments or derived profiles, thereby limiting flexibility and scalability. Here, we introduce TREAD (Transfer learning-based REpeat Annotation using Protein EmbeDdings), a supervised framework that reformulates repeat detection as a residue-level annotation problem and operates directly on embeddings from protein language models. Instead of constructing explicit probabilistic profiles, TREAD learns repeat-specific features implicitly, enabling residue-resolved scoring and flexible repeat segment extraction. Across complementary benchmarks based on RepeatsDB and Pfam, TREAD consistently matches or outperforms the widely used profile-based tool HMMER, particularly in low-data and high-divergence settings. The model exhibits robustness to score thresholding and demonstrates better generalization to independent test sets, including those containing remotely related families. To illustrate the practical utility of TREAD, we applied it to survey {beta}-propeller proteins across the AlphaFold Database and representative proteomes to generate a comprehensive census of this fold. This analysis highlights extensive propeller diversity, identifies lineage-specific expansion patterns across the tree of life, and suggests previously unrecognized relationships between propellers and other repeat folds. Together, TREAD provides a flexible and scalable alternative to profile-based repeat annotation and establishes a general motif-centric framework for protein sequence annotation.
papers.title: Beyond profiles: supervised repeat annotation using protein embeddings

papers.abstract: Purpose: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disease that affects motor control but can also influence sensory perception. Changes in vision and proprioception are well-documented but less is known about how PD alters auditory perception, particularly perception of speech acoustic properties. The current study examined perception of speech rate and intensity in PD and the relationship of auditory perception to disease severity. Method: People with PD were compared to age- and hearing-matched controls using perceptual tasks focused on discrimination and learning of speech rate and intensity. For rate discrimination, speech, non-speech, and visual stimuli were included to determine whether performance differences for PD participants and controls were specific to speech. Disease severity was assessed using the MDS-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) and the relationship to performance on perceptual discrimination and learning tasks was evaluated. Results: People with PD performed significantly worse than controls in the rate discrimination task for all types of stimuli. There were no significant group differences for intensity discrimination. However, participants with greater PD disease severity demonstrated significantly poorer intensity discrimination accuracy. Performance on learning tasks utilizing rate and intensity manipulations did not differ between PD and control participants and was unrelated to PD disease severity. Conclusions: People with PD had difficulty discriminating rate differences across speech, non-speech, and visual stimuli, indicating that challenges with rate perception are not limited to speech. The relationship between intensity discrimination and disease severity may suggest common dopaminergic networks between motor symptoms and auditory perception in PD.
papers.title: Perception of speech rate and intensity in Parkinson's disease

papers.abstract: Lipids are the predominant building blocks of plant membranes and are essential for plant growth and development. They are crucial for survival during times of stress as lipids are involved in multiple signaling pathways, and their relative abundances can change in response to environmental factors. To better characterize the lipid composition of the vital food crop maize, we generated a comprehensive glycerolipid atlas using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry. We surveyed the lipid profiles of three different maize genotypes: B73, a temperate inbred; CML312, a subtropical inbred; and Palomero Toluqueno, an open-pollinated variety from the Mexican highlands. We collected leaf samples from 4 developmental stages and 6 leaves. From one growth stage, we also sampled along with three leaf zones: base, center, and tip. The genotype and leaf number were the major drivers of lipid differences. Phosphatidylcholine, lysophosphatidylcholine, and triacylglycerol genotypic differences were particularly high. We generated an eFP browser to be integrated into the maize genome browser, as well as a separate web interface to easily browse and compare lipid levels across tissues and genotypes, available at https://rrellan.shinyapps.io/Zea-Lip/.
papers.title: Zea Lip: An atlas of glycerolipid profiles across leaf development in maize

papers.abstract: Host specialization can restrict gene flow in fungal pathogens, yet sexual compatibility may persist when mating occurs on a shared alternate host. We tested this possibility by crossing wheat-adapted Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici and barley-adapted P. striiformis f. sp. hordei on Berberis vulgaris. Despite contrasting host specialization and genome-wide sequence differentiation, reciprocal crosses produced 18 viable aeciospore-derived progeny. Chromosome scale parental assemblies revealed physically unlinked homeodomain (HD) and pheromone receptor (PR) mating-type loci, consistent with a conserved tetrapolar mating system. All progeny inherited one HD haplotype from each parent, representing all four parental HD haplotype combinations. Phenotyped progeny displayed host-interaction profiles distinct from either parent, including compatibility with selected genotypes of both wheat and barley. These findings demonstrate that host-associated differentiation in P. striiformis can coexist with incomplete intrinsic reproductive isolation between the tested parental isolates, allowing sexual hybridization to generate novel host phenotypes.
papers.title: A conserved tetrapolar mating system permits sexual hybridization and recombinant host phenotypes in wheat- and barley-adapted Puccinia striiformis

papers.abstract: The universe of possible protein sequences is astronomically large, yet our understanding of sequence-structure relationships is derived almost entirely from the infinitesimal fraction used by life. Determining which physical properties are already accessible to unevolved polypeptides, and which require subsequent evolutionary refinement, is central both to understanding protein emergence and to expanding protein design beyond biological sequence space. Here, we explore this largely uncharted space using a high-throughput FRET-based selection of a library containing millions of random protein sequences, complemented by fluorescence imaging, biophysical characterization and sequence-based modelling. We find that random sequence space contains multiple physical phenotypes that cannot be captured by a simple distinction between soluble and aggregated proteins. Individual sequences can produce substantial FRET in both the cytosol and visible assemblies, while assemblies differ in packing density and cellular responses. Repeated selection for stronger FRET reduces population solubility indicating that proximity-based selection alone does not necessarily favor biology-like protein states. These experimentally defined phenotypes are predictable from sequence. Our results reveal resolvable and learnable variation within unevolved protein sequence space, providing a route to investigate how far random sequences lie from soluble, stable protein solutions and to learn from regions of the protein universe not previously sampled by evolution.
papers.title: Learning the structural diversity in random protein sequence space

papers.abstract: C4 photosynthesis evolved from the ancestral C3 pathway through coordinated leaf anatomical and metabolic reorganization that concentrates CO2 to reduce photorespiration. Quantitative understanding of these structure-function relationships remains limited. Here we used anatomy-aware metabolic modeling of a mesophyll-bundle sheath cell system to analyze the interdependence between leaf anatomy and photosynthetic metabolism on the C3-C4 spectrum. Our model faithfully recapitulates the transitory steps from C3 to C4 photosynthesis, reveals a crucial role for plasmodesmata in enabling the C3 to C4 transition, and points at potential pre-C2 metabolic states that provide benefits under conditions that favor elevated photorespiration. Incorporating bundle cell suberisation with our model predicts reduction of PSII activity and dominance of the NADP-ME C4 subtype in leaves with suberized bundle sheath cells and proposes a role for oxygen evolution at PSII as a potential driver for this mechanism. Varying bundle sheath leakage and photorespiratory conditions along the C3-C4 spectrum identify conditions under which C3-C4 intermediate photosynthesis provides energetic benefits and underlines the notion of intermediate photosynthesis as a stable evolutionary state. Overall, our study sheds new light on the quantitative relationship between leaf anatomy and metabolism and its interaction with the environment and suggests targets for climate-adaptation in C3 plants.
papers.title: Metabolic modeling links leaf anatomy to environment-specific benefits on the C3-C4 spectrum

papers.abstract: The authors have withdrawn their manuscript because a subsequent audit of the analysis pipeline found that several steps reported as completed had no supporting output, including the selection of the initial set of loci, and that the RNA-protein interaction analysis cannot distinguish RPTOR isoforms, so the proposed RPTOR-208/ABCC8 interaction and the conclusions built on it are not supported. Therefore, the authors do not wish this work to be cited as reference for the project. If you have any questions, please contact the corresponding author.
papers.title: WITHDRAWN: Post-GWAS functional annotation of the RPTOR locus identifies rs12950541 as a candidate regulatory variant for type 2 diabetes and metabolic traits

papers.abstract: Those living with right hemisphere damage (RHD) often struggle with engaging in aspects of conversation that require understanding what a speaker means. There is growing evidence that conversation relies on deducing the speaker's perspective, an ability known as theory of mind (ToM). However, whether individual differences in conversation after RHD relate to ToM deficits is unknown. Here, we related individual differences in conversational success to ToM in 31 speakers during the early stages of RHD (median 5 days post-stroke) in comparison to 16 age- and education-matched controls. We measured conversational success as the number of differences identified between two images while participants conversed with study coordinators. A non-verbal false belief task measured ToM abilities. Baseline cognitive tasks assessed visual inattention, inhibitory control/visual selective attention and working memory. Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed that the ToM ability to explicitly infer others' perspectives while managing conflict with one's own reliably predicted conversational success ({beta} = 0.42, p = .023; {beta}'s = .44 - .64 across sensitivity models). Adding false belief ToM substantially increased model fit ({Delta}R2 = .115, Cohen's f2 = .15), independent of baseline cognitive abilities and demographic factors. These findings provide the first empirical evidence in unilateral RHD that the ability to reason about a partner's knowledge and manage conflict with one's privileged perspective is critical for successful conversation. Results support theoretical models of ToM as a cognitive basis for everyday conversation. The clinical implications underscore the importance of socio-cognitive screening and ToM-based interventions to enhance communication outcomes in stroke rehabilitation.
papers.title: Theory of mind predicts conversational success in early right hemisphere stroke recovery

papers.abstract: Background: Datasets related to infectious diseases are essential for public health decision-making, yet their reuse remains limited by persistent barriers to data sharing and integration. Achieving data that are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) is widely recognized as essential for accelerating scientific discovery and enabling coordinated responses to emerging threats, but the needs of the global pathogen data community have not been systematically characterized. Aim: This study, conducted by the Pathogen Data Network (PDN), aims to identify infrastructural and educational priorities among stakeholders working with infectious disease-related data, namely researchers, educators, healthcare professionals, bioinformaticians, and policymakers who generate, curate, or use pathogen data, in order to guide community-responsive support for data sharing and interoperability. Methods: A cross-sectional stakeholder survey was disseminated as an open, non-probability (convenience) survey to prospective participants reached through PDN networks, targeted mailing lists, and open professional and social-media channels. A total of 136 responses from researchers, healthcare professionals, bioinformaticians, and educators were analyzed descriptively to identify prioritized barriers, training needs, and preferred support mechanisms. Results: Respondents consistently identified structural constraints as the primary impediments to effective data use, including limited funding (74%), data-aggregation challenges (68%), and a shortage of skilled personnel (52%). Respondents identified bioinformatics for infectious disease research (68%) as the highest priority for training, followed by guidance on using the integrated pathogen data and tools portal provided by the PDN, the Pathogens Portal (51%). The Pathogens Portal was also ranked as the most essential PDN resource (72%). Preferred training formats included virtual short courses (68%) and webinars (66%). Notably, while researchers emphasized technical subjects like machine learning, educators prioritized foundational case studies. Conclusion: These findings provide an evidence-based descriptive summary of community needs and suggest that barriers to FAIR pathogen data are predominantly systemic rather than purely technological. The survey framework and openly available dataset offer a reusable template for assessing needs in other communities and regions. By aligning training, infrastructure development, and outreach with empirically identified priorities, organizations supporting infectious disease research can strengthen the interoperability and reuse of data and establish a benchmark for future community-driven improvements.
papers.title: Community needs for FAIR pathogen data: a cross-sectional survey of infectious-disease researchers and educators

papers.abstract: Current digital twin brain (DTB) models are typically optimized using single-modality functional neuroimaging data, which restricts their ability to simulate brain dynamics across multiple spatiotemporal scales. Here, we show that a two-stage DTB (TS-DTB) modeling framework jointly constrained by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) data. Validation in both the healthy young and Alzheimer's disease (AD) cohorts demonstrates that the TS-DTB model simultaneously captures subject-specific features of multi-scale brain dynamics. In particular, the TS-DTB models of AD patients successfully recapitulate spectral-temporal signatures of cognitive decline, suggesting a model-inferred association between these deficits and simulated excitation-inhibition (E-I) imbalances. By simulating responses to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), we further reveal that acute EEG normalization in AD patients is computationally associated with putative E-I rebalancing via model-inferred synaptic reconfiguration and background suppression. Overall, these findings underscore the potential of the TS-DTB to advance the mechanistic understanding of the brain and inform personalized digital therapeutics.
papers.title: An EEG-fMRI Jointly Constrained Digital Twin Brain and Its Application in Alzheime's Disease

papers.abstract: Individual phenotypes often depend on the genotypes of other individuals within a group. These phenomena are termed "indirect genetic effects" (IGEs) and have been distinguished from direct genetic effects (DGEs) using quantitative genetic models. Recent studies have utilized high-resolution polymorphism data to enable genomic prediction (GP) and genome-wide association study (GWAS) of IGEs. To accelerate this practice, here we integrate polygenic and oligogenic IGEs using a multi-kernel mixed model. This model incorporates two random effects with a single covariance parameter for polygenic effects, while including neighbor allelic similarity to test SNP-marker effects for oligogenic effects. Our simulations demonstrated that the present model could infer a trade-off between DGEs and IGEs with a slight improvement in GWAS/GP performance. By applying our method to three species of woody plants, we found evidence for intergenotypic competition in aspen and apple trees, but limited evidence in climbing grapevines. Based on GWAS, we also detected significant variants associated with competitive IGEs on the apple trunk growth. Our study offers an alternative implementation for GWAS/GP of IGEs and thereby provides an effective tool to dissect the genetic architecture of mixing ability within a plant species.
papers.title: Dissecting oligogenic and polygenic indirect genetic effects through the lens of neighboring plant genotypes

papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Inactivation of ANGPTL3 (angiopoietin-like protein 3, A3) is a proven therapeutic strategy for lowering plasma lipid levels independently of the LDL receptor (LDLR), yet the optimal approach to inactivate A3 remains unclear. A3 is proteolytically cleaved and circulates as full-length (A3-FL), N-terminal (A3-Nter) and C-terminal (A3-Cter) fragments. The specific contribution of each form of A3, and of its paralog, ANGPTL8 (A8), in modulating circulating levels of ApoB-Containing Lipoproteins (ABCLs) remain poorly defined. Clarifying these relationships will inform next-generation A3-directed therapies. METHODS: We performed liver perfusion studies to directly compare the number and composition of VLDL particles secreted from mice with and without A3. To amplify effects on cholesterol metabolism, we generated Ldlr-/- mice expressing wildtype A3 (A3-WT), A3-FL or A3-Nter, with or without co-expression of A8, and analyzed plasma lipids, circulating A3 and A8 complexes, and intravascular lipase activities. Complementary in vitro assays and structural modeling were used to assess relative endothelial lipase (EL) inhibition by A3 alone or in complex with A8. RESULTS: Liver perfusion studies revealed that A3 inactivation does not alter the rates of hepatic secretion of VLDL in wildtype or Ldlr-/- mice. Inactivation of A8 alone lowered plasma LDL-cholesterol (C) levels by ~20%, an effect dependent upon the expression of both EL and A3. Maximal inhibition of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) required co-expression of A8 plus both A3-FL and A3-Nter, indicating that A3 cleavage, in addition to A8 expression, is essential for maximal LPL inhibition. In contrast, A8 expression, but not A3 cleavage, was required for optimal EL inhibition. CONCLUSIONS: A8 acts in concert with A3 to differentially modulate LPL- and EL-mediated lipolysis, which antagonizes hepatic clearance of newly-secreted atherogenic ABCLs. This mechanistic framework refines our understanding of A3-targeted lipid lowering and highlights the therapeutic potential of dual A3- plus A8-directed strategies to treat dyslipidemia and prevent atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
papers.title: Dual Control of Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Levels by ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL8

papers.abstract: Predicting whether aggregate community properties remain stable as environments fluctuate is a central challenge of ecological research. A critical open question is, however, how well the fundamental niche of species can predict this aspect of community stability. We conceptualised community performance (CP) curves by aggregating species-specific performance across environmental conditions and asked whether the variability of these curves explains community temporal variability. In Lotka-Volterra and in mechanistic consumer-resource simulations, CP variability explained on average 92% of the variation in total abundance variability. Explanatory power remained above 75% across gradients of interaction strength and coexistence conditions. Derivation of the expected community variability - CP variability relationship for the Lotka-Volterra case explains this high explanatory power despite interaction effects. In a purpose-designed microcosm experiment, CP variability explained 67% of variation in the temporal variability of total community biomass. Explanatory power of CP variability therefore retains substantial information about community stability even in strongly interacting systems, providing a tractable basis for forecasting stability when species interactions are unknown.
papers.title: Community performance curves predict temporal stability despite interaction effects

papers.abstract: Predictive coding has influenced many conceptual accounts of delusions, the impervious and often bizarre beliefs that accompany a range of neuropsychiatric conditions. However, these explanations remain incomplete and have rarely been tested using formal modelling. Here, we present a formal account of delusional beliefs based on hybrid predictive coding, which sheds new light on the computational mechanisms underpinning two core features of delusions: their thematic recurrence and imperviousness to contradictory evidence. In simulation experiments, we demonstrate that a combination of contextually inadequate initialisation of beliefs and excessive certainty in them (a hallmark of psychosis) triggers a reorganisation of the generative model relating observed events to hidden causes. This reorganisation enables the maintenance of delusional beliefs that are thematically stable, internally consistent with external inputs, and impervious to contradictory evidence, all without an increase in global prediction error and even after certainty has returned to normal levels. Overall, our results suggest that delusions emerge and are maintained by generative models learned under atypical conditions. These findings provide mechanistic insights into the computations that may underpin delusions and provide fresh ideas for potential therapeutic strategies that focus on re-training generative models.
papers.title: Delusions Emerge and Persist due to Generative Model Reorganisation: Insights from Hybrid Predictive Coding

papers.abstract: Fitness landscapes offer a compact representation of adaptation, yet are rarely inferred from sparse multi-environment data. We present a Bayesian approach to infer an effective multi-host phenotypic fitness landscape from cross-inoculation assays by linking successful infection probabilities to Fisher's geometrical model and to an explicit decomposition of establishment routes. The model estimates (i) the distance matrix among host-specific phenotypic optima, (ii) target-host permissiveness through the widths of fitness peaks, (iii) target-specific differences in the efficiency with which phenotypic suitability translates into successful infection, and (iv) the conditional probabilities that successful infections are attributed to direct establishment, rescue from standing variation in the source inoculum, or de novo rescue in the target host. We apply the approach to an experimental evolution dataset for endive necrotic mosaic virus evolved on five Asteraceae hosts and challenged in a full cross-inoculation design. The inferred landscape can be visualized as a phenotypic map of the host community, revealing pronounced heterogeneity in target-host permissiveness and a geometry broadly concordant with host phylogeny. By grounding assay-derived distances in an explicit mechanistic model, the approach provides a parsimonious representation of multi-host constraints that can be used to discuss establishment barriers and potential springboard hosts in heterogeneous communities. More broadly, it offers a general method for inferring effective fitness landscapes from sparse multi-environment data.
papers.title: Inferring the multi-host fitness landscape of endive necrotic mosaic virus from cross-inoculation experiments

papers.abstract: The genetic diversity preserved in wheat landraces provides an important resource for broadening the genetic basis of modern wheat breeding, but its utilisation is constrained by the limited availability of effective genome-editing technologies for diverse genetic backgrounds. Here, we developed an integrated genome-engineering framework to modify Rht-1, a major regulator of plant height, in genetically diverse bread wheat landraces from the A.E. Watkins Collection. We combined CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion, cytosine base editing and prime editing to create defined Rht-1 variants in landraces representing five underutilised ancestral groups (AG1, AG3, AG4, AG6 and AG7). CRISPR/Cas9 editing generated targeted deletions of the conserved DELLA motif while retaining the downstream GRAS domain in-frame, yielding altered Rht-1 variants with potential utility for functional analysis and breeding. We further developed a wheat-adapted TaCBE6b-intron system and used cytosine base editing to engineer premature-stop variants in Rht-D1. Utilising prime editing with an adapted ePPEplus system enabled precise G-to-T conversion at the Rht-D1 locus, generating the nucleotide substitution characteristic of the Green Revolution semi-dwarf Rht-D1b allele. Prime-editing activity varied substantially among Watkins genotypes, with editing detected in WATDE0394, WATDE0549, WATDE0639 and WATDE0706. At the individual-plant level, amplicon sequencing confirmed D-genome editing, with edited Rht-D1 haplotypes reaching 100% of NGS reads in an individual WATDE0394 plant, and exceeding 50% in several plants from WATDE0394, WATDE0549 and WATDE0706. The engineered Rht-D1 variants were associated with reduced plant height; notably, a WATDE0394 plant carrying a 100% edited D-genome haplotype reached 69 cm compared with approximately 131 cm for the control. All T1 progeny of this plant were homozygous for the prime edit, as assessed by KASP markers. Reducing plant height in these genetically diverse landraces addresses their tall architecture and associated lodging susceptibility, a practical constraint on their direct use in breeding populations. Together, these results demonstrate that complementary genome-editing technologies can generate defined Rht-1 variation in genetically diverse wheat landraces while introducing agronomically relevant plant-height variation. The resulting founder lines provide valuable resources for functional analysis of DELLA-mediated growth regulation and a foundation for precision pre-breeding, composite cross populations, and the development of resilient wheat.
papers.title: Integrating Green Revolution Rht-1 Alleles in Diverse Wheat Landraces Using CRISPR/Cas9, Cytosine Base Editing and Prime Editing

papers.abstract: Proteomics needs instruments that combine depth with quantitative precision. Here we describe the ZenoTOF 8600 system, a quadrupole time-of-flight instrument that combines triple-quadrupole ion optics with an optical detector, the Zeno trap and electron-activated dissociation. The MS2 ion current increases tenfold over its predecessor, the ZenoTOF 7600+ system. In scanning quadrupole data-independent acquisition (ZT Scan DIA), every fragment records the Q1 profile of its precursor, so wide isolation windows keep their sensitivity while abundant precursors attain the selectivity of a window about ten times narrower. ZT Scan DIA identifies up to 38% more precursors than variable-window DIA and improves quantitative accuracy. The platform quantifies up to 5,200 protein groups in a single HeLa cell, 5,000 from 1 nL of mouse brain tissue, 10,000 in a single run and 5,700 at 500 samples per day, and targeted assays reach 20 amol on column and quantify S129 phosphorylation of -synuclein.
papers.title: Scanning DIA on the ZenoTOF 8600 system records a precursor dimension for every fragment at tenfold higher ion flux

papers.abstract: Bacteriophages rely on breaching the bacterial cell wall as the first step of infection. We characterise ORF11, a putative tail-spike lysin from the 19 kbp Minhovirus SHEF14, a podovirus infecting Enterococcus faecium. The ORF11 2.5 Angstrom crystal structure reveals that ORF11 comprises four domains: a predicted glycosyl hydrolase (D1) a cysteine, histidine-dependent amidohydrolase/peptidase (CHAP, D4), separated by a helical linker (D2) and a CHAP like domain (D3). The crystal form reveals a dimeric assembly with the predicted glycosyl hydrolase (D1) and CHAP peptidase (D4) domains located adjacent to each other (but at opposite ends of the dimer) within one subunit and separated by domains D2 and D3- positioned at the dimer interface. The presence of the D3 CHAP-like domain is unusual among related bacteriophage tail-lysins from related small podoviruses but conserved in E. faecium Minhoviruses. Biochemical assays using recombinant ORF11 and LC-MS/MS confirmed dual peptidoglycan degrading activity. ORF11 functions as both an N-acetylglucosaminidase and a D,D-endopeptidase, cleaving the bond between the D-alanine in position-4 and the D-aspartate residue at the end of the side chain. Together, these results provide the first structural description of an Enterococcus podovirus tail-spike lysin and demonstrate bifunctional enzymatic activity. This dual action likely facilitates initial surface recognition and localised peptidoglycan degradation during infection of E. faecium, offering new insights into how small-genome phages target this clinically significant antimicrobial-resistant pathogen.
papers.title: Structural Basis for Dual Peptidoglycan Hydrolysis by an E. faecium Minhovirus Tail Spike Lysin

papers.abstract: Regeneration restores lost tissues through diverse cellular strategies that vary across species and tissue contexts. In many systems, regeneration involves blastema formation; however, how blastema formation is coordinated in tissues employing multiple stem/progenitor populations remains unclear. Here, we investigate tentacle regeneration in the hydrozoan jellyfish Cladonema, in which our previous work identified two distinct proliferative populations: resident homeostatic stem cells (RHSCs), which contribute to tissue production during homeostasis and regeneration, and repair-specific proliferative cells (RSPCs), which are transiently induced upon injury to form the blastema. While extensive cell death occurs shortly after injury, it is largely dispensable for blastema formation. Using pharmacological inhibition and cell proliferation analyses, we identify ERK/MAPK signaling as a key regulator of blastema formation. ERK/MAPK signaling is rapidly activated at the injury site and promotes proliferation of RSPCs. In contrast, inhibition of Notch signaling disrupts nematocyte differentiation and increases proliferative activity in RHSCs, indicating that Notch signaling governs the balance between differentiation and proliferation in RHSCs. Together, these findings reveal a division of labor between conserved signaling pathways in regulating distinct proliferative populations during tentacle regeneration.
papers.title: Division of labor between ERK/MAPK and Notch signaling in regulating distinct proliferative populations during jellyfish tentacle regeneration

papers.abstract: Atrial cardiomyopathy is characterized by altered atrial structures, yet its underlying genetic basis remains inadequately explored. TIE1 mutations are reported in lymphedema patients, but whether they exhibit cardiac defects alongside lymphatic abnormalities remains unknown. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing showed high Tie1 and Tek expression in atrial endocardial cells. TIE1 deficiency severely disrupted atrial morphogenesis, with only minor ventricular defects. Bulk RNA-seq showed reduced transcripts for endothelial development and cardiac trabeculation in Tie1 mutants. Separate RNA-seq analysis of the atria and ventricles further confirmed these findings, revealing a more pronounced downregulation of trabecular genes, including Tek, in the atria upon Tie1 loss. Endothelial deletion of Tek impaired trabeculation, particularly in atria. Consistently, Tie1 loss combined with a single null Tek allele disrupted both atrial and ventricular trabeculation. Strikingly, atrial morphogenesis defects appeared within 48 hours of induced endothelial Tie1 loss coupled with Tek heterozygous deletion, implying a critical endocardial role in organizing the atrial muscular network. The synergy of TIE1 and TIE2 in remodeling atrial trabeculae was confirmed postnatally, whereas TIE1 insufficiency alone had no obvious effect. Together, TIE1 is differentially required for atrial versus ventricular development, acting synergistically with TIE2 to regulate endocardial cell-coordinated assembly of atrial internal muscular network.
papers.title: Endocardial TIE1 synergizes with TIE2 to regulate the atrial internal muscular network assembly

papers.abstract: Human behavior differs substantially across individuals. While artificial neural networks (ANNs) are regarded as promising models of human perception, they are often assumed to lack such individual differences. Here, we demonstrate that multiple instances of the same ANN architecture exhibit substantial individual differences in behavior that mimic those observed in humans. We trained and tested 60 ANN instances from three architectures on a digit recognition task and found notable individual differences in overall accuracy, confidence, and response time (RT). Critically, these individual differences in ANN instances mapped consistently onto the individual differences produced by 60 humans performing the same task, with the mapping strength often approaching the human-to-human benchmark across all three behavioral metrics (accuracy, confidence, RT). The mapping generalized even across behavioral metrics: an ANN instance that aligned with an individual human on accuracy also aligned with the same individual on confidence and RT. These findings extended to a more complex, 10-choice blurry object recognition task, though the human-ANN mapping was generally less robust than the human-human benchmark. Overall, these findings open the possibility of using ANN ensembles as computational proxies for probing the mechanisms underlying human variability.
papers.title: Individual differences in artificial neural networks capture individual differences in human behavior

papers.abstract: Root system stiffness is a measurement that describes the resistance of a root system to rotation. Previous work has shown that genotypes with a higher root system stiffness are also more susceptible to root lodging. In this study, we deconvolve the contribution of root architecture, individual root-level mechanics, and root-soil interaction to root system stiffness in maize inbred lines. Collectively, larger above- and below-ground root systems and stiffer individual brace roots contribute to a higher root system stiffness. When considering all traits in predictive models, the below-ground root architecture primarily drives the prediction of root system stiffness categories. These below-ground traits describe the size and distribution of the root system. Analysis of a roothairless3 mutant revealed a reduction in root system stiffness that could not be decoupled from a reduction in root size. Together these results link root system stiffness to the size and distribution of the below-ground root system and highlight the importance of this measurement for both root lodging resistance and root phenotyping.
papers.title: Maize root system stiffness is determined by the size and distribution of the below-ground root system

papers.abstract: Identifying robust neuroimaging markers associated with schizophrenia is essential for advancing research and informing clinical understanding. However, a major obstacle to clinical translation is the limited ability of neuroimaging-based classification models to generalize across scanning sites. In this study, we first establish best performing within-site models, and then systematically investigate cross-site generalization in first-episode schizophrenia (FES) classification and evaluate strategies for mitigating site-related distribution shifts. Using data from two acquisition sites (n=544), we examine ComBat, CovBat, optimal transport, and deep adaptation. Across functional, structural, and diffusion-based features, both traditional machine learning (TML) and neural network (NN) models achieved comparable performance in within-site classification, with resting state fMRI functional connectivity providing the most robust unimodal features. When models are transferred across sites, performance degraded substantially across all approaches, by 5 to 12 percentage points of balanced accuracy. Distribution-alignment methods partially mitigated this degradation. Harmonization recovered 6 to 8 points for functional connectivity in one transfer direction, mainly by correcting a displaced decision threshold. Deep adaptation recovered similar gains but less consistently. Increasing model complexity alone did not result in systematic performance gains. Across the classifiers tested on this pair of sites, multimodal feature fusion did not consistently outperform functional connectivity alone. Overall, our findings indicate that controlling for site effects was more critical than model complexity for achieving generalizable classification in FES. These results come from two sites of a single coordinated study, and whether they hold for more heterogeneous sites remains to be tested.
papers.title: Domain Adaptation Improves Cross-site Classification of First-episode Schizophrenia from Multimodal Neuroimaging Data

papers.abstract: Resting-state brain activity is dominated by oscillations in the alpha band (8-13 Hz). The dominant frequency within this band, the individual alpha peak frequency (IAPF), has been widely used as a global marker of inter-individual variability in perceptual and cognitive functions, as well as clinical phenotypes. However, the traditional approach implicitly assumes a single oscillatory rhythm varying along a parametric continuum. Here, we analyzed resting-state EEG data from more than 2000 participants across multiple independent datasets using unsupervised spectral decomposition methods. We identify three distinct and highly stable alpha components, or archetypes, that jointly and compositionally determine the IAPF. These components exhibit dissociable age-related trajectories as well as distinct scalp topographies and cortical sources. Together, these findings indicate that individual differences in alpha activity do not reflect variation along a single frequency dimension, but rather differences in the relative contribution of discrete alpha generators. These results call for a reevaluation of many reported associations between alpha frequency, brain function, and clinical phenotypes, and suggest that estimates of alpha-component expression may provide more precise and informative biomarkers than conventional global IAPF measures.
papers.title: The compositional nature of the human alpha rhythm

papers.abstract: Long-read single-cell RNA-sequencing enables isoform-level quantification in individual cells, yet methods for delineating cell population-specific isoforms remain limited. Here, we develop Hypatia to systematically compare isoform complexities across three complementary dimensions, including isoform usage, diversity, and expression. Our analyses demonstrated that Cramer's V improved the precision of detecting isoform usage shifts, at the cost of detecting fewer events in sparser data. Results further revealed Tsallis entropy as a refined, tunable measure of isoform diversity, improving comparability across genes and cells. Critically, integrating these analyses in real datasets provided complementary views of isoform variation across cell populations, highlighting Hypatia's important applications.
papers.title: Hypatia: Comparative Isoform Profiling Across Cell Populations from Long-Read Single-Cell Transcriptomes

papers.abstract: Adaptive optimizers reduce sensitivity to coordinate-wise gradient scale, but they usually still require the user to choose an overall learning rate and often a schedule. We introduce YamAdam, an adaptive optimizer that requires no user-specified optimizer hyperparameters. YamAdam combines short-memory Adam moments with both decay factors fixed at 1/2, a projection that removes only the historical component opposing the current mini-batch gradient, a one-time calibration of a reference update radius, and subsequent scaling based on dimensionless directional statistics. We evaluate YamAdam without user-specified optimizer settings on six workloads spanning image classification, image reconstruction, tabular classification and regression, and language modeling. The comparison contains 30 fixed settings from 10 optimizer families, with every setting reported separately. Our primary measure, {Delta}TTT, is the comparator-minus-YamAdam difference in budgetnormalized time to five predefined targets, averaged equally across workloads. All 30 comparator settings produced a positive {Delta}TTT, ranging from +0.003526 to +0.210524. Across 540 setting-workload-seed comparisons, YamAdam was faster in 504, tied in 14, and slower in 22. Across 2,700 target observations, both methods reached 2,634 targets and only YamAdam reached 66; no target was reached only by the comparator or by neither method. These results show that an optimizer requiring no user-specified optimizer hyperparameters can attain predefined targets rapidly across heterogeneous workloads.
papers.title: An Adaptive Optimizer without User-Specified Hyperparameters through Historical Projection and Self-Calibrated Scaling

papers.abstract: Multiple classes of selfish genetic elements, including transposable elements, meiotic drivers, and viruses, are suppressed by small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) that guide RNA interference (RNAi). These are interlocked within continually evolving genetic conflicts that are characterized by extremely rapid dynamics of change in both sequence and copy number. Indeed, it was shown that across Drosophila, the core RNAi machinery evolves under positive selection, and that the RNAi effector AGO2 has additional copies in some species. This contrasts with the core microRNA (miRNA) machinery in Drosophila, which evolves under negative selection and maintains one-to-one orthologs not only amongst flies, but even to mammals. Here, we analyze >300 long read genome assemblies of Drosophila species to generalize these attributes. Not only do we find recurrent expansion of AGO2 across ~100 species, including lineages with ongoing amplification of AGO2, we also find dozens of species with extra copies of the other core RNAi factors, r2d2 and dicer-2. In many cases, these additional RNAi factor copies co-exist, or are nested, within a lineage bearing an ancestral expansion of AGO2. Transcriptome data provide evidence that core RNAi factors, including certain lineage-specific copies, are biased for testis expression. Finally, we use small RNA data to annotate hairpin RNAs (hpRNAs) in D. pseudoobscura, one of the species with prominent amplification of RNAi factors. We find rampant de novo hpRNA loci in this species, whose siRNAs are predominantly expressed in testis. All together, these findings highlight evolutionary plasticity of the fly RNAi pathway and affirm that it is preferentially deployed in the germline of the heterogametic sex. When considered alongside abundant genetic data for recurrent sex ratio meiotic drive against the Y chromosome, these genomic data strongly imply that a fundamental role of endogenous RNAi is to control sex chromosome conflicts.
papers.title: Recurrent expansion and rapid evolution of the Drosophilid RNAi pathway in testis

papers.abstract: Despite their global importance, the genomic foundations of domestication in perennial fruit trees remain incompletely integrated across demography, selection, and structural variation. Pear (Pyrus spp.), domesticated in Europe and East Asia, provides a powerful system to compare alternative evolutionary trajectories within a balanced genomic framework. Using lineage-specific reference genomes, we analyzed nucleotide and transposable element (TE) polymorphisms across 396 well-documented wild and cultivated individuals spanning both regions. We uncovered weak domestication bottlenecks and extensive wild-crop gene flow, consistent with a protracted evolutionary process. In Europe, dessert and perry P. communis diverged independently based on fruit use. In East Asia, P. pyrifolia diversified geographically in China and Japan, following distinct domestication trajectories. Selection scans identify lineage- and population-specific targets associated with fruit texture, metabolism, and immunity. We find no support for the cost-of-domestication hypothesis: cultivated pears show a lower realized burden of deleterious mutations than their wild relatives. TE insertion patterns largely reflect demographic history, and are not enriched near the genes under positive selection. Together, our results support a protracted, multi-regional model of pear domestication shaped by recurrent gene flow and lineage-specific genomic architectures.
papers.title: Contrasting genomic routes to domestication in Occidental and Oriental pears

papers.abstract: Genomics data are sequences, and exploration in these data involves mapping these sequences to function and understanding that mapping. Analogous to a sentence composed of words, a sequence's function is understood through its constituent subsequences, or k-mers. The presence of k-mers, their positions, and their relationships with other k-mers (k-mer associations) all affect sequence function. Understanding the sequence function requires determining the contributions of each of its k-mers and the impacts of their positions and k-mer associations. k-mer associations are inherently combinatorial and may be hierarchical. Although these associations may be impactful for biological phenomena, k-mer associations cannot be understood by humans and severely obfuscate model analyses, yielding generalizations, simplifications, and approximations. Ignoring k-mer associations, however, yields concepts that are human-understandable and exact. To determine whether ignoring k-mer associations is appropriate, models that learn or ignore k-mer associations can be compared. Oyster is a novel NN that learns k-mer composition and k-mer positions while ignoring k-mer associations, the first with these abilities to our knowledge. Oyster is a glass-box model as the exact position-specific contributions of k-mers are directly extracted from the model weights. Oyster is compared with models that consider k-mer associations using two case studies spanning two important genomics topics: protein-DNA interactions and enhancer activity. Across these case studies it was found that while models that consider k-mer associations perform better than Oyster models, the predictions of the Oyster models were in strong agreement, serving as faithful proxies. Human-understandable concepts were extracted from the Oyster models revealing concepts that align with the literature as well as novel ones.
papers.title: Oyster: A Neural Network for Modeling Genomic Sequences with Exact Position-Specific k-mer Contributions

papers.abstract: Tuberculosis eradication efforts are severely hampered by antimicrobial resistance and bacterial persistence. We previously reported that the VapBC12 toxin antitoxin (TA) system in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis) regulates disease progression and antibiotic persistence. In this study, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying VapC12 dependent modulation of bacterial growth and antibiotic susceptibility. We identified a Cholesterol Recognition Amino acid Consensus (CRAC) motif in the VapC12 toxin that is critical for cholesterol binding and interaction with its cognate antitoxin, VapB12. Heterologous expression of VapC12 in Mycobacterium smegmatis induced toxicity, providing a model to investigate its functional activity. We determined the crystal structure of VapB12 at 1.6 Angstorm resolution and used molecular modelling to predict the VapBC12 complex structure. Structure-function analyses identified specific residues critical for complex assembly and toxin activity. Mechanistically, our findings suggest that cholesterol activates VapC12 by competitively displacing VapB12 from the CRAC motif, thereby restricting M. tuberculosis growth. Finally, we showed that pharmacologically inhibiting VapC12 alleviates cholesterol-mediated growth restriction and enhances antibiotic activity. Collectively, these findings establish a mechanistic link between cholesterol sensing, toxin-antitoxin regulation, and antibiotic susceptibility in M. tuberculosis, highlighting VapC12 as a potential target for therapeutic strategies to combat tuberculosis persistence.
papers.title: Cholesterol-activated VapC12 toxin modulates growth and drug susceptibility in Mycobacterium tuberculosis

papers.abstract: Natural sequences have long been the assumed ground truth for protein sequence design methods. But natural sequences encode more than the structural fold, carrying evolutionary history that reflects ancestry, drift, and function. Deep learning models for protein sequence design inherit this signal, achieving higher native sequence recovery but lower predicted foldability. Motivated by this trade-off, we introduce Caliby, a Potts model-based sequence design method capable of conditioning on structural ensembles. By conditioning on synthetic ensembles generated from an input backbone, Caliby samples sequences consistent with shared structural constraints while averaging out native sequence confounders. This strategy improves designability while reducing native sequence recovery, and generalizes across sequence design models. Mechanistically, designed sequences show reduced covariation between non-contacting residues and lower energetic frustration, indicating more precise structural encoding. We demonstrate experimental applicability by designing thermostable proteins, functional lanthanide binders, and soluble membrane protein variants, including a pentameric assembly confirmed by cryo-EM.
papers.title: Isolation of structural constraints by ensemble-conditioned protein sequence design

papers.abstract: Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) widely used in breast cancer treatment, paradoxically increases endometrial cancer risk. Although progesterone receptor (PR) shares estrogen receptor alpha (ERa) binding sites in Ishikawa endometrial adenocarcinoma cells, that could explain in part progestin regulation of estrogen effects, whether long term tamoxifen exposure alters this ERa/PR interplay in endometrial tumors remains unknown. Given the absence of endometrial tumor PR cistrome data, we compared ERa cistromes from tumors of users and non-users with Ishikawa cells ERa and PR cistromes to investigate how long-term SERM exposure might affect ERa binding signatures. Here, we show that non-user ERa binding exhibits greater similarity to the PR cistrome than tamoxifen users. These shared ERa-PR binding sites are not enriched in estrogen response elements (EREs) but in AP-1 and SOX motifs, suggesting indirect or tethered ERa recruitment, and are associated with genes involved in inflammatory pathways, such as MYC. In contrast, tamoxifen exposure appears to shift ERa binding toward PR-independent regions enriched in ERE motifs, and that could regulate early estrogen response pathways genes, including the oncogene NRIP1. Our findings suggest that exposure to tamoxifen may redirect ERa binding toward genomic regions responsive to estrogen, whereas ERa binding in non-users retains features associated with PR-occupied regulatory sites. These results provide bases for further investigation about the role that SERM treatment could play in remodeling the endometrial tumor epigenetic landscape and point to the hypothesis that this remodeling may involve altered ERa/PR regulatory interplay, potentially contributing to endometrial tissue dysregulation.
papers.title: Comparative cistromic analysis reveals a shift in tamoxifen-associated endometrial tumor ERα binding toward sites less frequently shared by progesterone receptors

papers.abstract: A growing body of work suggests that mutation bias - whereby some types of mutations occur more often than others - can influence the genetic basis of adaptation and the distribution of fitness effects of new mutations. For instance, the loss of specific DNA repair genes shifts the mutation spectrum from a transition-biased to a transversion-biased state in Escherichia coli. This reversal of the ancestral mutation bias enhances access to under-sampled variants, increasing the beneficial mutation supply. But are these effects strong enough to alter adaptive outcomes? We show that mutation bias reversal indeed increases adaptation rate in E. coli by about 5%, and halves the variation in adaptation rates across replicate populations. Even though replicate populations of a strain diverge and adaptation slows down over time, the effect of beneficial supply on adaptation rate gets stronger. The advantage of bias reversal accrues due to greater beneficial mutation supply, with ~2-3 times as many beneficial mutations as strains with reinforced bias. Overall, mutation bias strongly influences the genetic basis of adaptation and alters the types of accumulated genomic mutations that may shape subsequent evolution. Our results show that mutation bias is important for predicting evolution, and highlight multiple ways in which mutational processes can shape the genetic and phenotypic outcomes of adaptation.
papers.title: Mutation bias is a key predictor of adaptation rate

papers.abstract: Next-generation neural mass models capture the collective behavior of brain regions through an exact mean-field reduction of the spiking neural networks, retaining key microscopic properties while remaining computationally efficient. This explicit link to single-neuron dynamics makes them a natural framework for studying how neuromodulators, such as dopamine (DA), shape macroscopic network activity. Integrating its effect is a key step toward biologically grounded brain models. Because the spiking network underlying such a reduction is fully known, the reduced model can be directly validated against it. Here, we perform a systematic comparison between a recently proposed DA-modulated mean-field model and its corresponding spiking network across multiple dynamical regimes, evaluating its ability to capture the qualitative organization of the network activity, and transitions between dynamical states. This comparison identifies the conditions under which the reduction accurately reflects the behavior of the full network, and highlights its theoretical limitations.
papers.title: Linking microscopic and mean-field descriptions ofdopaminergic modulation in neural circuits

papers.abstract: Amyloid assembly in vivo occurs in complex proteomic environments where multiple aggregation-prone species coexist. A{beta} and medin are two highly prevalent amyloids in ageing humans, and medin co-localizes with A{beta} in cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). Yet the structural consequences of their interaction remain unclear. Here, we determine the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of fibrils formed from defined in vitro mixtures of A{beta}40 and medin. From the same reaction, we resolve three fibril populations: (i) a previously described A{beta}40 polymorph that also forms in isolation, (ii) a novel A{beta}40 polymorph with A{beta}42-like features, including ordered N- and C-terminal regions, and (iii) the first atomic structure of full-length medin fibrils. Biochemical and immunogold analyses demonstrate association between A{beta} and medin within the mixed assemblies. However, the cryo-EM map of the novel A{beta} polymorph does not unambiguously resolve medin within the ordered A{beta} core. These findings are consistent with two non-exclusive mechanisms by which the polymorphic landscape is reshaped in mixtures: transient heterotypic amyloid interactions that redirect A{beta} folding pathways, or partial and structurally heterogeneous incorporation of medin into the fibril architecture. Regardless of the precise structural mechanism, our data demonstrate that interactions between coexisting amyloids can remodel their polymorphic landscape, revealing how mixed amyloid systems generate emergent conformations.
papers.title: Atomic structures of medin and Aβ fibrils reveal polymorphic remodeling in mixed amyloid systems

papers.abstract: Modelling quantitative genomics data remains challenging due to imbalanced target distributions, non-independent observations, and substantial computational costs. This study examines the challenges and current methods, proposes new methods, applies these methods across two case studies: a controlled setting with synthetically generated data and on real genomics datasets. Effective modelling of imbalanced data starts with density estimation. Density estimation via binning facilitates downstream analytical steps. Minimum Transformation Binning is a novel method that improves current binning methods for density estimation. Data splitting of imbalanced and non-independent observations is best accomplished by objective data splitting which entails randomly generating splits, scoring them, and selecting the best scoring one. This study conducts an empirical comparison of scoring functions toward an optimal objective data splitting method, finding the use of all-against-one absolute relative difference to be the best scoring function. Model fitting methods can be divided into loss functions and data balancing. Two methods have been previously proposed based on weighting error functions by the reciprocal or complement of the density estimation. This study conducts a comparison of these methods on the case studies, finding that reciprocal density weighting significantly outperforms non-weighted and complement density weighting. This study also tests model fitting with reciprocal weighted sampling per epoch for imbalanced regression. While this method does not generally improve performance, it uses significantly less resources in model fitting which can be beneficial for hyperparameter optimization. Together, this study provides a unified framework for effective modelling of imbalanced regression, especially imbalanced genomics data.
papers.title: Binning-based Methods for Model Fitting and Data Splitting Improve Machine Learning Imbalanced Regression

papers.abstract: Loci under strong balancing selection, such as sex-determining, mating-type, and self-incompatibility loci, are frequently flanked by regions of suppressed recombination. The reasons why recombination suppression evolves around these loci remain poorly understood. Here, we propose that one reason may be that loci under balancing selection facilitate the emergence of pseudo-overdominance, a phenomenon under which linked partially recessive deleterious mutations in repulsion mimic overdominance. Pseudo-overdominance arises under certain conditions when linkage disequilibrium gradually builds up between recessive deleterious mutations, often due to strong genetic linkage and genetic drift, forming complementary haplotypes. Homozygous and recombinant offspring are then selected against because they carry homozygous recessive deleterious mutations. Using individual-based simulations, we demonstrate here that the presence of loci under balancing selection (overdominant) eases the establishment of pseudo-overdominance by facilitating the maintenance of partially recessive deleterious mutations and linkage disequilibrium in their flanking regions. This occurs particularly in regions with low recombination rates and a high load of partially recessive deleterious mutations, which can be found in specific genomic regions in natural populations. We additionally show that selfing, while generally hindering pseudo-overdominance establishment, can in contrast facilitate its establishment around a permanently heterozygous locus, likely because recessive deleterious mutations are protected from being purged near such a locus and selfing increases genetic drift. Once established, we further showed that pseudo-overdominance can in turn favor the evolution of recombination suppression around permanently heterozygous loci, preventing the creation of unfit homozygous recombinant offspring. These results suggest new avenues for understanding the evolution of loci under balancing selection, sex chromosomes, mating-type chromosomes in selfing fungi, supergenes, and shed new light on the mechanisms driving genome evolution.
papers.title: Loci under balancing selection facilitate the emergence of pseudo-overdominance and recombination suppression

papers.abstract: Audio-visual stimuli are typically detected faster and more accurately than unisensory ones, but it remains unclear whether this benefit reflects true integration of evidence or other effects such as independent processing and modality repetition. We address this with three biologically motivated models of audio-visual integration, built on Wong and Wang model, a mean-field recurrent framework originally developed for unisensory decision-making. The OR model takes in independent unisensory processes through winner-take-all competition, and the SUM model implements full linear summation of sensory evidence. These two sit at opposite ends of the integration spectrum. The REPEAT model adds switch and repeat costs, whereby responses are faster when the modality repeats across trials. We simulated 121 participants whose unisensory evidence accumulation rates varied from modality dominance to balanced integration. We fitted the simulated reaction times and accuracy with a drift diffusion model and compared the resulting multisensory drift rates with the optimal prediction from the unisensory rates, as well as with empirical audio-visual detection data. The OR and SUM Models reproduced established unisensory response patterns from behavioural data from in children, children with autism, adults, older adults, and people with Parkinson's disease. Drift diffusion analysis revealed suboptimal integration in the OR Model and optimal integration in the SUM Model. However, the SUM Model also produced supra-optimal responses under certain conditions, inconsistent with behavioural data. The REPEAT Model captured the role of priming in sensory repetition effects, distinguishing it from true multisensory integration. Together, these models highlight how biologically grounded mathematical frameworks can shed light on the mechanisms underlying multisensory integration, particularly the nuanced contributions of modality repetition and integration efficiency.
papers.title: Modelling Audio-Visual Reaction Time with Recurrent Mean-Field Networks

papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics enables comprehensive characterization of proteins, but label-free approaches are challenging to scale to thousands of samples per day (SPD). Multiplexed data-independent approaches (plexDIA) can increase throughput but lack the mass tags to enable it. Here, we systematically screened a library of 576 compounds and identified several small molecules that, when conjugated to peptides, improve their detection and sequence identification. The lead molecule, PSMtag, substantially increases the detection of fragment b-ions, which increases the confidence of sequence identification and enhances de novo sequencing. PSMtags allow 9-plexDIA, using only stable isotopes of carbon, oxygen and nitrogen. As a result, it allows increasing sample throughput for plexDIA workflows. We demonstrate 1,130 SPD with 9-plexDIA from single-cell-level human proteomes, acquiring 27,520 protein datapoints in the same time label-free methods acquire 3,216. Our approach constitutes an expandable framework for developing mass tags to overcome existing limitations in multiplexed proteomics.
papers.title: PSMtags improve peptide sequencing and throughput in sensitive proteomics

papers.abstract: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is a major target for deep brain stimulation (DBS) in Parkinson disease (PD), yet its molecular organization and relationship to the adjacent para-subthalamic nucleus (pSTN) remain incompletely defined. Here, we performed comparative molecular mapping of the STN and pSTN in mouse and macaque, complemented by a human tissue sample, three-dimensional imaging, and publicly available spatial transcriptomic datasets. The STN showed a largely conserved molecular framework across species with gradients across rostrocaudal and dorsolateral axes. However, HTR2C was found enriched in the ventral STN of macaque and human tissue samples, while broadly distributed across the mouse STN. HTR2C showed opposite gradient of PVALB. In the mouse STN, Nts expression revealed an additional mediolateral gradient. Publicly available transcriptomic datasets showed concordant expression patterns. In both species, TAC1 characterized the canonical pSTN but also an extended population reaching dorsally along the medial aspect of the STN. TAC1-positive cells were thus found in the region traversed by tyrosine hydroxylase-positive fibers of the medial forebrain bundle (MFB). Together, these findings reveal a spatially heterogeneous, multiaxial molecular organization of the STN and a spatially complex molecular organization of its neighboring brain areas, refining the molecular and anatomical framework of the subthalamic region.
papers.title: Comparative molecular mapping reveals molecular gradients and spatially organized populations in the subthalamic and para-subthalamic regions

papers.abstract: In a community effort, we audited error control in twelve crosslinking mass spectrometry pipelines using two ground-truth designs that expose a lower bound on false identifications. Some pipelines passed, whereas for others these verifiably false identifications alone exceeded the requested false discovery rate up to 29-fold at the protein-protein interaction level. The audit also tracked improvement between software versions, supporting its use for regression testing.
papers.title: A community audit of error control in crosslinking mass spectrometry

papers.abstract: Maternal microorganisms contribute to the development of the infant gut microbiome, but plasmid sharing between mothers and infants remains poorly characterized. We reanalyzed longitudinal shotgun metagenomes from 65 mother-infant pairs to identify highly similar plasmid sequences across 117 comparisons at infant ages of 0.5, 3, and 12 months. We assessed associations with delivery mode and examined the predicted hosts and gene content of shared plasmids. Plasmid sharing was detected in 27 comparisons (23.1%) at 0.5 and 3 months, but not at 12 months. Among plasmids with predicted hosts, Bacteroides-associated sequences were prominent. Compared with plasmids detected only in mothers, shared plasmids were enriched in genes associated with mobilization (mbpA, mbpB, mbpC), replication (repL), and toxin-antitoxin systems (yoeB). Vaginally delivered infants had higher total plasmid counts at 0.5 months than cesarean-delivered infants, although plasmid sharing did not differ significantly by delivery mode. These findings provide a basis for understanding the genetic characteristics of plasmids shared during early gut microbiome development.
papers.title: Mother-infant sharing of gut plasmid sequences during early infancy and their genetic characteristics

papers.abstract: Distinguishing resident microglia from engrafted peripheral myeloid cells is important for interpreting CNS inflammation. P2RY12, TMEM119, and FCRLS are widely used to identify microglia, but their ability to distinguish cellular origin after prolonged engraftment remains context dependent.
