papers.abstract: Goal-directed behavior often requires sustained effort across a sequence of interdependent decisions, yet the determinants of persistence in such contexts remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how individuals regulate persistence in a novel sequential effort-based task in which they controlled an avatar through successive checkpoints to reach a final goal and could make repeated attempts following failure. At each attempt, participants could choose either to persist in the same task or to disengage toward an easier but less rewarding alternative. We found that decisions to persist or disengage were jointly shaped by multiple interacting factors. Disengagement increased with task difficulty and lower skill level. It also increased with repeated attempts and varied with time-on-task, indexing fatigue, and with accumulated errors, indexing lack of progress. Conversely, proximity to the goal promoted persistence and shaped decision dynamics with greater hesitation when disengaging near the goal. Notably, clearing the first checkpoint produced a sharp increase in persistence, suggesting that early success plays a pivotal role. Furthermore, persistence reflected both retrospective and prospective evaluations of effort, with prior investment promoting commitment and anticipated effort reducing it. Finally, disengagement was preceded by short-term performance decline but not by a detectable increase in decision conflict. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive account of persistence in sequential effortful tasks, showing that decisions to persist or disengage are jointly shaped by multiple factors related to fatigue, (lack of) progress, goal proximity, and early success.
papers.title: Determinants of persistence in sequential effort-based decision-making

papers.abstract: The creatine (Cr)-creatine kinase (CK)-phosphocreatine (PCr) system maintains ATP homeostasis in tissues with high energy demands, but its role in early human placental development remains poorly understood. We characterized Cr-CK-PCr system components across gestation and investigated its function in trophoblast development. Proteins involved in Cr biosynthesis, transport, and utilization were examined in first-trimester, second-trimester, and term human placentae (n=3-6/group). Components showed gestational age- and compartment-specific localization. The biosynthetic enzymes AGAT and GAMT localized predominantly to fetal villous mesenchyme and broadly across villous compartments, respectively. CKB was enriched in fetal mesenchyme, whereas CKMT1 was broadly expressed across trophoblast subtypes. The main Cr transporter SLC6A8 was abundant in syncytiotrophoblast early in gestation but shifted predominantly to fetal blood vessels at term. To determine functional importance, primary human trophoblast stem cells (hTSCs) were treated with a creatine analog, cyclocreatine (cCr; 0-40 mM), for 48 h. Treatment with 20 mM cCr reduced proliferation (P<0.001), decreased EGFR expression (P<0.05), induced cell-cycle arrest (P<0.0001), and increased apoptosis (P<0.0001). cCr also impaired mitochondrial and glycolytic function (P<0.01) with morphological evidence of mitochondrial stress. Consistently, treatment of primary human trophoblast organoids with cCr reduced organoid growth and EGFR expression (P<0.05). Together, these findings demonstrate that the Cr-CK-PCr system is dynamically expressed across human placental development and that disruption of Cr/PCr metabolism compromises trophoblast bioenergetics, proliferation, and survival, supporting its importance in placental development and providing a foundation for investigating its contribution to pregnancy disorders associated with altered placental energy metabolism.
papers.title: Creatine phosphagen system regulates energy metabolism and growth of trophoblasts

papers.abstract: Genomic changes are central to cancer, so sequencing is essential for understanding tumor evolution and advancing precision medicine, but resolving somatic variants and methylation is challenging in regions with repeats, reference gaps, and germline variants. To identify the full spectrum of somatic variants, including complex rearrangements, we construct and curate near-complete, haplotype-resolved assemblies of the most recent common ancestor of an early-passage, broadly-consented hypodiploid pancreatic cancer cell line and matched normal tissues. The tumor assembly recapitulates all 35 chromosomes observed by karyotyping, including translocation-induced hybrid chromosomes containing dynamic dicentric and fused centromeres, nested foldback inversions causing 14 breakpoints with a haplotype switch in a single derivative chromosome, and centromeric satellite tandem duplications up to 136 kbp. Our tumor-normal assembly-based benchmark expands previous multi-technology ensemble benchmark approaches, adding >8,000 somatic small variants altering ~40 kbp and 149 somatic SVs altering 939 kbp, including 2,764 small variants and 126 SVs not represented on GRCh38. Additionally, 5,111 somatic small variants change representation because they alter germline variants on GRCh38, impacting mutational signatures. Most source-resolved somatic LINE insertions originate from two non-reference germline LINE insertions with accessible promoter elements. These assemblies demonstrate that centromeric, acrocentric, telomeric, and other polymorphic regions, conventionally excluded from analysis, harbor extensive somatic and epigenetic changes and provide curated paired tumor-normal benchmarks to advance algorithms for repetitive regions of cancer genomes.
papers.title: A near-complete human pancreatic cancer genome

papers.abstract: Quantitative fluorescence microscopy is frequently confounded by spatially varying illumination and temporal intensity drift. Although BaSiC is a widely adopted retrospective correction method, it can fail when foreground content is strongly correlated across images, a common regime in time-lapse, tiled and volumetric acquisitions, and its application often requires manual parameter tuning that limits reproducibility and scalability. We introduce BaSiCPy, a foreground-aware implementation of BaSiC that improves illumination profile estimation under correlated foreground structures, provides automatic hyperparameter selection and accelerates large-scale processing through GPU support. BaSiCPy is distributed as an open-source Python package with graphical and programmatic interfaces, facilitating integration into contemporary bioimage analysis workflows.
papers.title: BaSiCPy: Scalable and Robust Shading Correction for Optical Microscopy Images

papers.abstract: The optimization and control of bioprocesses require robust in silico models that can accurately capture the complex and dynamic behavior of living cells. While hybrid models that combine machine learning with mechanistic equations have emerged as a powerful tools, they often require relatively large datasets and might yield inconsistent predictions that violate the stoichiometry of metabolism. In this study, we introduce FBA-Hyb, a multi-scale hybrid modeling framework that tightly integrates genome-scale metabolic networks via flux balance analysis (FBA) into its architecture. In our FBA-Hyb framework, artificial neural networks predict key FBA inputs (substrate uptake rates and FBA objectives) while a surrogate FBA module translates them into the metabolic fluxes that govern the bioprocess. A key novelty is that the FBA optimization step is replaced by a surrogate generated with symbolic regression, which encapsulates the FBA model into a compact analytical expression. This allows easy backpropagation through the integration of the neural controlled differential equation based FBA-Hyb bioprocess model. We validated FBA-Hyb against a standard hybrid model (Std-Hyb) using two Escherichia coli fed-batch case studies. In the first study, FBA-Hyb achieved a 42% average improvement in predictive accuracy (R2) during a leave-one-process-out cross validation. Crucially, FBA-Hyb maintains strict stoichiometric feasibility even during extrapolation. Meanwhile, an alternative approach based on standard architectures leads to stoichiometrically inconsistent solutions in 22% of the cases analyzed. In the second case study, we demonstrate how FBA-Hyb effectively simulates unmeasured chemical species and discovers a metabolic shift in sulfate-limited regimes during bioprocessing. By providing a modular, biologically consistent, and computationally efficient architecture, FBA-Hyb offers a robust foundation for the next generation of bioprocess models and sustainable process optimization.
papers.title: Integrating Metabolic Networks into Hybrid Bioprocess Models

papers.abstract: Transgenerational plasticity can prepare descendants for environmental stress, but its generality and adaptive value remain unclear. Here we tested for adaptive transgenerational effects of exposure to the bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas vranovensis across five Caenorhabditis species. Pathogen exposure reduced rate-sensitive fitness in all five species, but behavioural responses varied across species and generations. In C. elegans, exposed parents and their F2 descendants showed increased pathogen avoidance. In C. remanei, pathogen exposure increased attraction in females, whereas their F2 female descendants showed greater avoidance. We found no F2 behavioural response in C. kamaaina, C. tropicalis or C. briggsae. Remarkably, however, ancestral exposure increased F2 larval survival on the pathogen in C. elegans, C. remanei and C. tropicalis. In C. tropicalis this survival benefit occurred without behavioural avoidance. The two species showing transgenerational avoidance had the closest sequence matches between the bacterial small RNA Pv1 and its candidate neuronal target maco-1, suggesting a possible molecular basis for variation in the response. Our results show that shared susceptibility to a pathogen does not imply similarity in transgenerational response, and that ancestral exposure can benefit descendants without inheritance of pathogen avoidance.
papers.title: Transgenerational pathogen defence extends beyond behavioural avoidance

papers.abstract: Importance: Adolescent body mass index (BMI) is linked to brain microstructural alterations, but it is not known if this association is uniform across the BMI range. Objective: To characterize the shape of the association between adolescent BMI and brain microstructure across the BMI range. Design: Baseline, and 2-, 4-, and 6-year follow-up brain imaging and BMI from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive DevelopmentSM Study, analyzed between June 2025 and June 2026. Setting: Multicenter, population-based study including 21 sites distributed across the US. Participants: 10,361 adolescents (5,034 [48.5%] female; aged 9-18 years) from this population-based cohort study were included after quality control of complete data. Exposures: Centers for Disease Control BMI extended percentiles and percent from median BMI. Main Outcome and Measure: The primary outcome was the restricted normalized isotropic (RNI) signal fraction derived from diffusion imaging which indexes water confined within spherical cellular structures and is sensitive to microstructural properties including cellularity. Results: A total of 10,361 participants (5,034 [48.5%] female; aged 9-18 years) contributed 21,629 imaging observations across four timepoints. Higher BMI percentile was associated with greater RNI in bilateral reward- and appetite-related subcortical gray matter and white matter tracts, with effects varying spatially within structures, and with generally greater magnitude in males. Across these structures, the association increased steeply above the 80th percentile. This acceleration reflected compression of the percentile scale at high BMI; when BMI was reparameterized as percent from median, the association with RNI was approximately linear. Conclusions and Relevance: Our results suggest that BMI is associated with brain microstructure in a graded manner within white matter tracts and subcortical gray matter related to reward, executive function, and appetitive control. This indicates that the effect of BMI on microstructure is not confined to weight extremes and should be accounted for when modeling brain-body-behavior relationships during adolescence.
papers.title: Assessing nonlinear associations between body mass index and brain microstructure across adolescence in the ABCD Study

papers.abstract: Poplar (Populus spp.) is globally important for timber and afforestation, and is also a model system for woody perennials. However, the molecular control of reproductive organ development, particularly that of the epidermal trichomes on seeds known as seed fibers (fluff), which cause environmental and health concerns, remains poorly understood. Here, integrating single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) with spatial transcriptomics, we constructed a spatiotemporal atlas of female poplar capsules that resolves the cellular composition of the organ and positions each cell type within its native tissue context. We traced the developmental trajectory of seed fibers, showing that they originate from placenta epidermal cells, and identified three functionally distinct fiber cell subtypes involved in initiation, photosynthesis and elongation. Network analysis identified candidate regulators including PtoPDF2, PtoMYB38 and PtoHDG11. PtoPDF2 activates PtoMYB38 and PtoSTK2 by binding L1-box motifs in their promoters, revealing a module that governs seed fiber initiation. Together, our study provides a framework for seed fiber development in poplar and candidate targets for breeding low-fluff cultivars.
papers.title: Single-cell spatiotemporal transcriptomics reveals the origin, cellular heterogeneity and regulatory network of seed fiber cells in poplar

papers.abstract: RNA-binding proteins regulate essential steps of RNA metabolism, yet identifying RNA-interacting regions and prioritizing sequence variants that alter binding remain challenging from protein sequence alone. Here we present catRAPID signature 2.0 HERCULES (Hybrid framEwoRk for RNA-binding domain loCalization and mUtation anaLysis using physicochemical and languagE modelS), an approach combining a fine-tuned ProteinBERT model with residue-level physicochemical descriptors to predict global RNA-binding propensity, localize interaction sites and estimate the impact of amino acid substitutions. The language model captures domain-scale sequence context, whereas the physicochemical module provides sensitivity to local residue changes. On an independent benchmark, HERCULES discriminates RBPs from non-RBPs with an AUROC of 0.86. At residue resolution, it enriches high-scoring positions within annotated interaction regions across canonical, non-canonical and putative domain classes, while maintaining strong performance on an independent InterPro benchmark. Protein microarray experiments using disease-associated repeat RNAs (CGG, CAG and interrupted CAACAG repeats) independently support multiple non-catalogued candidate RBPs prioritized by HERCULES. Using curated UniProt variants associated with impaired RNA binding, HERCULES also prioritizes deleterious substitutions from predicted changes in binding propensity. By integrating protein-level classification, residue localization, variant-effect prediction and experimental validation, HERCULES provides an interpretable framework for prioritizing RNA-binding proteins, interaction regions and mutation-sensitive sites. HERCULES is freely available at https://tools.tartaglialab.com/hercules and as an open-source Python package at https://github.com/tartaglialabIIT/hercules.git.
papers.title: HERCULES: a deep-learning framework for RNA-binding region localization and mutation-effect prediction

papers.abstract: Germline-targeting vaccines aim to elicit HIV-1 broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), but determinants of serum bnAb induction remain unclear. We previously showed that Q23-APEX-GT2 primes diverse V2-apex bnAb precursors in outbred rhesus macaques (RMs). To assess their maturation into authentic bnAbs, we infected immunized RMs with CAP256.SU SHIV. Four of six developed heterologous serum neutralization breadth, with one neutralizing ~70% of viruses tested. Early autologous neutralization and B-cell priming efficiency post-prime correlated with post-infection breadth. Longitudinal lineage tracing in lymph-nodes and blood revealed that recruitment and expansion of diverse long-CDRH3 V2-apex B-cell precursors, followed by early dominance of one or two clones, predicted serum breadth. Structural analyses showed that non-neutralizing lineages failed despite cross-reactive Env binding, owing to unfavorable V2-apex approach angles and limited glycan engagement. Together, these findings identify priming efficiency and early clonal dominance as key determinants of serum bnAb induction and provide a framework for HIV vaccine design.
papers.title: Early clonal dominance at priming sets the trajectory for broad HIV serum neutralization

papers.abstract: Coordination of the functionalities among key organelles is essential for maintaining the complexity and adaptability of the eukaryotic cell. Functionally versatile proteins, such as GTPases, often assume important roles in this process. A ribosome-binding GTPase called Developmentally-regulated GTP-binding (Drg) protein is a conserved family of GTPases that promotes protein synthesis and regulates cytoskeletal dynamics, suggesting their importance for cell growth and proliferation. Mitochondrial proteostasis requires coordination between cytosolic translation and the targeting, import, and assembly of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins. However, the ribosome-associated factors that support this coordination remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the conserved GTPase Drg1, one of the two Drg paralogues in eukaryotic cells, as a translation factor required for mitochondrial homeostasis and cellular fitness. Human Drg1 and its cofactor Dfrp1 are associated with translating ribosomes and co-sedimented with polysomes. Deletion of Drg1 in HEK293T cells caused altered mitochondrial architecture, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production, and impaired expression of a mitochondrially targeted reporter. Re-expression of wild-type Drg1 restored ATP production and reporter expression, whereas a GTPase-deficient Drg1 mutant failed to provide comparable rescue in ATP production, demonstrating that Drg1 catalytic activity is required for its cellular function. Mitochondria-directed APEX2 proximity proteomics further connected Drg1-dependent translation to proteins involved in mitochondrial protein import, respiratory-chain function, and mitochondrial protein synthesis. Reporter analyses indicated that Drg1 loss preferentially compromises productive translation toward the 3' region of the coding sequence. Together, these findings establish Drg1 as a ribosome-associated translation factor that supports the synthesis and homeostasis of proteins required for mitochondrial function. At the molecular level, loss of cellular homeostasis that is caused by compromised translation of cytoplasmically synthesized proteins functionally related to mitochondria underpins the observed phenomenon. Our results reveal a previously underappreciated connection between the cytosolic translation machinery and mitochondrial maintenance and provide a framework for understanding how defects in a conserved translational GTPase impair cellular energy metabolism and physiology.
papers.title: Ribosome-Associated GTPase Drg1 Links Cytosolic Translation to Mitochondrial Homeostasis

papers.abstract: Envelope biogenesis in Staphylococcus aureus is concentrated at the septum and encompasses peptidoglycan synthesis, teichoic acid production, and the targeted secretion and anchoring of YSIRK/GXXS signal peptide-bearing surface proteins. How S. aureus spatially restricts these processes to the dividing crosswall remains unclear. EzrA is a membrane-anchored protein structurally related to eukaryotic spectrins that has been implicated in linking cell division to envelope synthesis, yet its precise contribution remains undefined. Here, we show that EzrA spatially couples peptidoglycan synthesis with the surface display of septal proteins. In ezrA null cells, newly synthesized peptidoglycan is incorporated in a dispersed pattern rather than confined to the septum, teichoic acid synthesis is increased, and surface protein display is elevated. In wild-type cells, nascent peptidoglycan and nascent Staphylococcal protein A anchoring sites colocalize at the septum; this spatial coupling is lost in the absence of EzrA. ezrA null cells also exhibit impaired nucleoid occlusion, with septal ingression over the chromosome leading to chromosome guillotining. Together, these findings suggest that EzrA constitutes a spatial organizing system at the septum, coordinating multiple envelope biogenesis processes while linking septal organization to nucleoid occlusion, a parallel spatial positioning system, to ensure faithful chromosome segregation and cytokinesis.
papers.title: EzrA coordinates septal organization and nucleoid occlusion in Staphylococcus aureus

papers.abstract: The visual system operates by segmenting visual inputs into distinct perceptual objects. Segmentation is dynamic, as revealed by the tempo of perceptual choices and neural activity in the visual cortex. Dynamics for natural stimuli however, are poorly understood because natural scene segmentation is ambiguous and subjective. We measured subjective human segmentation maps for natural images using an innovative paradigm, and uncovered richer spatiotemporal dynamics than predicted by current theories of segmentation. To explain these dynamics, we introduced Iterative Bayesian Inference algorithms for segmentation that iteratively integrate visual inputs with the prior expectation for local smoothness. When visual inputs were consistent with such a spatial prior, iterative inference was faster. Such a predicted relationship between spatial prior and inferential dynamics was evident in our data and correctly reflected each individual participant's spatial biases. We conclude that iterative Bayesian inference sets the tempo for a fundamental function of natural vision.
papers.title: Natural scene segmentation dynamics reveal iterative Bayesian inference

papers.abstract: The RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway relays extracellular signals into a cellular response and its dysregulation leads to many pathologies, particularly cancer. Much is known about the individual components of the pathway, however, details of their interactions and how specificity is maintained is still poorly understood. Here, we determined cryo-EM structures of the MAP2K MEK1 activating its substrate MAPK ERK2, the final event in the cascade. We define the molecular details of specificity and activation of ERK2 and examine the mechanism of substrate recognition using solution techniques and molecular dynamics. Binding of the substrate MAPK leads to release of the MAP2K catalytic machinery, a mechanism enhanced in many gain of function disease mutations. Further, we observe that ERK2 release is not required for nucleotide exchange, suggesting how a processive mechanism could proceed. Our data advance the understanding of MAPK signalling specificity and provide a starting point for drug development.
papers.title: Molecular basis of mitogen-activated protein kinase ERK2 activation by its upstream kinase MEK1

papers.abstract: Erasing outdated memories is crucial for adaptive behavior. Yet once a cue-outcome association is learned, repeated cue exposure without outcome suppresses conditioned behavior without erasing the underlying memory. This allows rapid behavioral recovery when outcomes are reintroduced. Here, we confirm this limitation for standard prospective extinction protocols that present cues without the associated outcome, but show that true memory erasure is achieved by inverting the paradigm: presenting outcomes without associated cues, i.e., retrospective extinction. We demonstrate that orbitofrontal cortex activity at outcome is necessary for the rapid behavioral recovery following prospective extinction, and that mesolimbic dopamine activity at outcome is necessary for retrospective extinction. These findings reconceptualize extinction mechanisms and suggest complementary strategies to mitigate relapse and erase maladaptive memories.
papers.title: Memory erasure by dopamine-gated retrospective learning

papers.abstract: Bacterial defense systems undergo rapid evolutionary changes, yet the specific contributions of the genomic compartment (chromosomal versus mobile genetic element [MGE]) to these dynamics remain unclear. We analyzed 6,907 genomes from 213 species of Enterobacteriaceae using a phylogenetic birth-death model to quantify gain, loss, expansion, and reduction of defense (DEF) and anti-defense (anti-DEF) gene families. We found that DEF turnover differs from the background dynamics of the genomic elements that carry them. Direct comparisons among DEFs further revealed differences in loss and copy-number dynamics across genomic compartments, with the highest rates on chromosomes, intermediate rates on plasmids and ICEs/IMEs, and the lowest rates on prophages, whereas the relative balance between gain and loss and between expansion and reduction remained similar across chromosomes and MGEs. MGE-associated anti-DEFs showed higher loss, expansion, and reduction rates than DEFs, whereas chromosome-associated anti-DEFs showed lower gain rates than DEFs. Finally, we found that gains and losses of DEFs and anti-DEFs were positively correlated across bacterial lineages, with positive associations observed for both matching (that is, antagonistic) and non-matching pairs. Together, these results show that genomic background affects the overall flux of DEFs and anti-DEFs, and that turnover of DEFs and anti-DEFs is evolutionarily coupled across lineages.
papers.title: Co-evolutionary dynamics of defense systems and anti-defense genes in chromosomes and mobile genetic elements of Enterobacteriaceae

papers.abstract: Glycosylation heterogeneity of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) necessitates precise glycoengineering to optimize effector functions, such as those mediated by Fcgamma-receptors (FcgammaRs). However, current enzymatic remodeling methods are limited in scope, producing only a narrow spectrum of glycoforms and unable to achieve complete control over defined asymmetrical structures. Here, we report a multi-step, fully enzymatic platform for the solution-phase synthesis of a comprehensive library of biantennary mAb glycoforms, offering complete control over the alpha1,3- and alpha1,6-mannose arm architecture. This strategy uses a single domain of the beta-N-acetylglucosaminidase StrH (GH20-2) to achieve regioselective hydrolysis of the GlcNAc residue on the alpha1,3-mannose arm of the intact antibody, thereby introducing asymmetry. Next, the remaining terminal GlcNAc residue at the alpha1,6-antenna can be enzymatically extended with a beta1,4-galactoside and sialoside or alpha1,3-galactoside. Remarkably, after this extension, recombinant GnT-I can reintroduce the GlcNAc at the alpha1,3-mannosyl antenna, allowing precise control over glycan branching and composition. This robust, two-stage enzymatic remodeling methodology, demonstrated on infliximab and cetuximab, unlocks a broad chemical space of biantennary Fc glycans for comprehensive functional studies. We employed these well-defined glycovariants to determine the minimum structural requirements for anti-alpha-Gal IgE binding and to systematically evaluate binding affinities toward FcgammaRs, providing new insights for the rational design of next-generation immune-therapeutics.
papers.title: Asymmetrical Glyco-Engineering of Monoclonal Antibodies Provides Insights into α-Gal Immunogenicity

papers.abstract: Background and Hypothesis: Alzheimer's disease with psychosis (AD+P) is a subgroup of AD patients with more rapid cognitive deterioration. While our previous study showed that AD+P is associated with loss of prefrontal cortex postsynaptic density (PSD) proteins, identifying proteins in the broader cellular environment that influence PSD loss addresses a critical knowledge gap about synaptic dysfunction mechanisms in early disease stages. Study Design: We conducted a proteomic analysis comparing prefrontal grey matter cortex tissue homogenates from elderly normal controls (n=18), individuals with AD+P (n=61), and individuals with AD-P (n=48). Study Results: AD+P showed the most pronounced alterations relative to controls (178 proteins with q<0.05), although alterations in AD-P and AD+P relative to controls were highly similar (R2=0.965, p<0.001). Weighted-gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA) identified four modules significantly associated with disease status comparing AD subjects to controls, but none differed significantly between AD+P and AD-P. We identified 15 proteins significantly correlated with PSD yield across all samples, including ENPP6, linked to AD+P by GWAS. Additionally, PSD yield-associated proteins showed minimal overlap with altered AD proteins (1 of 137). Proteins negatively correlated with PSD yield were enriched for presynaptic endocytosis, whereas the one WGCNA module significantly correlated with PSD yield was enriched for inflammatory terms. Conclusions: Our findings suggest a model in which AD+P arises from the combination of quantitative alterations within a shared AD proteome profile and a superimposed set of protein alterations correlated with PSD yield that confer distinct mechanisms of synaptic vulnerability and psychosis risk.
papers.title: Proteomic analysis in Alzheimer's disease with psychosis reveals a shared AD proteomic landscape and a separate molecular signature of postsynaptic density disruption

papers.abstract: The authors have withdrawn this manuscript because the work has since been expanded with substantial new data and reorganized into two separate manuscripts, each with a revised author list. Therefore, the authors do not wish this work to be cited as reference for the project. If you have any questions, please contact the corresponding author.
papers.title: WITHDRAWN: Omnidirectional 3D Printing of Anisotropic Nanofibrous Peptide Hydrogels

papers.abstract: Obesity is a global health challenge increasingly linked to environmental obesogens. Tributyltin (TBT), a model obesogen that activates PPARgamma and RXR, promotes transgenerational obesity in mice, but whether developmental and ancestral exposure impairs energy balance remains unclear. Brown adipose tissue (BAT) contributes to energy expenditure and thermoregulation through UCP1-dependent and -independent pathways. We tested whether TBT exposure disrupts BAT function in F1 and F3 descendants of exposed F0 dams. We measured body composition before and after high-fat diet (HFD) challenge and assessed resting core body temperature, BAT gene expression, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) content, and mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) capacity. TBT-line males accumulated more fat after HFD without changes in lean mass despite similar mass-scaled food intake. Before HFD, core body temperature was lower in F1 and F3 TBT-line males, indicating impaired thermal homeostasis before increased adiposity. Candidate-gene qPCR did not show uniform suppression of thermogenic genes; instead, Ucp1 mRNA increased while Ucp2 mRNA decreased in F1 males, indicating dysregulation. Transcriptomal profiling revealed altered thermogenic signaling and consistent downregulation of mitochondrial electron transport chain genes across F1 and F3 males. Relative mtDNA content was unchanged, whereas complex-specific respirometry revealed reduced complex I- and II-associated respiratory capacity, providing evidence of impaired electron transport. No consistent effects occurred in females. These findings identified an early, male-associated BAT phenotype characterized by thermogenic dysregulation, reduced mitochondrial ETC capacity, and impaired thermal homeostasis. They support a model in which impaired BAT mitochondrial function contributes to later susceptibility to diet-induced obesity.
papers.title: Ancestral tributyltin exposure produces male-specific brown adipose thermogenic dysregulatoin

papers.abstract: Endemic human coronaviruses (HCoVs), such as HCoV-HKU1, account for ~30% of common colds each year and can cause serious upper and lower respiratory infections, yet no licensed vaccines or therapeutic antibodies target HCoVs. Despite being endemic to the human population, little is known about the antigenic landscape of HCoV-HKU1. Here, we characterized key interactions between the HCoV-HKU1 spike (S) protein and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) isolated from convalescent HCoV-HKU-1-positive peripheral blood mononuclear cells collected prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. We isolated 14 mAbs that bound distinct regions of S, including the receptor-binding domain (RBD), N-terminal domain, and S2 subunit. Structural and functional studies revealed three groups of RBD-specific mAbs targeting diverse footprints within and around the TMPRSS2 receptor-binding site: (1) H501-022, which recognizes the TMPRSS2-binding site and thereby blocks receptor engagement; (2) H501-008, which binds a distinct epitope outside the TMPRSS2-binding site that is shared with HCoV-OC43; and (3) H501-018, which recognizes both up and down RBD conformations at a distinct, non-overlapping epitope outside the TMPRSS2-binding site. H501-008 weakly neutralized live HCoV-OC43 in vitro and protected mice against lethal HCoV-OC43 challenge. Notably, the three RBD-specific mAbs potently neutralized HCoV-HKU1 pseudovirus in TMPRSS2-overexpressing cell lines, but exhibited limited neutralizing activity against authentic HCoV-HKU1 infection in primary human airway epithelial cells. Together, these findings structurally define the antigenic landscape within and around the HKU1 receptor-binding site and demonstrate that receptor-binding site recognition alone is insufficient to predict physiologically relevant antibody-mediated neutralization.
papers.title: Structural Definition of Neutralizing Epitopes within and around the HKU1 Receptor-binding Site Reveals Cell Context-Dependent Neutralization

papers.abstract: The eyes of insects exhibit extreme morphological variation through changes in size and shape. While the model organism Drosophila melanogaster has been used to elucidate the underlying gene networks and cell-signalling pathways that regulate the patterning and growth of the eye, insight into the regulators of nutrient-dependent sizing and allometry within and between the sexes remains poorly understood. Using a screen approach of the well characterized and ancient Insulin/TOR pathway, we show that perturbations of different nodes of this pathway modulate the impact of nutritional variation on the sizing and scaling of the eye to varying degrees, and that this is further influenced by sex. When starved, wild-type flies decrease in eye size and body size proportionately in females, yet males change eye-to-body size disproportionately. Subsequently we used previously validated RNAi lines to knockdown each component of the Insulin/TOR pathway in an eye-specific manner to characterize their individual influence in modulating nutritional plasticity of eye sizing. Surprisingly, this resulted in a range of size and scaling variation, components modulating the plastic response on eye size mean, eye-to-body slope, intercept, as well as eye size variance, some effects ranging in magnitude from shutting off plasticity to amplifying, and some which were sex-limited. More generally, the morphospace of a trait can evolve within and across the sexes through modifications of plasticity genes.
papers.title: Keeping an Eye on Plasticity Genes: Insulin/TOR Pathway Components Mediating Nutritional Plasticity of Eyes Within and Between Sex

papers.abstract: It is widely accepted that susceptibility to infection increases with age, usually attributed to immune system dysregulation. However, factors beyond decreased resistance mechanisms may increase susceptibility, such as changes to physiological or metabolic processes determining overall tolerance, and this may differ between individuals. We hypothesised that age-related increases in susceptibility reflect changes in both immune system function and disease tolerance, with their relative importance varying by population and sex. We assessed age-related susceptibility to bacterial pathogens in an outbred D. melanogaster population and 22 isolines. We leveraged this variation to investigate age-related infection susceptibility and lifespan, and to estimate frequencies of declines in resistance or tolerance mechanisms. Susceptibility increased early in life, and was widespread across infections and populations. Despite strong correlation between the sexes in baseline susceptibility and its decrease over age, susceptibility at old age did not correlate. Increased susceptibility was associated with impaired resistance (bona fide immunosenescence), but more frequently with reduced tolerance, which could be detected early in life, and remained low. We find susceptibility at old age predicts lifespan in males only. In conclusion, increased infection susceptibility is an early-arising ageing phenotype occurring in both sexes and driving male mortality. Infection susceptibility followed a power-law (Weibull) rather than the exponential (Gompertz) pattern typical of mortality, with each doubling of age approximately doubling susceptibility. We argue that the term 'immunosenescence' should be limited to dysregulation of resistance mechanisms, and consideration of population variation, sex, and ageing of non-immune functions is critical to fully understand age-related loss of pathogen control.
papers.title: Harnessing variation in Drosophila melanogaster reveals different routes to increased infection susceptibility over age and sex-dependent association with lifespan

papers.abstract: Inter-individual differences in learning-related activation in the hippocampus and its subregions predict specific differences in memory abilities. The complexity of these relationships creates a setting that is ripe for theoretically informative investigation, but that can also yield reports of spurious relationships that do not reflect underlying neurobiological associations. Across-study replication is therefore a critical step toward understanding how individual differences in hippocampal activity drive individual differences in memory ability. In the domain of verbal memory, Wig et al. (2008) identified a negative relationship between task-induced activation in right posterior HPC (pHPC) and out-of-scanner verbal memory test performance. Replicating this result in an independent sample of 86 participants, we identified the same negative correlation between pHPC activation during an in-scanner Lithuanian-English paired associate learning task and out-of-scanner California Verbal Learning Test (CVLT-II) performance. In a follow-up exploratory voxel-wise association analysis, we observed the same negative correlation between CVLT-II performance and task-induced activity across three regions of the medial temporal lobe: the left perirhinal/entorhinal cortex, right parahippocampal gyrus, and left posterior hippocampus. This replication and accompanying extension represent a critical step toward understanding how pHPC supports verbal memory by answering basic questions concerning the reliability and selectivity of this previously identified relationship.
papers.title: Lower Levels of Task-Induced Hippocampal Activation Predict Better Performance on a Separate Verbal Memory Evaluation

papers.abstract: Seed amplification assays sensitively detect misfolded alpha-synuclein (alphaSyn) templating activity in homogenates but erase tissue coordinates, whereas Ser129-phosphorylated alphaSyn (pS129) immunostaining preserves anatomy without measuring functional seeding competence. Here we report multiplexed immunofluorescence-integrated quiescent seed amplification (IF-QSAA), coupling in situ QSAA with multichannel immunolabelling on the same brain section. Combining mouse alphaSyn monomer, high sulfate and 70 degrees C quiescent incubation under an agarose overlay generates localized, fibrillar thioflavin T-positive products with high seed specificity. Across preformed-fibril-inoculated mouse brains and human Parkinson's disease (PD) tissue, QSAA reveals white-matter seeding enrichment, resolves hemispheric asymmetry earlier than pS129, and recovers endogenous seeding signals from archival formalin-fixed PD tissue lacking pS129 immunoreactivity. Using a QSAA-first workflow with 80 degrees C citrate retrieval and spectral unmixing, IF-QSAA identifies selective neuronal and microglial associations and resolves core-halo QSAA-pS129 dual-positive pairs. IF-QSAA thus co-maps functional seeding and molecular histopathology.
papers.title: Spatial mapping of α-synuclein seeding activity and pathology using immunofluorescence-integrated quiescent seed amplification

papers.abstract: Dynamic mRNA modifications have a crucial impact on the fate and metabolism of a transcript, including splicing, subcellular localization, stability, and translation. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is one of the most prominent modifications found in mRNA. It is catalyzed by Methyltransferase 3 (METTL3), which forms part of the core (catalytic) m6A writer complex together with Methyltransferase 14 (METTL14) and Wilms' tumor 1-associating protein (WTAP). The m6A writer complex has local preference for A within the consensus DRACH (D = G/A/U, R = G/A, A, C, H = A/U/C) motif. Within the transcript, m6A sites are enriched after the last splice site of the last exon and in the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) in proximity to the stop codon. Finally, m6A can also be removed from a transcript by eraser proteins fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) and AlkB Homolog 5, RNA Demethylase (ALKBH5). A variety of m6A reader proteins in different subcellular localizations recognize m6A and mediate m6A's regulatory function on mRNA metabolism. Established functions of m6A include promoting transcript decay, transcript stability, translation, splicing, and nuclear export. Finally, recent studies note the role of m6A in preventing formation of anomalous double stranded RNA (dsRNA) structures and their recognition by innate immune sensors. Adenosine deamination is also a highly prominent mRNA modification. The majority of A-to-I deamination is catalyzed by ADAR1 protein which deaminates A to inosine (I) in the context of dsRNA. Inosine pairs preferentially with cytosine and therefore is decoded as guanosine (G) by the cell's translational machinery. Two different ADAR1 isoforms exist, the constitutively expressed (and nuclear) p110 isoform and the interferon-inducible (and mostly cytoplasmic) p150 isoform which plays an important role during interferon responses. A-to-I editing occurs most frequently in repetitive elements such as short interspersed nuclear elements (SINE), introns, and the 3'UTR, due to their propensity to form dsRNA structures. Importantly, these dsRNA structures can activate cytoplasmic dsRNA sensors like MDA5. ADAR1 binding and editing of such structures prevents activation of innate immune sensing pathways. Both m6A and A-to-I deamination target adenosine, suggesting a potential for interactions. While several studies have investigated each modification independently, questions regarding their interplay remain unresolved (and conflicting) in part because the assignment of m6A or A-to-I instances used different (and incompatible) methodologies. In our LPS/IFN-g;-stimulated RAW 264.7 macrophages, ~60% of expressed genes (n = ~12,800) are annotated as m6A-modified and ~12% as harboring A-to-I editing sites, with ~10% of genes classified as harboring both mark types. Recent advances in direct RNA sequencing have made it possible to directly assess the co-occurrence of these two adenosine modifications within individual RNA molecules. Here we revisit this problem focusing on the transcriptome of macrophages for three reasons: First, macrophages readily adapt their phenotype and function, in response to changes in tissue physiology and external stimuli. This means that we can match changes in modification events to specific (and well understood) functional outputs, from the upregulation of activation markers to the phagocytic ability of cells proficient or deficient in modification enzymes. Second, there is already a body of literature on m6A and A-to-I occurrences within macrophage transcriptomes (which can serve as a positive control, despite the fact that their interplay on individual RNA molecules cannot be assessed due to earlier identification methods). And third, macrophage cell lines (including the RAW 264.7 [RAW] cell line studied here) have been used in the past for studies on RNA processing, providing a system in which post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms can be mechanistically assessed. Here, we generated RAW cells deficient for METTL3 or ADAR1, and used Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (validated with Illumina sequencing, where appropriate), to characterize the relationship between these two mRNA modifications and their impact on macrophage function.
papers.title: m6A regulates ADAR1 mediated RNA editing during macrophage activation

papers.abstract: Incorporating colloidal quantum emitters into integrated photonics would greatly advance quantum optics. However, placing individual sub-10 nm colloidal particles onto micron-sized photonic structures with nanometer-scale precision remains challenging. We introduce topography-modulated origami placement, which uses DNA origami to place colloidal nanomaterials within lithographically defined, shape-matched resist wells. The method patterns origami templates onto photonic chips with high yield and nanometer-scale precision. A soft-silicification-passivation step stabilizes deposited origamis while preserving DNA binding sites that selectively attach and align colloidal quantum rods, controlling their position and emission polarization. Placed quantum rods demonstrated room-temperature single-photon emission. We integrated individual quantum rods with waveguides, micro-ring resonators, and bullseye microcavities, and achieved cavity-coupled single-photon emission. This approach offers a general platform for integrating colloidal quantum materials into photonic systems.
papers.title: DNA-directed nanometer-scale integration of single colloidal quantum emitters with on-chip photonics

papers.abstract: Non-coding variants contribute to blood cell trait variation, but their effects on silencers remain poorly defined. Here, we used ReSE, a high-throughput silencer screening system, to assess sequences encompassing 14,720 non-coding variants from fine-mapped loci associated with 15 blood cell traits. In K562 cells, we identified 805 variants with differential silencer activity, comprising 425 loss-of-silencer-function and 380 gain-of-silencer-function candidates. Luciferase reporter assays confirmed allele-dependent repression, and endogenous editing of selected variants was accompanied by altered expression of nearby genes. K562 cells harboring the rs2857078 alternative allele showed downregulated globin expression and reduced mature erythrocyte markers upon erythroid differentiation. By integrating single-cell hematopoietic chromatin accessibility with evolutionary conservation, we further prioritized functional silencer variants despite their low fine-mapping posterior inclusion probabilities. Together, these findings implicate silencer perturbation as a regulatory mechanism contributing to blood cell trait variation and related disorders, and provide candidates for mechanistic investigation of non-coding associations.
papers.title: Genetic variants within silencer elements shape human blood cell phenotype diversity

papers.abstract: Cancer progression arises through the somatic evolution of oncogenes (OGs) and tumour-suppressor genes (TSGs). According to Knudsons two-hit hypothesis, both alleles of a TSG must typically be inactivated for tumorigenesis to proceed, whereas a single activating mutation can drive an OG. However, this diploid framework does not apply to genes in the male X chromosome, which is hemizygous, so that a single loss-of-function mutation can inactivate an X-linked TSG. Here, we adapt classical population genetics models of adaptation in haploid and diploid asexual populations to somatic evolution, and we test their predictions using somatic mutations from the COSMIC database. After excluding mutations in genes with reported copy-number alterations or promoter methylation, we find that TSGs in tumours from male patients show a higher ratio of loss-of-function (nonsense and frameshift) to synonymous mutations than autosomal TSGs, and that complete losses of X-linked TSGs are more frequent in males. Importantly, we find no such differences in tumours arising in females. X-linked OGs also show a higher rate than autosomal OGs in males and, as predicted by the model, the pattern is reversed in low-proliferation tumours, although this last difference is not statistically significant. Neutral (synonymous) mutation rates differ between sexes but not between the X chromosome and autosomes. Our work shows that ploidy and chromosomal context can be incorporated into models of somatic evolution, and it provides a framework to explore sex differences in tumorigenesis.
papers.title: Somatic evolution of cancer genes in sex chromosomes

papers.abstract: Cell migration is a fundamental behavior involved in multicellular development, regeneration, and homeostasis, which is deregulated in cancer. Epithelial cells migrate individually when isolated and collectively within a tissue. However, how interactions between cells affect their ability to explore space and their sensitivity to guidance signals is poorly understood. Here, we show that isolated cells that are persistent random walkers adopt a superdiffusive behavior in an epithelium. The effect is stronger than external guidance cues and enables cells to reach greater distances than when isolated. This directional memory emerges from fractional Brownian motion that relies on velocity coordination between neighboring cells with intact cytoskeletal connections to intercellular adhesion complexes. Furthermore, we show how the stability and mechanosensitivity of adhesion complexes ultimately regulate the speed of collective migration and the sensitivity to guidance signals via dimerization of the adhesion protein vinculin. Together, our results show how cell speed, persistence, and directionality define the efficiency of spatial cell exploration on short, intermediate, and long time scales, respectively.
papers.title: Collective directional memory controls the range of epithelial cell migration

papers.abstract: Microbes in human brain and their potential contribution to neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) have long been debated. We recently developed a new method (the electronic tree of life, eToL) based on small subunit ribosomal RNA (rRNA) probes, further confirmed by large subunit rRNA analysis, to comprehensively address the spectrum of microorganisms in control and AD brain. We report a remarkable diversity of brain microbes in control brain. The most abundant are fungi, bacteria, and chloroplastida, and we report detailed identification of representative microbial species. The pattern is substantially conserved across different bilateran species from Drosophila to human. In terms of diversity, the human brain microbiome appears to be a subset (~20%) of the gut microbiome. Adenovirus type C was the major virus found in human brain; other viruses were not well represented. However, the spectrum of brain microbes differed between individuals as well as between brain regions examined from single individuals (amygdala, cingulate cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus); of these four regions, the highest microbial burden was in cingulate cortex. There was evidence of spreading of pathogens between brain regions in single individuals. Some microbes are over-represented in AD brain according to two measures: (i) absolute number of microbes normalized to endogenous human transcripts, and (ii) the number of brain specimens showing overabundance versus control. Species over-represented in AD brain according to both measures notably include bacteria (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus/Bacillus, Sphingomonas/Ralstonia) and fungi (Acrocalymma/Altenaria/Aureobasidium of the Aspergillus group; Komagataella of the Candida group, Cortinarius of the Schizophyllum group, and Tausonia of the Cryptococcus group), that are all related to known human pathogens. In addition, an uncharacterized chloroplastida (algae-related) species was more abundant in AD brain samples. Although these findings point to diverse microbial species, indicative of multiple causation, similar absolute levels of bacteria and fungi in AD brain samples could suggest synergy between pathogens. However, it is important to stress that not all AD samples were positive for these microbes, but this could be because the affected brain region(s) was not examined. These findings support the contention that infection, perhaps associated with declining immunity with age, may contribute to AD development.
papers.title: The remarkable complexity of the brain microbiome in health and disease

papers.abstract: Spontaneous phospholipid flip-flop sets the background against which flippases, floppases, and scramblases create and dissipate membrane asymmetry. How the associated free-energy barrier depends on lipid chemistry and on the surrounding membrane remains unclear, because experiments are few and contradictory and previous simulations covered only a small part of the lipidome. Here, we calculate Martini 3 flip-flop free-energy barriers for over 700 membrane--lipid combinations, the largest such dataset to our knowledge. A systematic single component bilayer panel of five headgroups, three linkages, and 35 tail families is complemented by mixed bilayers, from binary mixtures to organelle-inspired compositions, that place the same lipid in different membranes and thus separate the effects of lipid chemistry and the membrane environment. In single component bilayers, the barrier rises with tighter tail packing and depends strongly on headgroup and tail unsaturation but only weakly on linkage. Moving a lipid into a mixed bilayer shifts its barrier as much as most headgroup substitutions do, and the shift follows the change in local tail order. Within a shared membrane, headgroup differences are mostly smaller than between single component bilayers, so part of a headgroup effect arises from the membrane that the lipid forms. A Bayesian model combining chemical descriptors with local membrane structure predicts barriers for withheld lipid families and membranes with cross-validated errors of 2.8 and 3.8 kJ/mol. The calculated trends agree qualitatively with native-lipid vesicle experiments, although Martini 3 underestimates the barrier differences between lipids, gives lower barriers than atomistic models, and overstates the effect of cholesterol.
papers.title: Structural Determinants of the Energetic Barrier of Phospholipid Flip-Flop

papers.abstract: Transfer RNA derived fragments (tRFs) are emerging regulators of gene expression. Despite mounting evidence of their functional relevance in cellular and pathological processes, their roles in virus infection remain poorly understood. Here, we show that host tRFs are dynamically reprogrammed during Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) lytic replication and function as potent antiviral effectors. Transcriptome-wide profiling revealed extensive remodelling of the tRF landscape following viral reactivation, identifying a subset of tRFs; tRFs (tRF-His-GTG, tRF-Gly-CCC, and tRF-Lys-CTT) that are robustly induced independently of parental tRNA abundance. Functional analyses demonstrate that these tRFs suppress viral gene expression and infectious virion production. Mechanistically, we show that tRF-His-GTG and tRF-Lys-CTT engage canonical RNA silencing pathways by associating with AGO2 complexes and mediating sequence-specific repression of host target genes. Among these targets, we identify SHF as a critical pro-viral factor that promotes PI3K/Akt signalling, cellular survival and efficient viral replication. Collectively, our findings define a previously uncharacterised host defence pathway in which tRFs restrict KSHV replication by targeting host factors required for efficient viral propagation, thus expanding the functional repertoire of non-coding RNAs in antiviral immunity.
papers.title: tRNA-derived fragments restrict KSHV lytic replication through miRNA-like repression of host pro-viral signalling networks

papers.abstract: Benthic biofilms are biogeochemical hotspots in rivers, yet their endogenous viral communities remain poorly resolved at national scales. We analysed 447 biofilm metagenomes from 146 sites within England's River Surveillance Network (RSN), sampled in spring and autumn from 2021 to 2023, integrating viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), water-quality gradients, predicted host associations and auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs). We recovered 38,534 vOTUs, revealing extensive viral novelty, where 93% of the vOTUs could not be assigned to a known family. Viromes were dominated by Caudoviricetes and unclassified lineages and were extremely heterogeneous: no vOTU occurred in more than 8.3% of samples. Season, but not sampling year, structured virome composition (family-level PERMANOVA R2 = 0.050, p = 0.001; year p = 0.08), and within-site turnover between spring and autumn exceeded turnover between years. Bray-Curtis ordination linked virome structure weakly to pH, dissolved organic carbon, conductivity, nitrate-N and dissolved oxygen (envfit R2 [≤] 0.066), while threshold indicator taxa analysis (TITAN) identified vOTUs with abrupt change points along alkalinity, dissolved oxygen, nitrate-N and temperature gradients. Predicted host associations were concentrated in Pseudomonodota, Cyanobacteriota and Bacteroidota, with Microcoleus, Chamaesiphon and Flavobacterium among the dominant host genera. Virus-host networks were modular, and module abundances correlated with water quality variables (dissolved oxygen, pH, nitrate etc.), suggesting that environmental filtering acts partly through host ecology. Predicted virus-host associations formed a sparse network organised around a few highly connected viral lineages. Functional profiling showed that the biofilm virome was dominated by nucleotide metabolism, DNA methylation, phosphate-stress, glycan-modification and photosynthesis-related AMGs, with nrdA/nrdB ribonucleotide reductase as the dominant AMG signal. Few vOTUs (1.2%) were detected as proviruses, although provirus fractions were higher in selected host-linked lineages. Collectively, these results show that river biofilm viromes are seasonally structured ecological communities whose composition, host associations and metabolic potential reflect the physicochemical and biological state of rivers. We propose that biofilm viromes provide a complementary layer of information for understanding river health, microbial ecology and the propagation of anthropogenic pressures in freshwater systems.
papers.title: Ecological and metabolic signatures of biofilm viromes across a national river surveillance network

papers.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) poses a significant threat to global public health, and effective preventive measures are urgently needed. The widespread antibiotic resistance of KP underscores the critical need for vaccine-based strategies. Although numerous vaccine candidates against KP have been investigated, none has yet been licensed. mRNA-LNP vaccines against KP have only recently begun to be explored, and their ability to deliver conserved outer membrane protein antigens remains largely untested. In this study, we constructed an mRNA vaccine encoding the highly conserved outer membrane protein X (OmpX) of KP-the first mRNA-LNP vaccine targeting this antigen-and evaluated its immunogenicity and protective efficacy in mice. Immunoinformatics analyses predicted concordance between the in silico and in vivo outcomes: bioinformatics tools were used to evaluate the antigenicity, immunogenicity, physicochemical parameters, and secondary and tertiary structures of OmpX, and the C-ImmSim server was used to simulate the vaccine-elicited immune responses. We then performed mouse immunization and challenge experiments to characterize the humoral and cellular immune responses induced by the OmpX vaccine. The mRNA vaccine was immunogenic in mice, eliciting high titers of OmpX-specific antibodies. OmpX-Fc mRNA-LNPs also induced robust cell-mediated immunity, with significantly elevated IFN-{gamma} and IL-4 levels indicative of combined Th1/Th2 cellular responses. Serum from OmpX-immunized mice promoted significantly greater complement-mediated KP cell lysis than serum from the alum or luciferase mRNA-LNP control groups. Notably, OmpX-Fc mRNA-LNP immunization conferred complete protection against lethal KP challenge, with 100% survival and a significant reduction in visceral bacterial burden. These data establish a promising mRNA vaccine strategy for inducing broad immune responses and promoting serotype-independent immunity against KP.
papers.title: An OmpX mRNA-LNP vaccine induces protective humoral and cellular immunity against Klebsiella pneumoniae in a C57BL/6 mouse model

papers.abstract: Intercalating dyes are widely used to visualize DNA in single-molecule experiments, but their effects on DNA-processing proteins remain incompletely characterized. Here, we study the effects of intercalators on DNA loop extrusion by SMC complexes. Intercalating dyes become fluorescent upon DNA binding, enabling direct visualization of extruded DNA loops. As dye intercalation alters the biophysical properties of DNA by lengthening and unwinding it, we examine how that modifies loop extrusion. We systematically characterize the effects of intercalators, and find that they stiffen DNA, partly neutralize its charge, and can substantially reduce the binding and ATPase activity of SMCs. We assess four dyes and conclude that SYBR Gold and SYTOX Orange are less invasive intercalators than SYTOX Green or YOYO-1. While loop extrusion is qualitatively not affected by intercalation, quantitative values for SMC binding and looping rates differ significantly from those in the absence of intercalators. We present a new dye-free loop-extrusion assay (utilizing local fluorescent spots along DNA), and find that loop extrusion proceeds at 1.75{+/-}0.26 kb/s for S. cerevisiae condensin without dyes, while adding intercalators leads to a two-fold lower rate. Our findings establish that intercalators quantitatively modify loop extrusion parameters, and we offer practical recommendations for minimizing their impact.
papers.title: Intercalator effects on DNA loop extrusion by SMC proteins

papers.abstract: Transforming growth factor {beta}-activated kinase 1 (TAK1) is a serine/threonine kinase best known for its roles in immune and stress-response signaling, yet its physiological function in mature neurons remains poorly understood. Here we identify neuronal TAK1 as a regulator of excitatory synaptic integrity, hippocampal plasticity and memory. Conditional reduction of TAK1 in forebrain excitatory neurons impaired short- and long-term memory and was accompanied by attenuated long-term potentiation in the hippocampus. At the cellular level, TAK1 deficiency reduced dendritic spine density and suppressed excitatory synaptic transmission, whereas genetic or pharmacological disruption of TAK1 kinase activity recapitulated these synaptic deficits. Mechanistically, TAK1 localized to the postsynaptic compartment of excitatory synapses and associated with PSD-95. Phosphoproteomic analysis of isolated postsynaptic density fractions revealed coordinated changes in synaptic phosphorylation following TAK1 reduction, including decreased phosphorylation of the NMDA receptor subunit GluN2B at serine 920. Analyses of phosphodeficient and phosphomimetic GluN2B mutants supported a role for S920 phosphorylation downstream of TAK1 in maintaining dendritic spine density, excitatory synaptic transmission and spontaneous synaptic calcium activity. Notably, synaptic TAK1 level was reduced in the aged hippocampus. Re-expressing neuronal TAK1 in aged mice increased dendritic spine density, enhanced hippocampal synaptic plasticity, and improved memory performance. Together, these findings define a postsynaptic TAK1-GluN2B signaling axis that supports excitatory synaptic function and suggest that reduced synaptic TAK1 signaling may contribute to hippocampal vulnerability during aging.
papers.title: Postsynaptic TAK1-GluN2B axis supports hippocampal synaptic integrity and cognitive function during aging

papers.abstract: Bacterial specialized metabolites are bioactive compounds that have been mined extensively as antibacterials, antifungals, and other drugs. They are widely used as experimental probes of complex biological systems. Since their discovery, their functional characteristics have typically been investigated as single, soluble compounds. The discoveries in this work expand this model. First, we report the co-packaging in extracellular vesicles (EVs) of two specialized metabolite complexes, candicidin and antimycin A, the products of a supercluster of biosynthetic genes, by a Streptomyces soil isolate. Secondly, we report that the products of this supercluster have synergistic antimicrobial activity against fungal biofilms, whereas biofilms are tolerant to the individual compounds. Finally, we show that co-packaging these compounds in EVs ensures simultaneous delivery with enhanced potency. This research advances understanding of the elegant complexity that shapes the evolution and function of bacterial specialized metabolites. In particular, the enhanced antibiofilm activity of co-packaged metabolites compared to individual soluble compounds is notable given the relevance of biofilms to microbial ecology and to pathogenesis. Our work supports the evolution of coordinated activity of specialized metabolites to counter conditional environmental challenges, and highlights co-packaging in EVs as one mechanism for secretion and co-delivery of combinations of bioactive molecules.
papers.title: Extracellular vesicle packaging of a supercluster-encoded antimicrobial combination with enhanced potency against fungal biofilms

papers.abstract: The hippocampal CA3 region supports coordinated network activity and memory processes, but how molecularly distinct CA3 neuronal populations contribute to recurrent circuit function remains poorly understood. Here we identify St18 as a molecular marker of a distinct population of deep-layer, burst-firing CA3 pyramidal neurons and generate an St18-Cre mouse line for their selective genetic targeting. In contrast to canonical CA3 pyramidal neurons, St18 neurons preferentially innervate CA3 bilaterally, with only sparse projections to CA1. Moreover, St18 neurons are highly active during endogenous CA3 sharp-wave ripples, and their optogenetic activation evokes local ripple-like activity in CA3 but not in CA1. Furthermore, chemogenetic suppression markedly reduces CA3 ripple occurrence without significantly affecting CA1 ripple occurrence and selectively impairs spatial working memory performance. Together, these findings reveal the functional significance of a molecularly defined CA3 recurrent circuit, linking neuronal heterogeneity to hippocampal network dynamics and spatial working memory.
papers.title: A molecularly defined recurrent CA3 circuit regulates network dynamics and spatial working memory

papers.abstract: The gut microbiome's functional architecture can be conceptualized as a network of metabolic niches, yet clinical approaches to fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) do not leverage niche-level information to guide engraftment. Here, we present a culturomics-based framework that profiles the metabolic niche landscape of individual microbiomes to enable targeted, antibiotic-independent FMT. Using a panel of 60 diverse media conditions, we show that gut communities from genetically identical mice harboring distinct microbiomes exhibit reproducible, vendor-specific niche-occupancy profiles, with each condition selecting for compositionally distinct niche-associated communities (NACs). We demonstrate that antibiotic pretreatment prior to FMT compromises community resilience, yielding communities that lose donor taxa more rapidly and recover less taxonomic diversity after secondary perturbation compared to untreated recipients. By comparing donor and recipient niche profiles, we identify vacant metabolic niches in recipient microbiomes and show that NACs targeting these vacancies achieve stable engraftment persisting for over 72 days without antibiotic pretreatment, whereas NACs targeting occupied niches fail to colonize. Furthermore, complex NACs not only fill vacant niches but reshape the surrounding native community, while simpler NACs engraft with minimal collateral impact. This culturomics-guided framework provides a scalable, mechanistic approach for rational donor-recipient matching that could advance personalized microbiome-based therapies.
papers.title: Culturomics-Guided Precision FMT Enables Stable Antibiotic-Independent Engraftment via Metabolic Niche Targeting

papers.abstract: The pathogenesis of HIV-1-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) is partly driven by microglial dysregulation. Indeed, HIV-1-induced microglial dyshomeostasis is characterized by a sustained pro-inflammatory state and exacerbated microglia proliferation. Herein, in vitro studies were conducted in primary microglia to elucidate the transcriptomic alterations underlying EcoHIV induced microglia hyperproliferation. Consistent with, and expanding upon, prior studies, treatment with EcoHIV exacerbated microglia proliferation evidenced by the upregulation of Pcna and Mki67. With regards to microglial receptors and adapter proteins, the transcriptomic expression of Trem2 and Dap12 was suppressed and increased, respectively, in microglia treated with EcoHIV. Crucially, dysregulation of the Trem2/Dap12 signaling complex explained 51.4% of the variance in microglial proliferation in EcoHIV treated microglia. A preliminary investigation of the Trem2-mediated microglial survival and immunoregulation pathway affords additional support for a unique EcoHIV-induced transcriptomic profile. Specifically, independent of biological sex, EcoHIV treatment upregulated Syk and downregulated Ctnnb1 mRNA expression. Notably, biological sex regulates precisely how EcoHIV treated microglia respond to the suppression of Trem2 and compensatory hyperproliferative state. Collectively, primary microglia treated with EcoHIV exhibit a highly specialized and sex-dependent transcriptional state. Enhancing our understanding of how HIV-1 alters microglial homeostasis is crucial for the identification of novel therapeutic targets for HAND.
papers.title: EcoHIV Treated Primary Microglia Exhibit a Highly Specialized and Sex-Dependent Transcriptional State

papers.abstract: Inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) can alter protein function through noncovalent binding, yet its partners among human membrane associated proteins remain poorly characterized. PolyP is recognized through two modes: a structure-based mode driven by charge complementarity with sites assembled by protein folding, and a more recently defined sequence-based mode at histidine and lysine rich tracts. The sequence determinant is well defined and directly searchable; the structure-based mode has few characterized examples and no systematic search method, because its residues leave no contiguous sequence signature. Broad experimental binding screens are especially demanding for integral membrane proteins, which require specialized conditions. We therefore developed a computational workflow that searches predicted structures for surfaces able to accommodate a phosphate chain. We designed custom scores that integrate surface electrostatics, docking results and structural confidence to prioritize candidates. From 19,481 completed docking searches on 5,648 AlphaFold models representing 2,925 UniProt protein entries, we nominated 82 entries as candidates for noncovalent polyP binding. Predicted polyP contacts in 18 candidate entries overlapped experimentally characterized functional residues, linking the predicted interfaces to established sites of ligand recognition, regulation and membrane attachment. The workflow ranks computational results rather than measuring binding, providing specific targets for experimental investigation.
papers.title: A structural screen for candidate polyphosphate binding surfaces in human membrane associated proteins

papers.abstract: Neuropeptides form modulatory communication channels that tune neuronal circuits and their functions, often through selective targeting of distinct cell populations. Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) is an important neuropeptidergic regulator of fear and stress. However, its receptors are surprisingly ubiquitous across most brain areas and cell types, making the physiological roles and functional mechanisms difficult to predict. Here, we investigate the cell type-specific effects of PACAP in the temporal association cortex (TeA), a brain region implicated in fear learning and memory. Adcyap1r1, encoding the PACAP receptor PAC1, was broadly expressed across the majority of neuronal and non-neuronal cells. Yet, PACAP engaged highly diverse molecular pathways across functionally distinct cell types that were differentially recruited during auditory fear learning and retrieval, providing a framework for how broad receptor expression can yield specific network modulation. Our data underscore the importance of dissecting cellularly resolved peptidergic signaling to understand functional mechanisms of neuropeptides.
papers.title: PACAP engages distinct signaling programs across cortical neuronal and non-neuronal cell types

papers.abstract: Giardia lamblia (syn. G. duodenalis, G. intestinalis) is a flagellated intestinal protozoan and a common cause of waterborne diarrhoeal disease. Its environmentally resistant cysts can persist in untreated groundwater, yet boreholes in Nigeria are widely assumed to be safe and are rarely screened for protozoan parasites. We examined borehole water from ten quarters of Gombe metropolis (Malam Inna, Tudun Wada, Pantami, Orji, Tumfure, Bolari, Jekadafari, Nassarawo, Kumbiya Kumbiya and Kagarawal) in a cross-sectional study with two sampling rounds two weeks apart. One 15 L sample was collected per site per round (20 samples in total), concentrated by sedimentation and centrifugation, and examined as unstained normal-saline wet mounts by light microscopy. Samples were scored positive when at least one cyst with morphology consistent with Giardia was seen. Two of 10 samples (20%) were positive in each round; overall, 4 of 20 samples (20%; 95% Wilson CI 8-42%) were positive. Three of ten sites were positive at least once: Jekadafari in both rounds, indicating repeated detection, and Tumfure and Pantami in one round each. Positivity did not differ between rounds (Fisher's exact test, p = 1.000). Because identification relied on morphology alone, without staining, immunofluorescence, PCR or viability testing, and because pH, turbidity and temperature were not measured on site, these results are presumptive detections from a small, non-random sample of boreholes. They nevertheless indicate that the underground origin of borehole water does not by itself guarantee freedom from parasitic contamination. We recommend routine parasitological monitoring, wellhead protection and household water treatment, and molecular confirmation (PCR and genotyping) in follow-up work.
papers.title: Presumptive detection of Giardia lamblia cysts in borehole water in Gombe metropolis, north-eastern Nigeria: a two-round cross-sectional study with implications for water safety

papers.abstract: Microbial decomposition of complex organic matter is a major control on the global carbon cycle, and its efficiency hinges on how microbes acquire resources. Decomposition requires costly extracellular enzymes to break down complex polymers, whereas the resulting soluble products are captured far more cheaply through membrane transporters. How microbes balance investment between these two processes is a fundamental axis of microbial life history, yet it has remained difficult to quantify across their vast diversity. Using genomic repertoires for carbohydrate depolymerisation and uptake, we developed a simple ratio distinguishing depolymerisation-optimised from uptake-optimised strategies, and applied it to more than 249,000 environmental and host-associated bacterial genomes. These strategies were strongly phylogenetically structured and differed by habitat, with uptake-optimised bacteria unexpectedly more prevalent in diffusion-limited soils than in aquatic environments. In an 18-month field-scale plant litter decomposition experiment, uptake-optimised bacteria dominated during early decomposition, when fungi were more abundant and strongly expressed hydrolytic enzymes, shifting towards depolymerisation-optimised bacteria at later stages. A simple genomic ratio therefore captures ecologically meaningful resource-acquisition strategies that vary with phylogeny, habitat and successional stage. The balance of these strategies could shape community-level extracellular enzyme investment, with consequences for decomposition and carbon cycling.
papers.title: A life-history axis of resource acquisition in bacteria: depolymerisation versus uptake

papers.abstract: The inhalation of Aspergillus fumigatus spores into the human pulmonary tract places conidia in direct contact with host immune cells which deploy a coordinated killing mechanism aimed at conidia clearance and preventing invasive infection. The fungus also employs cellular processes that aid its survival during these host mediated stresses, which allows the conidia to sustain growth while resisting attacks by the host immune cells. Ribosomal biogenesis plays a vital role in growth, survival, and stress adaptation in eukaryotic cells. In filamentous fungal pathogens, this process supports the transition of inhaled spores into invasive hyphae and is therefore an important aspect of fungal pathogenicity. It is, however, unclear whether ribosomal biogenesis factors contribute to stress survival beyond their canonical ribosomal roles and provision of support for vegetative growth. In this study, we investigated the role of A. fumigatus ribosomal biogenesis factor BFR2 in contribution to fungal stress survival and resistance to neutrophil killing.
